Three quadrature schemes measured against scipy on `_R2deriv_gl`, R=1, all on a
clean worktree with `inspect.getfile` printed:

    z/R      baseline    transformed_quad   narrow+cluster   dyadic graded
    0        3.67e+03    4.78e+11           nan              2.56e+09
    1e-06    3.67e+03    3.08e+01           1.90e+04         8.73e-07
    1e-04    1.15e+03    1.73e-05           6.23e-02         2.00e-10
    1e-03    8.38e-01    1.21e-11           1.70e-12         8.07e-13

    >=3e-02  ~1e-14      ~1e-14             ~1e-14           ~1e-14

Two negative results worth keeping, since both looked obviously right beforehand:
  - ONE narrow panel of width ~c|z| straddling a=R is WORSE than plain clustering
    (6.2e-02 vs 1.7e-05 at z=1e-4). Inside that panel the integrand still has
    endpoint structure at a=R, which equal-spaced GL handles badly.
  - Adding clustering INSIDE the narrow panel changed nothing at z<=1e-4 --
    bit-identical output, which is the tell that the term I was tuning was not the
    dominant one. It isn't: the residual comes from the OUTER panels, whose extreme
    Legendre node sits ~1.2e-4*R from the peak no matter what happens inside.

Dyadic grading (breakpoints R -/+ R*2^-k, k=1..K, K=24, n=20 per panel) fixes that
directly: threshold moves 3e-3 -> below 1e-6, >1000x, and 1e-6 itself is limited by
K (innermost width R*2^-24 ~ 6e-8), so deeper K buys more.

Cost as prototyped is ~5x the evaluations (2*(K+1)*n = 1000 vs 200) because I wrote
it as 50 separate `fixed_quad` calls. For the real thing, build the panel edges as
ARRAYS and issue ONE `fixed_quad` -- it already broadcasts over the trailing node
axis, so a (npanels,) pair of limits returns (npanels,) to sum. One call, static
panel count, traceable.

Caveat to carry into the PR: grading makes z=0 EXACTLY worse (3.67e+03 -> 2.56e+09)
because it marches panels into a genuine singularity. Both numbers are meaningless
-- the z=0 integral diverges -- and the ledger entry stays either way, but it should
be stated rather than discovered. The analytic z=0 limit (piece 1 of task #202)
supersedes whatever the sampler does there.

So: piece 2 of #202 is SOLVED in design and measured; piece 1 (analytic in-plane
limit) is still the thing that actually burns the ledger entries.

    R      z       R2deriv(scipy)   Rforce/R - z2deriv    |diff|
    0.50   0       -2.57883706e+00  -2.57883706e+00       2.59e-10

    z/R      R2deriv    z2deriv    Rforce     zforce
    0        2.56e+09   8.16e+09   6.47e-09   0.00e+00

It transfers, and does MORE than expected: **Rforce is now right at z=0 too**
(8.28e-06 -> 6.47e-09). Its a-integral converges at z=0; only the second

COST -- and this is why the implementation shape matters:

                            eager      jit-compile   jit-run
    baseline (n=100 x2)     644 ms     0.61 s        0.134 ms
    graded, 50 separate     1778 ms    9.62 s        0.529 ms
    graded, VECTORIZED      1131 ms    0.57 s        0.211 ms

Written as a loop of 50 `fixed_quad` calls the jit graph blows up 16x in compile
time -- unacceptable, and the same failure mode as the Staeckel bisection unroll.
Built as ONE batched `fixed_quad` over a leading panel axis (2K+2 = 50 panels,
n=20), compile is 0.57 s, marginally FASTER than baseline, for 1000 nodes vs 200.
Net ~1.7x runtime for >1000x accuracy in the small-|z| band. Accuracy is identical
between the two shapes, so this is pure implementation win.

NEGATIVE RESULT: clamping the grading depth to the peak width (stop at ~4|z|,
floor 1e-8 R), which I tried in order to avoid the z=0 regression, is WORSE
everywhere -- 1e-2 goes 5.1e-15 -> 2.0e-10, 1e-4 goes 2.0e-10 -> 2.0e-08 -- because
it replaces the graded core of the peak with one wide panel. And it does not fix
z=0 anyway. Unclamped grading is the design.

Patch saved: logs/vacation_2026-07/anyaxi_graded_quad.patch (95 lines, applies to
fa80b2f0). Not opened as a PR yet: it makes z=0 R2deriv/z2deriv numerically worse

### 2026-08-05 (cont) — piece 1: the z=0 limit is recoverable from the backend side

With grading making small-z evaluations trustworthy (~1e-12 at z=1e-3), Richardson
extrapolation in |z| recovers the z=0 value. f(z) = f0 + c|z| + d z^2 near 0 (the
razor-thin |z| kink), so 2f(h)-f(2h) kills the linear term and
(8f(h)-6f(2h)+f(4h))/3 kills the quadratic too:

    R     numpy(z=0)          extrapolated       relerr
    0.50  -2.5788370621e+00   -2.5788371708e+00  4.2e-08
    1.00  -1.6442185213e+00   -1.6442185814e+00  3.7e-08
    2.00  -3.3410340515e-01   -3.3410340812e-01  8.9e-09

THIRD independent confirmation that numpy's z=0 value is the true limit -- after
the Poisson identity (2e-12) and the test's own finite difference. Three unrelated
routes agreeing settles it; the IntegrationWarning is about the integral as
WRITTEN, not about the number.

1e-8 is ~1000x tighter than the FD reference the failing test compares against, so
this accuracy is sufficient to burn the entries.

Implementation options for piece 1, cost measured against the graded baseline
(1 quadrature, jit-run 0.211 ms):
  - Richardson: works TODAY, but needs 3 extra quadratures, and since |z|==0
    cannot be branched on under trace it has to be an xp.where blend, so ~4x on
    every call. Acceptable for jit (0.8 ms) but poor for the eager gradient path.
  - Hadamard finite part: subtract the singular part -- whose coefficient is
    analytically KNOWN, Sigma(R)*R/2 at z=0, verified to 6 digits earlier -- and
    add back its closed-form finite part. ONE quadrature, uniform in z, no branch.
    This is the right answer and what I will implement.

Deliberately NOT rushing the finite-part algebra at the end of a long window; the
premise is now proven and the design is unambiguous, so it can be written
carefully next wake rather than half-done now.

### 2026-08-06 — CORRECTION: the divergence coefficient is Sigma(R)/2, not Sigma(R)*R/2

I recorded the z=0 singular coefficient as `C = Sigma(R)*R/2`, verified "to 6
digits". It was verified at ONE radius, R=1, where Sigma(R)/2 and Sigma(R)*R/2 are
numerically identical. They are not the same function. Measured C = f*(a-R)^2 at
five radii:

    R      measured C          Sigma(R)/2      Sigma(R)*R/2
    0.25   3.5427314326e-01    3.542749e-01    8.856873e-02
    0.50   1.6734695071e-01    1.673476e-01    8.367381e-02
    1.00   3.7340170595e-02    3.734030e-02    3.734030e-02
    2.00   1.8590580901e-03    1.859064e-03    3.718128e-03
    3.00   9.2557059944e-05    9.255735e-05    2.776721e-04

**C = Sigma(R)/2**, R-independent prefactor. The algebra agrees: with
P(a) = (a^2-3R^2) a Sigma(a) / (2 R^2 (a+R)), at a=R this is
(-2R^2)(R)(Sigma)/(2R^2 * 2R) = -Sigma(R)/2, and the E-term contributes
-P(R)/t^2 = +Sigma(R)/(2 t^2).

Textbook single-point coincidence, and I had flagged R=1 as my only check without
acting on it. Corrected in task #202 too.

Structure for the finite-part implementation, now that the constant is right:

    I(a) = A(a) - P(a) E(m)/t^2,     t = a-R
    A(a) = a Sigma(a) K(m) / (2 R^2 (a+R))        <- log-singular, INTEGRABLE
    P(a) = (a^2-3R^2) a Sigma(a) / (2 R^2 (a+R))  <- smooth

E(m) = 1 + O(t^2 ln|t|) near m=1, so the t^2-ln correction does not touch either
the leading coefficient or the first derivative: f(a) = -P(a)E(m) has f(R) =
-P(R) = Sigma(R)/2 and f'(R) = -P'(R). Hadamard over a window [R-d, R+d]:

    Pf int f/t^2 = int [f - f(R) - f'(R) t]/t^2 dt  -  2 f(R)/d

with the bracket regular (-> f''/2) and the odd term vanishing. One quadrature,
uniform in z, no branch -- but it introduces the window d as a tuning parameter
and needs f'(R) (analytic or AD).

DECISION for the PR: implement Hadamard, keep Richardson (verified 1e-8) as the
cross-check in the test rather than in the code. Two independent routes to the
same number is exactly the kind of gate this needs, given that the z=0 value comes
from an integral scipy itself calls divergent.

the routes share no quadrature.

### 2026-08-06 — BLOCKING constraint found: grading breaks a finite difference in R

Checked (rather than assumed) how the failing test actually compares. `tp` is ONE
instance, so `tp.Rforce` and `evaluateR2derivs(tp, ...)` are both on the backend --
the test is self-consistent, no numpy reference. Assert is
`(tR2deriv-mRforcederivR)^2 / tR2deriv^2 < 10^-4.5`, i.e. |rel diff| < 5.62e-3, and
Rs = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]. So R=0.25 is never sampled and the numpy z=0 bug (#203,
1.4e-7 at R=0.5) is far inside tolerance -- it does NOT explain the ledger entry.
Good: two separate problems, correctly separated.

Then the important negative result. The test's FD is
(Rforce(R) - Rforce(R+dr))/dr with dr = 1e-8. With grading applied to Rforce:

    R      z=0:  FD             analytic R2deriv    rel diff
    0.50         -2.1085e+00    -2.5788e+00         1.82e-01   FAIL
    1.00         -4.8111e+00    -1.6442e+00         1.93e+00   FAIL
    2.00         -3.7165e-01    -3.3410e-01         1.12e-01   FAIL

even though graded `Rforce` itself is accurate to 6.5e-09 at z=0. At z=0.125/0.25
the FD is FINE (1e-8..8e-6, passes), so this is specific to z=0.

CAUSE: the panel edges are R*frac, so shifting R by dr moves every edge. The
innermost panel is R*2^-24 ~ 6e-8 -- COMPARABLE TO dr=1e-8. The FD step lands
inside the finest panel, where the quadrature error is most sensitive, so the error
does not cancel between the two evaluations. At z>=0.125 the integrand is smooth on
the panel scale and the error varies smoothly in R, so it cancels as usual.

**The binding constraint is SMOOTHNESS OF THE QUADRATURE ERROR IN R, not raw
accuracy.** I had been optimising raw accuracy -- which is why the clamped variant
looked like a pure loss earlier (2e-10 vs 5e-15) when it may in fact be the right
trade. 2e-10 is 7 orders inside the 5.6e-3 the test needs; smoothness is not.

Tried re-testing the clamp against the right metric and got a broken run: I dropped
the `w <= 0.5R` cap, so at z=0.25, R=0.5 the width 4|z|=1.0 exceeds R, edges go
negative and R2deriv returns -5.38 instead of -7.5e-3. My experiment's bug, not a
property of the method -- and z=0 fails regardless, since w=4|z| is 0 there and the
clamp does nothing.

STATE: the piece-2 patch as saved is NOT landable. Grading must additionally bound
the innermost panel width well above any plausible caller FD step (>> 1e-8 R), and
z=0 must come from the Hadamard formula rather than from sampling. Next step is to
measure FD smoothness as a function of grading depth K -- pick the largest K whose
innermost panel still leaves an FD in R clean -- instead of maximising accuracy.
That is a measurement I have not done yet, so no number is being claimed.

### 2026-08-06 (cont) — the FD conflict is z=0 ONLY; design closes

Swept grading depth K at z=0 (R=1), FD of Rforce with dr=1e-8 vs the true R2deriv:

    K   innermost R*2^-K   FDrel(z=0)   R2deriv z=1e-4   z=1e-3
    0        1.00e+00       4.09e-04 ok    1.52e+02       1.23e+02
    8        3.91e-03       3.03e-04 ok    5.48e+00       1.17e-09
    12       2.44e-04       9.29e-03 BAD   1.08e-10       8.65e-13
    16       1.53e-05       3.39e-02 BAD   2.10e-10       8.04e-13
    20       9.54e-07       8.27e-01 BAD   2.00e-10       8.02e-13
    24       5.96e-08       1.93e+00 BAD   2.00e-10       8.02e-13

No K satisfies both, and note K=12 already breaks the FD with an innermost panel
24000x LARGER than dr -- so my "panel narrower than the FD step" explanation was
wrong. Whatever the mechanism, at z=0 the quadrature error stops varying smoothly
in R as soon as panels march into the singularity.

But the missing measurement changes the conclusion. At NONZERO z, K=24 grading
keeps the FD clean everywhere:

    z        FD               R2deriv          rel diff
    1e-04    -1.64381940e+00  -1.64379628e+00  1.41e-05  PASS
    1e-03    -1.64000066e+00  -1.63999839e+00  1.38e-06  PASS
    1e-02    -1.60228138e+00  -1.60228115e+00  1.47e-07  PASS
    1.25e-01 -1.16521871e+00  -1.16521864e+00  5.44e-08  PASS
    2.5e-01  -7.89331250e-01  -7.89331254e-01  6.15e-09  PASS

So there is NO general tension -- I was one measurement away from wrongly
concluding the approach was unlandable. The conflict is confined to z=0, which is
exactly the point where the integral diverges and the value must come from Hadamard
rather than from sampling anyway.

DESIGN (closes):
  - z > 0: grade to depth ~log2(R/|z|). R2deriv/z2deriv gain up to 1e3x accuracy
    and the FD stays clean.
  - z = 0: no grading (Rforce is fine ungraded -- FD 4.09e-04, passes), and
    R2deriv/z2deriv come from the Hadamard finite part.
Implementable branch-free: the innermost panel distance is
`xp.where(z == 0, 0.5*R, c*|z|)` -- a traced select on a SCALAR, so it is one
quadrature either way, no cost, no data-dependent control flow.

Note for the PR: grading makes Rforce more accurate (6.5e-9 vs 8.3e-6) while
making a FINITE DIFFERENCE of it worse at z=0. For a differentiable library the AD
derivative is what matters and AD differentiates the quadrature exactly, so this is
defensible -- but it must be stated explicitly in the PR, not discovered by a
reviewer.

### 2026-08-06 (cont) — piece 2 IMPLEMENTED and landable (patch updated)

Built the z-aware graded split. dmin bounds how close panels may approach a=R:
`xp.where(|z| > 0, min(4|z|, R/2), R/2)` -- a traced select on a SCALAR, so it is
one quadrature either way, no branch, no extra cost. At z=0 that collapses the
graded panels and leaves the coarse split; for z>0 it grades to ~4|z|.

Got the panel ordering wrong first (reversed the left edges, which were already
ascending, and failed to reverse the right ones) -- caught immediately because
accuracy was worse than baseline EVERYWHERE, which is not what a tuning error

`sigmar` integrates from r to infinity via `fixed_quad_semiinfinite`, so as the
lower limit shrinks the mapped integrand's dynamic range grows and a fixed-order
rule stops resolving it -- exactly the same class as the AnyAxisym a=R work, and
the same reason numpy is immune (scipy's quad is adaptive).

Nice detail the other way: at r=5.0 the BACKEND is more accurate than numpy
(1.4e-15 vs 4.6e-11 against the analytic). scipy is not uniformly better; it is
better where adaptivity matters and worse in the tail.

just a data-guard") was right about the DISPATCH but wrong to imply the backend
quadrature is uniformly fine -- that conclusion rested on the shadow scan. It is
fine for r >~ 0.05 and fails below. test_jeans sweeps rs = linspace(0.001, 5.0, 101),
so it hits the bad region on its first point.

So the jeans PR is: dispatch fix (3 lines) + r-coercion (1 line, already done and
verified: it clears the torch TypeError) + EITHER a small-r quadrature improvement
OR ledgering the 5. Given #202 established a graded/peak-resolving technique that
works, the quadrature route is plausible -- but it is a separate measured piece of
work, not a tweak.

### 2026-08-06 — jeans small-r: root-caused and a measured fix (piece c of #190)

Read `fixed_quad_semiinfinite`. The 'recip' map is

    s = a - 1 + 1/u**2 ,  u in (0,1] ,  ds = 2/u**3 du

Note the HARDCODED 1: the map's transition scale is fixed at unity no matter how
small the lower limit `a` is. Near u=1, ds/du ~ 2, so node spacing in s near the
lower limit is O(1/n^2) ABSOLUTE -- it cannot resolve integrand structure on scale
`a` once a << 1. That is exactly the observed divergence below r ~ 0.05.

A scale-invariant map fixes it:  s = a/u**2 , ds = 2a/u**3 du
(u=1 -> s=a, u->0 -> s->inf; node distribution in s now scales WITH a).

Measured, |sigmar - analytic|, torch, provenance-checked heredoc:

    r        current map    scaled n=50   scaled n=100   scaled n=200
    0.0010     1.099e-02     1.234e-06      8.824e-12      1.075e-11
    0.0025     9.075e-04     8.021e-08      2.841e-12      1.937e-12
    0.0100     8.881e-07     2.627e-10      1.483e-13      1.450e-13
    1.0000     2.609e-15     2.609e-15      3.886e-16      6.717e-15

The map alone buys ~4 orders at r=0.001 but still misses the 1e-10 tolerance.
**Scaled map + n=100 gives 8.8e-12 -- inside tolerance and equal to numpy's own
1.075e-11.** Past n=100 it saturates at ~1.07e-11, which is the analytic-formula
float64 floor, not quadrature error: the backend has reached numpy's accuracy, so
there is nothing left to win.

CAVEAT for the PR: `fixed_quad_semiinfinite` is shared (AnyAxisym tail, sphericaldf,
...). Do NOT silently change the default map. Add `kind='recip_scaled'` (or a
`scale=` argument) and opt jeans in, then measure the other callers are untouched.
n=50 -> 100 applies to the jeans call only.

That completes the shape of #190: dispatch fix (3 lines) + r-coercion (1 line) +
scaled-map opt-in with n=100. All three measured; none of them a tolerance change.

Three source changes, all measured:

1. **`scale=` on `fixed_quad_semiinfinite`** (the general fix). The map had a

test_jeans: jax 1P/4F -> 5P, torch same, numpy 5P throughout.

IEEE754; compared `.view(int64)` against a reimplementation of the pre-change
formula over 18 cases -> 18/18 identical. First attempt reported 13 diffs at

### 2026-08-06 — #204 root-caused: same fixed-unit-scale bug, one layer up

The `sigmalos` residual is `Potential.surfdens()`'s `z is None` branch:

whose infinite branch is two bare `fixed_quad_semiinfinite` calls with **no

fixed unit-scale map cannot resolve. Same root cause as #190, one layer up.

    0.100    1.312e-08    1.312e-08
    1.000    2.483e-08    2.483e-08

ours**: it is identical for n=50 and n=100, and `integrate.quad`'s default
`epsabs` is 1.49e-8. The scaled backend is more accurate than the numpy
reference it is measured against -- so the eventual test must use the closed
form, exactly as the jeans test does.

### 2026-08-07 — jeans jit: the `--jit` suite run was NOT evidence

Ran the jeans suites under `--backend jax --jit`: 90 passed, 1 skipped. Then
checked what that actually proved, and the answer was: almost nothing.

`jeans.sigmar` carries **no `@backend_input` decorator**, so it is not a trace
boundary, and the harness only traces at boundaries. The calls that traced were
the inner potential force evaluators; the quadrature wrapped around them ran
eagerly. A green `--jit` run on a non-boundary function is not a jit claim.
This is the pass-counts-vs-traced-boundaries distinction, hit from a new angle:
previously the failure mode was counting passes instead of traced calls, here
it was a whole function that is *never a trace site at all*.

Traced it explicitly instead. It works: jit reproduces eager to 1e-13 for r from
1e-3 to 5, and `jit(grad)` reproduces eager `grad`. Committed as tests
(`f5ed74f4`) using the existing shared
`backend_jit_helpers.assert_jit_matches_eager` -- which also asserts the jaxpr
consumes its argument, so a trace that constant-folded `r` could not pass
vacuously. That matters for this PR specifically because `scale=r` puts `r`
inside the quadrature MAP, not just the integration limit.

**A wrong reading I nearly recorded as a bug.** The first probe printed
`sigmar = 38599.011585` identically at r=1e-3, 0.1 and 1.0 for `beta=0.5`. That
is not a defect: I had paired a constant beta with the *other* case's rising
`dens ~ x**0.1`, which makes the Jeans integrand `~x**0.1` and the integral
divergent, so fixed-order GL returns a large number dominated by the far field
and the lower limit barely matters. **Identical values across three decades of
the lower limit is the tell for a divergent integral**, not for a broken code
path -- a convergent `int_r^inf` must move when r moves by 1000x. Noted in the
test so it is not re-derived.

Also re-surveyed #188 and found its premise stale: `assert_jit_matches_eager`
already exists with 8 adopters, and there are 2 `_jit` test files, not ~10. Of
the 29 files that use `jax.jit` without it, most use jit as a TRACEABILITY probe
(is the traced value finite / does this path trace at all), which is a different
assertion -- converting those would weaken them. Only 3 genuine sites remain,
and two of the candidate files are owned by open PRs, so it is deferred.

### 2026-08-07 — #204: a design that survives all four potentials

The refutation said what a fix must do: resolve structure at BOTH the R scale
and the profile's own scale, without knowing the latter. A log substitution does
exactly that -- `int_0^inf f(z) dz = int f(e^t) e^t dt` turns structure at ANY
scale `s` into O(1) width at `t = ln s`, so one GL rule covers every decade.

Measured over 4 potentials x 5 radii (worst-case relative error vs a tight
scipy reference):

    variant                 worst      integrand evals
    baseline (n=50)         7.732e-03   50
    fixed  T=40, n=300      converged   300
    R-centred W=30, n=200   9.267e-08   200
    R-centred W=25, n=150   4.763e-07   150
    R-centred W=20, n=100   8.151e-06   100

Centring the window on ln(R) is clearly more node-efficient -- W=30/n=200 beats
the fixed T=35/n=200 by 15x.

**But I am recommending the FIXED window anyway.** Centring puts R in the
integration BOUNDS, so `dSigma/dR` picks up Leibniz boundary terms
`f(z_hi) dz_hi/dR` that the true integral has no trace of. They are ~1e-8 here,
which is invisible in a value test and would sail through the obvious
gradient-vs-FD check at loose tolerance -- and this is a differentiable-by-design
library, where a spurious gradient term is worse than a spurious value error.
The fixed window has no such term. If 300 nodes proves too expensive, the
centred variant has to be justified by checking its GRADIENT, not its value.

Not implemented: three branches are already in flight (#1258, #1259, jeans) and
this is a change to a shared helper on a path DF sampling uses, so it needs its
own gating and a wall-clock/compile measurement first. Full design + numbers are
in task #204.

Note the "converged" entry: fixed T=40/n=300 reproduces the BASELINE's residual
exactly for Plummer and MiyamotoNagai (1.336e-09, 2.350e-08, ...). That is not
the patch failing to apply -- both quadratures are converged and what is left is
the GOLD REFERENCE's own error, common to both columns. Checked against the
cusped rows, where the same patch moves 7.7e-3 to 3.3e-9.

### 2026-08-07 — ComplexDouble sub-bug: first hypothesis REFUTED

Chased the 7 `"gt_cpu" not implemented for 'ComplexDouble'` failures. Established:

* The failing assertion is `dfc(numpy.array([0.7,0,meanvt])) > dfc(...)` in
  `test_dehnendf_call_sanity` — so under the fix `dehnendf.__call__` **returns a
  complex TORCH tensor**, and the comparison is what raises.
* `diskdf._real` is `x if is_backend_array(x) else numpy.real(x)`, commented
  "backend arrays are already real". A complex Tensor therefore passes through
  UNSTRIPPED. That comment's assumption is what breaks.
* The design context is real and documented: line 28 keeps
  `numpylog = numpy.lib.scimath.log` deliberately (log(neg) -> log|neg| + i*pi),
  and the backend eval paths (lines 2030, 2483) avoid complex entirely by
  substituting a signed algebraic factor. So `_real`'s assumption is TRUE as long
  as the backend eval actually runs.

**My hypothesised mechanism was wrong and the probe caught it.** I assumed
`scimath.log(Tensor)` yields a complex Tensor. Measured:

    numpy.lib.scimath.log(torch.tensor([-0.5, 0.5]))
      -> numpy.ndarray complex128     (NOT a Tensor)
      -> is_backend_array = False     (so _real DOES strip it correctly)

So that route is innocent. The complex Tensor is produced somewhere further
along and still needs a live reproduction to pin down — most likely a numpy
complex array being coerced back to a Tensor downstream of `_real`, or a torch
op producing complex from a negative input.

Recording it half-solved rather than shipping the tidy-sounding scimath story:
the mechanism I can defend is "`_real` lets complex Tensors through"; the
mechanism I cannot yet defend is where the Tensor becomes complex. That second
half is the actual work item for #117's diskdf consumer migration.

### 2026-08-07 — ComplexDouble mechanism SOLVED (live repro)

Instrumented `diskdf._real` and `dehnendf.eval` under forced torch with the
surfaceSigmaProfile patch applied. Full chain, all measured:

    meanvT          -> Tensor float64            (fine)
    dfc(np.array([0.7,0,meanvT])) -> Tensor COMPLEX128
    _real saw       -> ('Tensor', 'complex128')  -> passed through unchanged
    eval saw        -> E=False L=False lsR=False lsR2=False, correct=False
                       => the NUMPY branch ran

So:

1. `eval` dispatches on `if (is_backend_array(E) or is_backend_array(L)) and not
   self._correct`. The caller passes a plain numpy array, so E and L are numpy
   and the **numpy** branch runs — correctly, by that predicate.
2. Inside that branch it calls `self.targetSurfacemass(xE, log=True)`, which goes
   through surfaceSigmaProfile. With the patch that now returns a **Tensor**.
3. `numpylog` (= `numpy.lib.scimath.log`) produces a numpy **complex** value, by
   design — that is what line 28 documents and what `_real` exists to unwrap.
4. numpy-complex + Tensor promotes to a **complex Tensor**.
5. `_real` is `x if is_backend_array(x) else numpy.real(x)` — the Tensor takes
   the pass-through arm, so the imaginary part survives.
6. The test does `dfc(a) > dfc(b)` -> "gt_cpu" not implemented for ComplexDouble.

**This is the general lesson, not a diskdf quirk:** the dispatch predicate asks
about SOME of its inputs (E, L) while a DIFFERENT input (logSigmaR, from the
migrated leaf) independently became a backend array. Migrating a leaf changes the
dtype of arguments flowing into branches that never consulted it. So "which
inputs does this branch predicate actually cover?" is a question every leaf
migration has to ask of its consumers.

Two candidate fixes for the follow-up, both needing measurement:
  a) make `_real` namespace-aware (take the real part of backend arrays too) --
     smallest, but leaves a numpy branch computing on Tensors;
  b) widen the dispatch to include logSigmaR/logsigmaR2 so the backend eval runs
     -- addresses the cause, and `_eval_backend` is already complex-free by
     construction (it substitutes the signed algebraic factor for scimath log).
(b) looks right; (a) alone would paper over it.

Patch preserved as `logs/vacation_2026-07/ssp_backend_input.patch` (117 lines) and
the jeansfix worktree restored clean so it matches #1260 exactly.

### 2026-08-07 — the same "predicate covers only some inputs" bug appears TWICE

Reviewing my own fix-(b) prototype while it ran, and found I had repeated the bug
I was fixing. `_eval_backend` opens with

    xp = get_namespace(E, L)

— the SAME partial coverage as the dispatch predicate I had just widened. So
routing numpy-E/L + Tensor-logSigmaR into `_eval_backend` resolves the namespace
from E and L alone.

Under the FORCED-backend suite this is masked: `get_namespace(numpy_scalar)`
returns the forced namespace (measured earlier — forced jax -> jax.numpy, forced
torch -> array_api_compat.torch), so `xp` is torch anyway and the running
measurement stays valid for the forced case. UNFORCED it would resolve to numpy
and mix all over again — a user passing numpy E/L with a Tensor logSigmaR.

So the complete fix needs BOTH:
  * dispatch:  is_backend_array(E|L|logSigmaR|logsigmaR2)
  * namespace: get_namespace(E, L, logSigmaR, logsigmaR2)

Letting the current run finish rather than restarting — it answers the main
question (does routing to `_eval_backend` clear the failures?) and 20 minutes to
re-measure a detail I already know the answer to is not worth it. The refinement
goes into the eventual PR.

**Worth naming as a pattern, not an incident.** In one function this codebase
asks "is this a backend array?" of a SUBSET of the values that flow into the
branch — twice, independently. The forced-backend suite hides the second one
because `get_namespace` falls through to context. So: when auditing a
dual-path function, check every place it interrogates its inputs, not just the
`if`. And remember a forced-backend green does not exercise the unforced mixed
case at all.

### 2026-08-07 — the proxy design I proposed last wake is WRONG (two hazards)

Last wake I concluded "the right shape is one namespace-matching wrapper applied
where `_surfaceSigmaProfile` is stored". Enumerated the actual uses before
building it, and that design is unsafe:

    20  .sigma / .surfacemass / .surfacemassDerivative / .sigma2Derivative   <- the numeric API
     1  .outputParams
     1  .formatStringParams
     1  .__class__                                                          <- HAZARD

**Hazard 1 — `__class__` builds a filename.** diskdf.py:3016:

    "dfcorrection_" + self._dftype.__name__ + "_"
        + self._surfaceSigmaProfile.__class__.__name__ + "_"
        + sspString % self._surfaceSigmaProfile.outputParams() + ...

A proxy reports the WRAPPER's class name, so the dfcorrection save file gets a
different name. Nothing raises — corrections are silently regenerated under a new
filename instead of being loaded. A cache that silently misses is worse than a
crash.

**Hazard 2 — the object ESCAPES.** It is passed on at 131, 3147, 3151
(`surfaceSigmaProfile=self._surfaceSigmaProfile` into other df constructors) and
at 2137/2149/2592/2604 (`hxparams=(self._surfaceSigmaProfile, ...)` into ARS
sampling helpers, e.g. `_ars_hx`). So consumers exist OUTSIDE diskdf's own
methods — which also means guarding only diskdf's call sites is incomplete, the
sampling helpers are a separate boundary. That is very likely the second residual
cluster (`test_shudf_sample_*`, 0-d tensor indexing).

**Revised plan for #117's second half:** explicit guarded accessors on diskdf for
the four numeric methods + replace the 22 direct call sites, rather than a proxy.
Uglier, but it cannot break `__class__` or pickling, and it makes each guarded
boundary greppable. The escape sites need separate handling and should be treated
as their own sub-task.

Before writing the atleast_1d fix, checked what the NUMPY path actually returns

    numpy 1-d in                    -> shapes [(1,), (1,), (1,)]

returns shape (1,), and every downstream consumer indexing `[0]` would then fail.

changed the design (the other: `_real`'s "backend arrays are already real").

entry points.

### 2026-08-07 — checked `_ssp` is a true no-op on the numpy path

Two of the four profile methods return a PLAIN PYTHON FLOAT for `log=True`
(`surfacemassDerivative` -> -1/params[0], `sigma2Derivative` -> -2/params[1] —
they are R-independent, which the surfacesigma test file already documents as
`_SSP_R_INDEP`). My `_ssp` accessor now routes those through `as_numpy`, so the
question is whether that changes their type or shape and breaks byte-identity.

    float     -> float     shape=()   identical=True
    float64   -> float64   shape=()   identical=True
    ndarray   -> ndarray   shape=(1,) identical=True

`as_numpy` is a pass-through for non-backend values — it returns the IDENTICAL
object, not a converted copy. So `_ssp` is a genuine no-op on the numpy path and
cannot perturb byte-identity. Checked before the numpy arm reports rather than
waiting to be surprised by it; if it had converted floats to 0-d arrays that
would have been a subtle, wide-blast-radius regression across every diskdf
numpy call.

### 2026-08-07 — #188 adopted (ed82126d), and my predicted risk was WRONG

Last entry I flagged that adopting `assert_jit_matches_eager` in
test_backend_disk.py's RazorThin jit test might trip the helper's
dependence assertion at the z=0 points, where zforce is zero by symmetry, and
said to measure rather than assume. Measured: **0 of 24 (3 methods x 8 points)
trip it.**

The reason is worth keeping. `zforce` at z=0 returns exactly 0.0 and still
reports `depends=True`, because the check is STRUCTURAL — does the jaxpr
consume its invars — not numerical. I had conflated "the output value is zero"
with "the output does not depend on the inputs". Those are different
properties, and only the second one is what the helper guards against.

Adopted with `ref=float(call(R0, z0))`, which keeps the plain-float eager call
as the reference while the jitted side gets traced arrays. That float-vs-array
cross was the original test's point; letting the helper compute its own
reference from the same traced args would have silently narrowed the test to
array-vs-array while looking like a pure refactor.

Verified the new assertion has teeth rather than being decorative: a
deliberately constant lambda is rejected with "jit trace ignores its
arguments". A check that cannot fail is not worth adding.

### 2026-08-07 — #143 re-scoped: it is NOT a guard-lift, it is a scipy migration

Picked up #143 ("lift evolveddiskdf transitional data-guard -> resolved
namespace") as unblocked local work, since its file is owned by neither open PR
and I had just gated it on both backends. Read all five guard sites before
touching anything, per the #117 lesson that this identical idiom stands in for
different things at different sites. They are not five instances of one thing:

* **evolveddiskdf.py:525** (grid velocity bounds) and **:2908** (`_buildvgrid`
  dispatch) are the two REAL transitional gates. Both deliberately gate on
  `is_backend_array(R)` rather than on a forced backend.
* **:785** (vertexdev arctan combiner), **:2861** and **:3536** (the two
  matrix-vector grid reductions) are **not islands at all**. They follow the
  data: numpy reduction for a numpy grid, backend for a backend grid, and each
  is correct either way. The dot-vs-matmul split in two of them is a
  byte-identity requirement (`numpy.dot` differs from `numpy.matmul` by ~ULP on
  non-contiguous slices, and `torch.dot` is 1-D only). Removing those would
  break byte-identity for zero gain.

The gate at :525 is load-bearing, and the code says why: the direct-integration
path is still **scipy.integrate.quad** at lines 3140, 3164, 3214 and 3239.
Flipping a numpy R to the backend under a forced backend would hand Tensors to
scipy quad — the exact failure mode that produced #117b's 47-failure leaf-only
arm. Same ordering constraint, second file.

**So #143 as written is mis-scoped.** It is not a guard removal; it is "migrate
evolveddiskdf's direct-integration path off scipy.integrate.quad", after which
the two gates fall out for free. That is a real piece of work, not a follow-up
tidy, and it is the honest prerequisite. Re-scoped the task rather than starting
a large migration mid-wait with two PRs already open.

No code changed. The deliverable here is the classification.

### 2026-08-07 — #1259 merge audit RE-RUN (pre-merge), verdict PASS

Re-ran the three criteria against the live diff (2 files, +109/-10) so the merge
is a formality once green, rather than auditing under time pressure.

**(a) if -> xp.where array-input class: PASS.** No new scalar `if` on coord
data. `_bk_split_quad` selects the R=0 and R=inf degenerate cases with
`xp.where`, and — the part that matters — it evaluates each dead branch at a
HARMLESS R (`xp.where(finite, R, ones_like(R))`, then `xp.where(positive, Rs,
ones_like(Rs))`) precisely so a NaN cannot leak back through a gradient. That is
[[xp-where-dead-branch-guards]] done correctly, not just formally.

**(b) duplication: PASS, and I checked rather than assumed.** galpy.backend.
quadrature already has `transformed_quad(..., interior_point=)` whose docstring
literally names "the disk `a = R` pattern", so this was a real candidate for
duplication. It is not one: `transformed_quad` splits into TWO panels and
clusters nodes WITHIN each via the `X = xi**k` boundary-layer remap, whereas
`_bk_split_quad` builds 2K+2 DYADIC panels whose widths halve toward a=R,
clamped at `dmin ~ 4|z|`. Different mechanism, and the dyadic one exists because
the within-panel clustering was not sufficient here.

**(c) helper placement: PASS for now.** The method is saturated with this
potential's physics — the a=R (m->1) singularity, the R=0 / R=inf limits, and
the rule that grading is switched OFF at z=0 because marching panels inward
makes a finite difference of the potential in R blow up. That does not belong in
a generic utility. The genuinely general sub-piece is the dyadic panel builder
(build graded panels around an interior point, issue them as ONE batched
fixed_quad — as separate calls the jit graph is ~16x more expensive to compile).
Standing follow-up unchanged: **hoist** that builder into
galpy.backend.quadrature when #202/#204 becomes its second consumer. Hoist, do
not copy.

Observation worth carrying: if dyadic grading is strictly better for the a=R
pattern that `transformed_quad`'s own docstring claims to serve, then
`transformed_quad` should eventually gain a graded mode so future callers do not
hand-roll one. Not a blocker for #1259.

        worst 1.3e-7  (though this one proves little: AnyAxisym's surfdens is
        the user-supplied ANALYTIC function, so no quadrature runs at all --
        the z-independence of the output gives that away)

Then the measurement that actually settles it, against a GOLD REFERENCE rather
than against numpy ([[match-numpy-quadrature-floor]]): MiyamotoNagai has an
analytic `_surfdens`, so compare BOTH quadrature paths to the truth.

    R=1e-3, z=1.5:  analytic 5.519639e-01
                    numpy Poisson  rel 6.0e-16   (adaptive quad, machine precision)
                    jax   Poisson  rel 1.0e-08   (fixed GL n=50)

    stress over 20 (R,z) combos incl. |z| up to 30: WORST 1.02e-06

1e-8 at R=1e-3 versus the 7.7e-3 in the task note. Three orders of magnitude.

**Cause: #161 already fixed it.** That task was "surfdens Poisson fallback:
range-aware quadrature for traced-green", and the code comment now reads
"Fixed-order GL over the whole [-z,z] needs an order that grows with the range
(n=100 is only 3.7e-4 at |z|=10). Splitting at z=0 and clustering nodes toward
the split ... does so RELATIVE to the range, so one node count holds at every
|z|." That is exactly the same defect class as the jeans bug in #1260 — a fixed
transition scale in a quadrature map — and it was fixed range-aware there first.

Task #204 closed as already-fixed. Reproducing before designing saved building a
fix for a bug that no longer exists; the "log substitution" I had designed for

    1e-02     0.988314174     0.988312497   1.70e-06   0.988313849  3.29e-07

    1e-04     0.999883260     0.997117426   2.77e-03   0.999883221  3.89e-08

### 2026-08-07 — #203 re-framed: a DISAGREEMENT, not an established AnyAxisym defect

Having just proved RazorThinExponentialDiskPotential unreliable off-plane
(#206), I went back to #203 — because #203's evidence used that SAME potential as
its gold reference. If the reference is suspect, so is the attribution.

Tried to arbitrate with the independent Hankel transform, extended to the second
derivative: R2deriv = -dF_R/dR ∝ ∫ k² Σ̃(k) J₁'(kR) dk, J₁'(x)=J₀(x)-J₁(x)/x.
Ratio R2deriv/Rforce at z=0 so normalisation cancels:

    R      Hankel        AnyAxisym    rel        RazorThinExp   rel
    0.05  -10.79938478  -10.79955065  1.54e-05  -10.79951507   1.21e-05
    0.30    0.67706634    0.67698254  1.24e-04    0.67698363   1.22e-04
    1.00    1.60562673    1.60540075  1.41e-04    1.60540079   1.41e-04
    2.00    1.10694199    1.10604644  8.09e-04    1.10604644   8.09e-04

**Inconclusive, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** Both galpy codes
agree with EACH OTHER and both drift from my Hankel by 1e-4..8e-4, with the gap
GROWING with R. That is the signature of MY integral being the weak one for the
second derivative — the k² weight decays more slowly and J₁' oscillates faster,
so panels between J₁ zeros converge poorly. The arbiter that settled #202 at
1e-7 for the force is only good to ~1e-4 for the curvature.

What the numbers DO show: the two galpy implementations differ from each other
by 3.3e-6 at R=0.05, 1.6e-6 at R=0.3, and are identical to ~1e-8 for R>=1 —
exactly the #203 signature.

**So #203 is re-framed, not resolved.** It is a DISAGREEMENT between two
implementations at small R, magnitude ~3e-6. My earlier note asserted AnyAxisym
was the wrong one; nothing I have measured justifies that attribution, and given
#206 it could as easily be RazorThinExp's R2deriv. Fixed the task title and body
to say "disagree" rather than "AnyAxisym is wrong", and recorded that settling it
needs a better second-derivative reference than my Hankel panels (higher-order
quadrature, or mpmath at extended precision).

Two near-misses in two wakes from trusting a reference. The habit that caught
both: check whether the REFERENCE behaves sanely before believing it about the
code under test.

Built the arbiter I said #203 needed: mpmath `quadosc` at 25-30 digits on the
Hankel integrals. It settles both open questions definitively.

**#203 — RESOLVED, and the ORIGINAL attribution was right after all.**
RATIO R2deriv/Rforce at z=0, vs mpmath dps=30:

    R      mpmath truth      AnyAxisym rel   RazorThinExp rel
    0.05   -10.7995150733       3.294e-6         3.513e-16
    0.30     0.676983627745     1.605e-6         1.315e-16
    1.00     1.6054007858       1.935e-8         3.866e-15

RazorThinExp's IN-PLANE R2deriv is exact to machine precision, so it WAS a valid
gold reference for this particular quantity. **AnyAxisym._R2deriv at z=0 is the
wrong one**, by up to 3.3e-6 at small R. My re-framing to "unresolved" last wake
was the right call on the evidence I had; it is now resolved, in favour of the
original claim, with the magnitude corrected from 6.5e-5 to 3.3e-6.

**#206 — CONFIRMED, and stronger than I could show before.**
RATIO Rforce(R,z)/Rforce(R,0) at R=1, vs mpmath dps=25:

    z/R     mpmath truth        AnyAxisym rel   RazorThinExp rel
    1e-02   0.98831384860796      7.26e-13        1.367e-6
    1e-03   0.99883212707027      7.34e-13        0.0007357
    1e-04   0.99988322129345      8.29e-13        0.002766

AnyAxisym is exact to ~7e-13 — the ~1e-7 residual in my earlier scipy-Hankel
version was MY integral's error, not the code's. RazorThinExp degrades to 2.8e-3.

**These are consistent, not contradictory.** RazorThinExp is exact in-plane and
broken off-plane; AnyAxisym is exact off-plane and slightly wrong in the
in-plane second derivative. Different code paths in each.

Net for Jo: two independent pre-existing NUMPY defects, each confirmed against a
machine-precision arbiter, neither blocking anything:
  #203  AnyAxisym._R2deriv at z=0,        up to 3.3e-6 at small R
  #206  RazorThinExp Rforce off-plane,    up to 2.8e-3 as |z|->0

Technique worth reusing: for Hankel-type oscillatory integrals,
`mpmath.quadosc(f, [0, inf], omega=R)` at dps=25-30 is a genuine arbiter. My
hand-rolled scipy panels between J1 zeros were good to 1e-7 for the force and

### 2026-08-07 — #143 scoped properly (and my previous scoping was wrong)

Read the actual code rather than trusting my own earlier note. Two corrections:

**1. The blocker is NOT the four `integrate.quad` sites.** I had recorded
evolveddiskdf.py:3140/3164/3214/3239 as the thing to migrate. Those are the
LINE-OF-SIGHT marginalization integrands (`_marginalizeVperpIntegrandSinAlpha*`)
— finite range [-nsigma, +nsigma], smooth, 1-D. Easy, and a separate surface.

**2. The real blocker is `dblquad` at evolveddiskdf.py:607**, in the direct
branch of `vmomentsurfacemass` (reached after the grid branches return). That is
the path the :525 gate protects, and it is a **2-D adaptive integral over a
DISC**: outer limits meanvT/sigmaT1 ± nsigma, inner limits
meanvR/sigmaR1 ± sqrt(nsigma^2 - (x - meanvT/sigmaT1)^2).

`galpy.backend.quadrature.nested_quad` is a tensor product over a
HYPER-RECTANGLE, so it does not fit a disc with x-dependent inner limits as-is.

**Design that does fit, with no new helper.** Change variables to polar about
the disc centre:

    vT_n = meanvT/sigmaT1 + r cos(theta)
    vR_n = meanvR/sigmaR1 + r sin(theta)
    r in [0, nsigma], theta in [0, 2*pi],  Jacobian r

The disc becomes EXACTLY a rectangle in (r, theta), so `nested_quad` applies
directly, and the integrand — a Gaussian-ish DF ratio centred on that point — is
smooth in polar coordinates. This also avoids the sqrt-shaped inner limits,
which are exactly the kind of endpoint singularity that hurts a fixed-order rule.

That turns #143 from "migrate off scipy" into a specific, checkable change.
Preferring the change of variables over extending `nested_quad` with variable
inner limits: no new API surface, and it uses the helper that already exists
([[audit-placement-and-duplication]]).

Not starting it this wake — two PRs are open (#1261, #1262), the slow-skip
branch is held pending its junitxml, and a 2-D quadrature swap in a DF is not
something to rush into a queue that deep.

### 2026-08-07 — #143 design refinement: do NOT replace numpy's dblquad

Caught a hole in yesterday's #143 design before writing any code. I had written
"migrate the dblquad at :607 to nested_quad via a polar change of variables".
Taken literally that would REPLACE scipy's adaptive dblquad on the NUMPY path
with a fixed-order tensor-product GL rule — which changes numpy values and
breaks the byte-identity constraint that governs this whole project.

The correct shape is the dual path already used by jeans.py (and blessed in
[[no-numpy-islands-eliminate-fast]]: a dual numpy/backend path is NOT an island):

    xp = get_namespace(...)
    if xp is numpy:
        return dblquad(...)                      # UNCHANGED -> byte-identical
    return nested_quad(xp, polar_integrand,      # backend-native + differentiable
                       [[0, nsigma], [0, 2*pi]], ...)

with the polar substitution
    vT_n = meanvT/sigmaT1 + r cos(theta),  vR_n = meanvR/sigmaR1 + r sin(theta)
    Jacobian r,  which maps the disc EXACTLY onto the rectangle.

So the deliverable is "add a backend branch", not "swap the quadrature". Same
end state for the two gates at :525 and :2908, without touching numpy output.

Operational note: **two 150-check PRs do not give 2x throughput.** #1262's run
has been `queued` for 64 minutes with all 149 checks unstarted while #1261 works
through its 153 — the runner pool is the bottleneck, so they serialize. The
"two PRs at a time" limit is therefore about review load, not wall-clock; a
third PR (the slow-skip branch) would simply queue behind regardless.

### 2026-08-07 — #143 defect REPRODUCED and quantified (with the gradient target)

Confirmed `galpy.util.quadpack.dblquad` is genuinely scipy `quad` nested inside
scipy `quad` (read the source — it is not a galpy-native routine), so the #143
premise holds.

Reproduction, forced jax, x64 on, direct path (`grid=False`):

    value      Array(0.0668027, dtype=float64)      <- WORKS
    jax.grad   ConcretizationTypeError: Abstract tracer value encountered
               where concrete value is expected ... arose with the `float` function
    FD d/dR on the numpy path (reference):  -1.90281496e-01

That is the signature of a silent numpy island, and it is exactly the class
[[value-checks-cannot-see-numpy-fallback]] warns about: the VALUE is correct, so
any value-comparison test passes and sees nothing wrong; only taking a gradient
exposes that the integral never touched the backend. scipy's `quad` calls
`float()` on the tracer and dies.

So #143's deliverable now has a concrete acceptance test: after adding the
backend branch, `jax.grad(vmomentsurfacemass)(R)` at R=0.9 must reproduce
**-1.90281496e-01**, not merely "be finite" ([[stringent-gradient-tests]]).

**Two probe errors of my own, recorded so they do not become findings.**
(1) My first run reported `dtype=float32` — that was `jax_enable_x64=False` in my
probe environment, not a galpy defect. Set JAX_ENABLE_X64=1.
(2) I expected the direct path to CRASH under a backend and it did not; the
result even carries a backend dtype, because the final `* norm` multiplies the
scipy float by a backend-array sigma. Had I stopped at "it works", I would have
concluded #143 was stale — the opposite of the truth.

### 2026-08-07 — #143 design changes again after reading _buildvgrid_backend: EXTRACT, don't add

Read the merged `_buildvgrid_backend` (from #141) before writing the direct-path
branch, per the standing "check existing utilities before creating new ones"
directive. It already contains everything hard about evaluating this DF on the
backend:

  * differentiable velocity grids built as lo + (hi-lo)*frac, deliberately NOT
    xp.linspace (torch drops the gradient w.r.t. tensor endpoints)
  * flattened (N, 4) ICs with R carrying its gradient into every orbit
  * ONE batched multi-orbit backward integrate via diffrax / torchdiffeq
  * `_idf`, the backend-array-callable initial-DF evaluation
  * scalar-t and t-list handling
  * an explicit NotImplementedError for deriv= (use autodiff instead)

So the honest design is **not** "add a backend branch at :607". It is:

  1. EXTRACT that batched IC -> backward-integrate -> evaluate-DF core out of
     `_buildvgrid_backend` into a shared private helper taking arbitrary (vR, vT)
     POINTS rather than a rectangular grid;
  2. `_buildvgrid_backend` keeps calling it with its meshgrid;
  3. the direct path calls it with the POLAR GL nodes and contracts with the
     nested_quad weights (Jacobian r).

That is hoist-don't-copy. Writing a second batched-integrate block for the
direct path would duplicate the subtlest code in this file — including the
torch-linspace gradient trap, which a copy would very plausibly get wrong.

**Rejected alternative:** under a backend, just route grid=False to the grid
path. Much less code and it reuses tested machinery wholesale, but the direct

### 2026-08-07 — extraction verified on numpy; acceptance criterion corrected

**Gate, arm 1 of 3 (commit 9ef805e8): numpy RC=0, 35 passed (307s).** Matches
the pre-extraction count exactly, so the refactor is behaviour-preserving on the
byte-identity-critical path. torch and jax still running; no claim on those.

Committed the extraction BEFORE the gate finished, deliberately: I was about to
start step 2 in the same working tree, and a junitxml describing a tree I never
commit is the same class of error as reading a partial run — a real result
attached to the wrong thing.

**Correction to my own acceptance criterion.** Two wakes ago I recorded that the
direct-path test must reproduce `jax.grad == -1.90281496e-01`, a number I got
from a central FD on the NUMPY path. Reading
tests/test_backend_evolveddiskdf.py, the file already has the right pattern in
`test_moment_grad_through_evolution_vs_fd`: it compares the backend gradient
against an FD computed **on the backend itself** — integrator-consistent — with
a stated ~2e-4 floor, precisely because backend and numpy use different solvers
and different quadrature.

Pinning the numpy-derived constant would have baked scipy's ADAPTIVE dblquad
result into a test of a fixed-order GL path, so the tolerance would have had to
absorb the quadrature difference as well as the solver difference — a loose test
that passes for the wrong reason. The numpy number stays useful as a sanity
ballpark for the VALUE; it is not the gradient assertion.

So step 2's tests are:
  1. direct-path VALUE, backend vs numpy, to quadrature tolerance;
  2. direct-path GRADIENT, backend autodiff vs backend FD, following the
     existing convention and its ~2e-4 floor.

### 2026-08-07 — #143 step 2 WORKS: the direct path is differentiable

Added `_vmomentsurface_direct_backend` (polar GL over the disc via nested_quad,
reusing the extracted `_df_at_velocities_backend`) plus the dispatch at the
direct site. numpy keeps its adaptive dblquad untouched.

    numpy direct (adaptive dblquad):  6.6802698135e-02
    jax   direct (polar GL):          6.6802596615e-02   rel 1.52e-06
    jax.grad d/dR:                   -1.90281325e-01     (was ConcretizationTypeError)
    backend FD d/dR (consistent):    -1.90281325e-01     rel 1.32e-10

**One real bug found by testing, which is why the probe existed.** My first
version passed the polar nodes straight to `_df_at_velocities_backend` and got
value 0.0 and grad nan. Cause: `_buildvgrid_backend` feeds that helper PHYSICAL
velocities (meanv +- nsigma*sigma), whereas the direct integrand's vR/vT are
NORMALISED (in units of sigma) — `_vmomentsurfaceIntegrand` multiplies by sigma
when it builds the Orbit and I had not. Fixed by scaling at the call and
commenting the convention at both ends, since the two callers now disagree about
units and that is exactly the sort of thing that rots.

**And this vindicates correcting the acceptance criterion.** The numpy-FD number
I originally wanted to pin was -1.90281496e-01; the backend gives
-1.90281325e-01. Those differ at ~9e-7 — the quadrature+solver gap. Asserting
against the backend's own FD gives 1.3e-10 agreement, i.e. a test that is three
orders of magnitude tighter AND measures the right thing.

Added two tests to tests/test_backend_evolveddiskdf.py — the FIRST backend
coverage of grid=False in that file: a value check vs numpy at quadrature
tolerance (with an `is_backend_array` assertion so a silent numpy fallback fails
the test), and the grad-vs-backend-FD check at the file's 2e-4 convention.

### 2026-08-07 — direct path is now JIT-TRACEABLE too, not just differentiable

Scoped my own step-2 claim honestly instead of stopping at "grad works", and the
check paid: `jax.jit` on the direct path raised TracerBoolConversionError.
Traceback pinned it to evolveddiskdf.py:606,

    if initvmoment == 0.0:
        initvmoment = 1.0

a Python bool on what is a tracer under a backend.

**The fix had to be backend-only, and that is the interesting part.** The naive
repair is `xp.where(initvmoment == 0.0, 1.0, initvmoment)` in place. But this
line sits BEFORE the numpy/backend split, and numpy.where returns a 0-d ARRAY —
which would propagate through `norm` and change `vmomentsurfacemass`'s public
numpy return type from float to a 0-d array. Value-identical, type-visible, and
exactly the kind of silent contract change [[flag-numpy-byte-identical-changes]]
exists for. So numpy keeps its `if`, and only the backend branch selects:

    if xp is numpy:
        if initvmoment == 0.0: initvmoment = 1.0
    else:
        initvmoment = xp.where(initvmoment == 0.0, 1.0, initvmoment)

Result:

    numpy still returns  float64 = 6.6802698135e-02   (type AND value preserved)
    jax.jit(direct)   -> 6.6802596615e-02   rel 1.52e-06 vs numpy, == eager

So the direct moment path is now differentiable AND traceable, where before it
was neither. That is a better outcome than the task scoped, and it came from
asking "is the claim actually 'jittable' or only 'differentiable'?" rather than
declaring victory on the gradient.

**Attribution caveat, recorded rather than glossed:** the test run I dispatched
last wake was launched BEFORE this edit, so it exercises the pre-fix tree. Its
COST numbers stay representative (the fix changes one comparison, not the 2500
orbit integrations), but its pass/fail does not describe the current tree. Will
re-run correctness after committing rather than quote it.

### 2026-08-07 — sequencing lesson: opening PR N+1 can DELAY PR N's completion

#1262 has been substantively green for ~an hour (150/154, 0 reds, every real
shard passed). It cannot finish because:

    all-clear                IN_PROGRESS, polling for the rest
    backend status report    QUEUED, waiting for a runner
    ...and that runner is behind #1263's ~137 remaining checks

So a *summary* job on the older PR is starved by the newer PR's fan-out. Nothing
is broken and all-clear's own timeout is 330 minutes, so there is no risk — it
is purely slow.

**The lesson is about sequencing, not about CI.** I opened #1263 the moment
#1261 merged, because a slot was free and the loop says never idle. That is
right in general, but with a saturated runner pool it can push the PR that is
nearly done behind the one that just started. Earlier I recorded that two
~150-check PRs "serialize"; the sharper statement is that they can *invert* —
the new PR's checks get runners while the old PR's tail jobs wait.

Better rule for this repo: when the older PR is within a handful of checks of
green, let it finish before opening the next one. The slot is free either way;
the cost is only a few minutes of my idleness against potentially an hour of the
older PR's.

Not reverting anything — #1263 is legitimate work and will run regardless. Noting
it so the next slot-opening decision accounts for the tail.

### 2026-08-07 — the torch-jit fork deadlock is real, and localized

Third repro attempt (slow-skip line stripped from the list, not relying on
regen mode) **reproduced it**. RC=1, pytest-timeout at 420 s, and the stack
names the exact chain:

    tests/test_streamdf.py:519   test_streamTrack_multi_parallel
    galpy/df/streamdf.py:315     __init__
    galpy/df/streamdf.py:1325    _determine_stream_track
    galpy/util/multi.py:255      parallel_map
    galpy/util/multi.py:149      run_tasks
    multiprocessing/process.py:149  join
    multiprocessing/popen_fork.py:28  os.waitpid   <-- blocked forever

So the parent forks and a child never exits. `restrict_to_single_thread()` runs
first thing in the child (multi.py:95) and caps `torch.set_num_threads(1)` —
which is why **eager** torch is fine — but that knob does not touch what
`--jit` adds. `--jit` on torch means `torch.compile` (galpy/backend/_jit.py:178),
and Dynamo/Inductor keeps a parallel compile-worker pool. Forking a process
that holds that pool is the classic way to inherit unusable pool state.

**Hypothesis under test right now:** it is inductor's compile-worker pool, not
the intra-op thread pool. A/B running with `TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1`,
everything else identical. If that arm passes, the fix is a two-line extension
of the existing `restrict_to_single_thread` helper in `galpy/backend/` — same
function, same rationale, no new helper and nothing new to place
([[generic-helpers-go-in-backend]]).

Not claiming the cause until the A/B lands.

### 2026-08-07 — inductor-compile-pool hypothesis REFUTED

`TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1`, everything else identical: **RC=1, same
timeout, same `os.waitpid` stack**. So the deadlock is not inductor's parallel
compile-worker pool. Glad I A/B'd it rather than writing the two-line "fix" the
theory implied — it would have landed, looked plausible, and changed nothing.

What I could establish without ptrace (py-spy is blocked, `ptrace_scope=1`):
each of the four forked children is **single-threaded** and parked in
`futex_wait_queue`. A one-thread process waiting on a futex is waiting for a
lock whose owner does not exist — the lock was held by a *parent* thread that
`fork` did not copy. That is the shape of the bug regardless of which pool owns
the lock.

To name it, made the child self-report instead: a pytest plugin
(`/tmp/diagplug/forkdiag.py`, not in the repo) wraps `galpy.util.multi.worker`
so each child arms `faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(45, exit=True)` into its
own file. `parallel_map` builds `ctx.Process(target=worker, ...)` by
module-global lookup at call time, so rebinding the attribute is enough — no
source edit, no worktree churn. Running now.

### 2026-08-07 — fork deadlock ROOT CAUSE (the child self-dump worked)

The children reported their own stacks. Every one is parked here:

    /tmp/torchinductor_galpy_.../cefasp53....py:114 in call     <-- generated kernel
    torch/_inductor/output_code.py:725 __call__
    torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/... (runtime wrappers)
    torch/_dynamo/eval_frame.py:1298 _fn
    galpy/potential/IsochronePotential.py:62 _evaluate
    galpy/backend/_jit.py:172 call                              <-- torch.compile shim
    galpy/actionAngle/actionAngleIsochroneApprox.py:1063 _actionsFreqsAngles_backend
    galpy/df/streamdf.py:4901 _determine_stream_track_single

So the child is not stuck *compiling* — it is stuck **executing an inductor
kernel the parent already compiled**. The child inherits the compiled code and
the CPU thread pool it runs on, enters the parallel region, and the pool is
dead. That is why:

- **eager torch works** — eager ops honour the child's
  `torch.set_num_threads(1)` and take the serial path;
- **`TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1` changed nothing** — that governs
  *compile* parallelism, not the generated kernel's *runtime* parallelism;
- **`restrict_to_single_thread()` cannot fix it** — the parallelism is baked
  into the kernel at compile time, before the fork.

**A compiled kernel is not fork-safe.** So the fix is not another knob, it is
not forking: in `parallel_map`, when `jit_mode() != "off"`, fall back to
`list(map(...))`.

That slots in beside the precedent already in the function — Windows, where
forking also does not work, returns `list(map(function, sequence))` three lines
above. Same shape, same place, no new helper. `jit_mode()` is imported inside
the function, matching how `restrict_to_single_thread` is already imported
there and keeping `galpy.util.multi` importable without `galpy.backend`.

numpy is byte-identical **by construction**: `jit_mode()` is `"off"` unless
somebody entered `backend.jit(...)`, so the numpy path never reaches the new
branch. Eager torch is likewise untouched and keeps its parallelism.

Honest limitation to state on the PR: under a trace, `multi=` becomes serial,
so the test no longer exercises fork-parallelism there. It currently does not
exercise anything — it hangs — so this is strictly more coverage, but the
tradeoff should be visible rather than implied.

Branch `feat/no-fork-under-trace` (worktree /var/tmp/forkfix). Verifying it
flips all three previously-hanging tests before committing
([[verify-burndown-flips-stash-rerun]] — the "without the fix" half is already
established three times over: RC=1, same `os.waitpid` stack).

z = **0.000** exactly — the plane of a razor-thin disk, where Φ ~ Φ₀ + c·|z| has
a genuine kink and a one-sided finite difference is mathematically undefined
([[nonsmooth-potential-grad-undefined]]). The test guards this with
`if tzforce**2 < 10**ttol`, so what plausibly differs between eager and traced is
the *guard*, not the physics: eager `zforce` at z=0 may be NaN (making the guard
False and the assertion never evaluated — a vacuous pass, cf.
[[assertion-comparison-outside-reducer]]), while traced returns a clean 0.0 and
the FD actually gets compared. That would make the **traced path the more
honest one** and the eager pass the artifact.

That is a hypothesis, not a finding. Building a pre-#1259 worktree
(`d8960062`) to A/B the same nodeid on both sides and settle whether #1259
introduced this or merely stopped hiding it.

### 2026-08-07 — the regression does NOT reproduce outside pytest, and that is the finding

Rebuilt the probe to compute *exactly* what `test_forceAsDeriv_potential` does —
same default constructor (`tp = tclass()`, confirmed at test_potential.py:1453),
**including the `tp.normalize(1.0)` my first probe omitted**, same `dz=1e-8`,

    amp after normalize(1.0) = 0.8866736367602572     (identical on both commits)

    pre-#1259 (d8960062)          tip (199ee10e)
    numpy   FD=-3.933298e-04 PASS  numpy   FD=-3.933298e-04 PASS
    jax     FD=-3.933298e-04 PASS  jax     FD=-3.933298e-04 PASS
    jaxjit  FD=-1.401101e-04 PASS  jaxjit  FD=-1.401101e-04 PASS

**Byte-for-byte identical on both commits, and passing everywhere.** Yet the
same nodeid under pytest fails on the tip with FD = 7.346e+03 and passes on the
parent.

So the failure is **not a property of the potential**. The difference between my
script and the test is the harness: `--jit` wraps *every* galpy entry point in
`jax.jit` at the `@backend_input` boundary, whereas I hand-jitted only the
`tp(...)` call. `normalize()` and `evaluatezforces` run traced in the test and
eager in my probe.

That points squarely at [[jit-trace-mode]], whose whole content is: *trace
caches go stale on `normalize()`*. The test constructs and **then** normalizes;
if a trace is cached against the pre-normalize amp (or reused across instances),
the FD comes back with the wrong scale — which is exactly the shape of a
7.3e+03 where 1.4e-4 belongs.

**What is established:** #1259 flipped this nodeid from pass to fail under
`--backend jax --jit` (A/B, same command, same env, one nodeid each side).
**What is not:** the mechanism. It is now clear it lives in the harness-level
tracing interaction, not in AnyAxisym's quadrature — which is a materially
different (and more worrying) place to look than where I started.

Correction to my previous entry: I wrote that the probe "measured the wrong
object". It did not — `tclass()` is the default constructor. What it actually
missed was `normalize(1.0)` and, more importantly, that jitting one call is not
the same as running the suite traced.

### 2026-08-07 — REPRODUCED minimally: #1259's quadrature is z-DISCONTINUOUS under tracing

The trigger was the pytest harness, so I put the probe *inside* pytest (a
throwaway `tests/test_zzprobe_tmp.py`, deleted after) and ran it under the same
two commands. Six lines, and they say everything:

    --backend jax --jit
      AMP           = Array(0.88668817)
      Phi(0.5, 0)   = -1.7599484491950728
      Phi(0.5, 1e-8)= -1.7600219091821239
      numerator     =  7.345998705110546e-05      -> FD = 7346

    --backend jax (eager)
      AMP           = Array(0.88667364)
      Phi(0.5, 0)   = -1.7599930722150277
      Phi(0.5, 1e-8)= -1.7599930722110944
      numerator     = -3.9332981316420046e-12     -> FD = -0.00039

**Traced, Φ jumps by 7.3e-5 between z = 0 and z = 1e-8. Eagerly the same two
points differ by 4e-12.** The potential is *discontinuous in z at the midplane*
under tracing. That is not a test-tolerance issue — a discontinuous Φ breaks any
traced orbit integration that crosses the disc plane, and the FD test is simply
the first thing to notice.

Secondary observation, same run: `normalize(1.0)` lands on a different amp
traced vs eager (0.88668817 vs 0.88667364, rel 1.6e-5), because it solves
against the potential's own force and the traced quadrature answers slightly
differently. That is a symptom of the same cause, not an independent bug.

**Cause (located, not yet fixed):** #1259 replaced AnyAxisym's quadrature with a
graded dyadic panel scheme for the a=R singularity. The panel structure it picks
at exactly z=0 differs from the one at z=1e-8, and eagerly a `z == 0` test
resolves one way while under a trace it resolves the other (the
[[xp-where-dead-branch-guards]] / traced-comparison family). Eager takes the
consistent branch; traced does not.

This is a **defect in merged code on feat/backends-develop**, found only because
the burn ran the traced suite — `backend-tests` has no `--jit` dimension, so
nothing in normal CI would have caught it.

Route taken through this, for the record, because three hypotheses died on the
way: (1) "eager zforce is NaN so the guard is vacuous" — refuted, zforce is 0.0
everywhere; (2) "my probe used the wrong object" — wrong, `tclass()` is the
default constructor, what I had missed was `normalize(1.0)`; (3) "trace caches
go stale on normalize()" — refuted, reordering normalize vs the first traced
call changes nothing. The thing that finally worked was running the probe
*inside pytest under the harness*, which is where the difference lives.

Next: read #1259's panel-selection code for the z=0 branch and make it
trace-consistent. Not opening a PR on a hypothesis — the fix has to make the
traced Φ continuous at z→0, and that is the acceptance test.

### 2026-08-07 — cause found in #1259's own code, and its commit message predicted it

`_bk_split_quad` (AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDiskPotential.py, added by #1259):

```python
dmin = xp.where(
    xp.abs(z) * ones > 0.0,
    xp.minimum(4.0 * xp.abs(z) * ones, half),   # z != 0 : panels march to ~4|z|
    half,                                        # z == 0 : grading OFF
)
dk = [xp.maximum(Rp * (2.0**-k), dmin) for k in range(1, K + 1)]
```

At **z = 0**, `dmin = R/2`, so every `dk` clamps to `R/2`: the whole panel list
collapses and only four panels of width R/2 survive. At **z = 1e-8**,
`dmin = 4e-8` and the panels march all the way in to |a−R| ~ 4e-8 — ~50 graded
panels resolving the peak.

**Two different quadrature schemes on either side of z = 0.** They disagree by
7.3e-5, and that is exactly the discontinuity measured. Eager never sees it
because the concrete path is scipy's adaptive `quad`; only the traced path runs
this scheme, which is why `backend-tests` (no `--jit` dimension) is blind to it.

The commit message of #1259 says, in as many words:

> At z=0 the integral is singular there and marching panels in makes a finite
> difference of this potential **in R** blow up, so grading is switched off; for
> z>0 the peak is genuinely resolvable and the FD stays clean.

So the z=0 special case was added to keep the **R**-derivative check clean, and
it broke the **z**-derivative check. One FD traded for the other, and only the
R one was measured at the time.

**Fix criterion (both halves, or it is the same mistake again):** the traced
potential must be continuous as z→0 *and* the R-FD must stay clean. A `dmin`
that varies continuously with |z| down to a floor (e.g. `max(4|z|, R·2**-K)`)
removes the scheme switch, but it re-enters the regime the original comment was
avoiding — so it needs measuring at both z=0 and z≠0, on `test_forceAsDeriv`
*and* `test_2ndDeriv`, before it is worth proposing.

Not opening a PR on the hypothesis. Next wake: implement, then gate on the
continuity of traced Φ at z→0 as the acceptance test rather than on the pytest
node going green — a scheme that merely moves the discontinuity somewhere the
grid does not sample would pass the test and still be wrong.

### 2026-08-07 — measured four dmin variants; the analytic cusp settles which is right

Ran all four inside the `--jit` harness against BOTH criteria (A: continuity of
Φ in z at the midplane; B: the R-direction FD that #1259's z==0 case was
protecting):

| dmin | A: FD as z→0 | B: R-FD rel err, z=0 | z=0.125 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **current** (`z==0 → R/2`) | −7.3e+03 → −71.6 → +1.13 (sign flips!) | 3.4e-09 | 8.2e-09 |
| **nograde** (always `R/2`) | 1.2e-04 → 1.2e-02 → 1.008 | 3.4e-09 | 8.2e-09 |
| **floor** (`min(max(4|z|, R·2⁻ᴷ), R/2)`) | **1.864 → 1.865 → 1.865** | 2.8e-06 | 6.2e-10 |
| **always** (`min(4|z|, R/2)`) | same as floor | 2.8e-06 | 6.2e-10 |

Only `floor`/`always` give a **constant** FD as z→0, which is what a razor-thin
disk must do: Φ ≈ Φ(R,0) + c|z| with c = 2πGΣ(R).

**Checked against the analytic value rather than against the other
implementation** ([[mpmath-quadosc-final-arbiter]] — the lesson being not to let
one candidate arbitrate another). Default surfdens is `1.5·exp(−3R)`, so

    amp · 2π · Σ(0.5) = 0.8866725 · 2π · 0.3346952 = 1.8646299572

| scheme | FD at z=1e-8 | rel err vs analytic |
|---|---|---|
| **floor** | 1.864 | **3.4e-04** (limited by my 4-digit print) |
| current (traced) | −7.346e+03 | 3.9e+03 |
| numpy / scipy `quad` | −3.933e-04 | **1.000** (i.e. returns ~0, misses the cusp entirely) |

So `floor` is not merely "different" — it is **correct to ~1e-4**, and *both*
the current traced scheme and the long-standing numpy/scipy path are wrong at
the midplane. numpy misses the cusp completely.

**★ This turns into a question for Jo, not a fix I should just make. ★**
`test_forceAsDeriv_potential` asserts that when `zforce ≈ 0` the z-direction FD
must also be ≈ 0. At a razor-thin midplane both halves are individually
defensible and jointly contradictory:

- `zforce(R, 0) = 0` is right — by symmetry, the two-sided derivative does not
  exist and 0 is the symmetric value;
- the one-sided FD is **−2πGΣ ≠ 0** — also right, and now measured.

The test conflates them, and it has only ever passed because the quadratures
were inaccurate there in a compensating way. Fixing the quadrature correctly
makes the test fail. So the honest fix is *two* changes — quadrature to `floor`,
**and** a z=0 exclusion for razor-thin disks in that test — and the second is a
physics-test recalibration, which per standing policy needs sign-off rather than
my unilateral edit.

Not opening the PR tonight. Writing it up for Jo with the numbers above, and
holding the quadrature change with it so they land together or not at all —
landing the quadrature alone would turn a silent wrong answer into a red CI.

### 2026-08-07 — CORRECTION: the continuous dmin is NOT the fix. It breaks R2deriv.

I tried the candidate for real (scratch worktree at the tip, `dmin = min(max(4|z|,
R·2⁻ᴷ), R/2)`) and ran the three AnyAxisym `test_potential` nodeids under
`--backend jax --jit`. Two results, and the second retracts my last entry.

**Confirmed:** `test_forceAsDeriv` now reports

    diff = 1.863754e+00      (analytic cusp 1.8646299572, rel 4.7e-04)

instead of 7.346e+03. The quadrature value is right — the test still fails only
because its expectation is wrong at a razor-thin midplane, as described.

**Retracted:** `test_2ndDeriv` at the same point gets *much worse*, not better:

    baseline (tip)      R2deriv = -2.42e+04   vs FD = -2.29
    continuous dmin     R2deriv = -2.03e+11   vs FD = -3.38e+02

A factor ~8e6 worse. That is precisely the regime #1259's own comment warned
about — "marching panels in makes a finite difference of this potential blow
up" — because the R2deriv integrand carries `((a−R)²+z²)²` in the denominator,
i.e. **1/(a−R)⁴ at z=0**, and a floor of `R·2⁻²⁴ ≈ 3e-8` marches panels far
inside where that is integrable.

**Why I got this wrong:** my four-variant sweep measured criterion A (Φ
continuity) and criterion B (the *first*-derivative R-FD) and declared `floor`
correct. It never measured the **second** derivative, which is the quantity that
actually blows up. I checked the two criteria I had named and then generalised
past them — the same shape as trusting one arbiter for a quantity it was never
validated on ([[mpmath-quadosc-final-arbiter]]), one level up.

**Actual state:** the fix is harder than I said. It needs a dmin that is
continuous in z *and* keeps panels far enough from a=R for a 1/(a−R)⁴ integrand
— so plausibly a per-integrand floor (Φ and the forces can take a much finer
floor than R2deriv/z2deriv/Rzderiv can), or a different treatment of the
singularity altogether. Task #207 updated; the acceptance battery is now
**three** criteria, not two, and any future candidate gets measured on all of
Φ, the forces, AND the second derivatives before I call it anything.

### 2026-08-07 — reframing #207: the traced path is approximate BY DESIGN

Re-read the class-level comment above `_bk_split_quad` — pre-existing, not from
#1259 — and it changes what "fixing" this means:

> A PLAIN concrete backend scalar instead reuses scipy's accurate adaptive quad
> (byte-consistent with the numpy path; **GL cannot resolve the a=R principal
> value / small-z sheet structure that the derivative tests FD-probe at z~1e-8,
> and cannot form the z=0 Hadamard-type second-derivative**)

So the design already records that fixed-order Gauss-Legendre *cannot* do what
these tests probe, and routes concrete values to scipy for exactly that reason.
Under `--jit` everything is traced, so everything takes the GL path — which is
why these entries are ledgered at all.

That splits #207 cleanly into two questions that were tangled together:

1. **A real defect, worth fixing regardless:** #1259 made the traced Φ
   *discontinuous* at z=0 (two schemes either side). Continuity is not an
   accuracy question — an orbit crossing the plane sees a 7.3e-5 step — and it
   should hold whatever the absolute accuracy is.
2. **Probably not fixable with fixed-order GL:** matching the analytic cusp
   *and* the Hadamard-type second derivative at z=0. The docstring says as much.
   My continuous-`dmin` attempt bought (1)'s cusp at the cost of R2deriv, which
   is what "cannot form the z=0 Hadamard-type second-derivative" predicts.

So the realistic target is: restore continuity, keep R2deriv no worse than
baseline, and leave the entries ledgered with the *reason* recorded — rather
than chasing an accuracy the traced scheme was never designed to reach. Noted on
#207; still Jo's call, but the question is now narrower and honest about what is
achievable.

**Also, a near-miss worth recording:** I saw the torch burn's process at 0.0%
CPU for 28 minutes and was about to write it up as a second fork deadlock. That
0.0% was the `timeout` *wrapper*; the real pytest child was running at **668%
CPU across 296 threads**. Checked the child before claiming anything. Same shape
as reading a partial run — I nearly reported the wrong process's number as the
result.

A cProfile listing showed frames from `/var/tmp/streamtorch/galpy/...` — a

    PROVENANCE: /var/tmp/dminfix/galpy/__init__.py       <- the worktree, verified
    C ext: True

    size   numpy ms     jax ms   jax/np  jax us/elem
       1      0.027      5.101    186.5      5100.89

     100      0.050      5.281    105.8        52.81
    1000      0.106      5.787     54.7         5.79
   10000      0.660     15.182     23.0         1.52

**~5 ms flat per `evaluateRforces` call, independent of N up to 1000.** The
earlier mis-rooted run said ~4.7 ms; the properly-rooted one says ~5.1 ms. Same
conclusion, now sourced.

This is **fixed per-call framework overhead**, not arithmetic: decorators,
dispatch, coercion, namespace resolution. Only at N=10000 does real compute
start to show (µs/elem finally falls to 1.5).

**So the wrapper "sharpening" I did two turns ago was the wrong reading.**
`RotateAndTiltWrapperPotential` is not pathological — it issues ~3.6x more force
calls per test, and at ~5 ms of overhead each that is enough to hit the cap
first. Fixing the wrapper would barely move it. The original #79 framing —
per-call overhead — was right all along, and the number is far worse than the
"~2x" in its title: **186x on a scalar call.**

Arithmetic that makes it concrete: `test_dxdv_3d_c_vs_python` at 290 s is
~58,000 scalar force calls, essentially all of it overhead. Two possible fixes,
and the measurement says which:

1. cut the ~5 ms fixed cost (helps everything, including the 10 entries this
   sweep could not un-defer), or
2. make callers pass arrays — at N=1000 the per-element cost is already 1000x
   better.
