### 2026-08-07 — where the 5 ms goes: jax's own dispatch, not a cacheable galpy constant

Profiled one `evaluateRforces` with verified provenance
(`PROVENANCE: /var/tmp/dminfix/galpy/__init__.py`):

    77103 function calls in 0.185 s for 20 calls  =>  ~3855 Python calls per force call

Self-time is spread thinly across **jax internals** — `ufunc_api`,
`dispatch.apply_primitive`, `array_constructors.asarray`,
`pjit._sharding_constraint`, `core.bind`, `lax._convert_element_type`. The only
galpy frames with meaningful self-time are `EllipsoidalPotential._Rforce` and
`_forceInt_all`, at 0.004 s each out of 0.185 s.

**My own prior hypothesis is refuted.** The earlier (mis-rooted) profile pointed
at `as_backend_constant` re-coercing GL nodes on every call — ~42% of cumtime —
and I flagged it as "plausible and cacheable". In the correct checkout,
`jnp.asarray` is still ~50% of cumulative time (220 calls, 11 per force call),
but `print_callers` shows **no galpy frame calls it**: it is jax's own per-op
input normalisation, invoked from inside `jnp.sqrt` and friends. There is no
cacheable galpy constant to hoist.

So the honest characterisation of #79: the ~5 ms is **jax's per-primitive Python
dispatch cost multiplied by the number of ops galpy issues** (~3855 Python calls
per force evaluation). No single hotspot, so no micro-optimisation will do it.
The three levers that actually apply:

1. **fewer ops** — fuse/vectorize galpy's own arithmetic in the hot force paths;
2. **jit** — eliminates per-op dispatch entirely, which is precisely what
   `--jit` mode already does (and why the traced shards are worth having);
3. **bigger arrays** — per-element cost is already ~1000x better at N=1000.

That is a materially different plan from "cache the coerced constants", which is
what I would have written up an hour ago. Recorded on #79 so the next attempt
does not start by chasing the hotspot that is not there.

### 2026-08-07 — the wrapper-vs-worker trap, twice in one session

Checked the with-fix interp arm and found the process at **0.0% CPU, 1 thread,
`sigsuspend`** — which reads exactly like a deadlock. It is the `timeout`
wrapper. The real pytest was its child at **92.6% CPU across 20 threads**,
working normally.

That is the second time today: the same thing happened with the torch burn
(wrapper 0.0%, worker 476-668% across 296 threads). Both times I checked the
child before saying anything, but the near-miss rate is the point — the cause is
that `pgrep -f "pytest ..."` matches `timeout -s SIGKILL 1800 python3 -m pytest
...` as well as the worker, and the wrapper is always the idle one.

Added to [[never-report-partial-run-as-result]]: pick the worker by `threads > 5`
or check `pgrep -P` before concluding anything from a CPU reading. A 0%-CPU
process is not evidence of a hang until you know it is the process doing work.

| `actionAngleAdiabatic_linear_angles_cylsep` | dev from linear trend **2.34757e-07** | `1e-7` | **tolerance** — off by 2.35x |
| `actionAngleStaeckelGrid_basicAndConserved_actions` | circular-orbit **e = 9.363e-12** | `1e-16` | **tolerance** — the bar asks a computed eccentricity to be zero to 1e-16 |
| `actionAngleAdiabaticGrid_outsidegrid_c` | off-grid Jr err **4.7e-3** | `1e-8` | **by design** — the backend path is grid-only (docstring), and the test evaluates at R=3.0 against an Rmax=2.0 grid |

So of the file's three traced failures, **two are tolerance and one is the
documented off-grid gap**. Nothing here is a correctness defect.

**And a ledger gap.** `actionAngleStaeckelGrid_basicAndConserved_actions` is
ledgered for **torch only**. Since `-jit` inherits the *same* backend's eager
entries, `jax-jit` does not cover it — so under jax-jit this is an **un-ledgered
failure**, the second traced-only gap found today after the #1259 regression. It
is not a jax-eager failure (CI's eager jax matrix has no entry for it), so
tracing genuinely changes the arithmetic here: eager jax lands under 1e-16,
traced jax lands at 9.4e-12. Fusion/reassociation, which is exactly what tracing
is allowed to do.

**This is the evidence for the tolerance batch that needs Jo** (#171). Two
entries, both with the measured number and the bar, plus a third that is a
design gap and should stay ledgered with that reason. I am not touching any
tolerance without sign-off; this is the proposal, measured.

Headline worth keeping: **test_actionAngle.py is 179/209 under jax --jit on its
first traced run** — the AA migration traces far better than anyone had checked.

### 2026-08-07 — found two bugs in my own sweep tool, before running the thing it is for

I am about to dispatch `workflow_dispatch(jit=true)` — the authoritative run for
every `-jit` ledger entry — and `ledger_sweep.py` is how I would read it. Checked
the tool against that specific job first, and it was wrong twice.

**1. The artifact name does not say "jit".** backend-tests.yml uploads
`backend-junit-${{ matrix.BACKEND }}-${{ SHARD_ID }}`, and `BACKEND` is `jax` or
`torch` regardless of `JIT_FLAG`. So a traced run is **indistinguishable from an
eager one by filename**, and the sweep would have compared traced outcomes
against the EAGER ledger keys — reporting every eager entry the traced run
happened to pass as STALE. Confidently, and wrongly. Added an explicit `--jit`
flag that re-keys `jax`→`jax-jit`; demonstrated on a fixture, where the buggy
path claims `1 STALE` and the fixed path correctly says the eager entries were
simply not measured.

**2. It did not implement conftest's inheritance rule, and the fix is asymmetric.**
`_load_backend_nodeids` makes `<b>-jit` inherit `<b>`'s eager entries, so a
traced failure already covered by an eager entry is not a gap. But staleness
does **not** inherit: an eager entry describes eager behaviour, so a traced PASS
must never mark it stale. Coverage uses the union; pruning uses only the literal
`<b>-jit` entries. Getting that backwards would have pruned the *eager* ledger
from a traced run — the worst possible outcome of this whole exercise.

Verified: a jit run where an eager-jax-ledgered nodeid fails now reports
**CONFIRMED (inherited)** rather than an un-ledgered gap.

The pattern is the one that keeps repeating today: the instrument was built for
the general case and quietly did not fit the specific job. Checking it against
the job — before trusting its output — is what caught both.

provenance printed:

    df.oortA(1.0)          pre-#1261      tip
      eager numpy            2.49 s      3.17 s
      TRACED (use+jit)       2.90 s     25.26 s      <- 8.7x

Then the profile of the traced call on the tip:

    133332  tottime 0.950  cumtime 36.644   galpy/df/diskdf.py:466(_ssp)
    133332          1.153          33.657   galpy/backend/_input.py:153(wrapper)
    133332          4.252           9.987   galpy/backend/_jit.py:181(traced_call)
    1333320/133332  2.283           4.747   galpy/backend/_jit.py:104(_static_key)
    133332          0.498          19.279   galpy/backend/_coerce.py:69(coerce_coords)

**`_ssp` accounts for 36.6 s of the 45.9 s call, across 133,332 invocations.**

**And my `getattr` suspicion was wrong.** The cost is not the indirection — it is
that #1261 put `@backend_input("R")` on `expSurfaceSigmaProfile`'s methods (that
is *how* it removed the numpy island), so under `--jit` **every one of those
133k leaf calls becomes a traced boundary**: `_static_key` hashing (10 sub-calls
each), `coerce_coords`, and a jax dispatch, per call.

Fourth mechanism hypothesis I have formed today, and the fourth to be corrected
by measuring it. The pattern is consistent enough to be worth naming: I am
reliably good at finding *where* and reliably bad at guessing *why*.

**The general lesson, which outlives this bug:** `@backend_input` is a
*boundary* decorator. Putting it on a **hot leaf** that already-coerced code
calls in a loop multiplies the boundary cost by the loop count. Removing a numpy
island by decorating the leaf is correct for dispatch and can be catastrophic
for traced performance. The leaf needs its coercion done once by its caller, not
133k times by itself.

Fix directions (to be measured, not assumed, when #208 comes up):
  * mark the leaf `@backendNative` so it does not re-enter the boundary
    ([[backendnative-must-be-innermost-decorator]]), or
  * have `_ssp` call an undecorated inner implementation and keep the decorated
    method as the public entry point.

Either keeps #1261's island removal while paying the boundary once.

### 2026-08-07 — #208 fixed, after two more wrong mechanisms

The `getattr`-indirection story from the profile was still not the mechanism.
Instrumenting the accessor settled it:

    _ssp branch counts: {'backend_array': 0, 'plain': 133332}
    R types seen      : {'float': 24, 'float64': 133308}

**Not one of the 133k calls passes a backend array.** `oortA` runs scipy's
adaptive quadrature, which calls the integrand with plain scalars. Under a
FORCED backend a plain `numpy.float64` still resolves to that backend --

    plain ctx      : numpy
    forced jax ctx : jax.numpy        <- this is the whole regression
    nested numpy   : numpy

-- so #1261's decoration put the entire scipy-quad scalar path onto jax: coerce
a scalar in, evaluate, convert back out, 133,332 times. Values were right the
whole way; it was 133k scalar round-trips.

My first fix bypassed the boundary when `is_backend_array(R)` -- **dead code, it
never fired once**, and measured 25.12 s against a 25.26 s baseline. Second
attempt pinned numpy unconditionally: fixed traced, but taxed the numpy path 35%

    slowprune  C-ext loaded: False    (unfixed tip -- the tempting arm)

Running the without-fix arm in `slowprune` would have made orbit sampling fall
back to Python, come back far slower, and "prove" my diskdf fix responsible for
a speedup it has nothing to do with.

The asymmetry is worth naming: a missing `.so` makes **correctness** results
optimistic (tests pass) *and* **attribution** results self-serving (your change
looks load-bearing). Both errors point the same direction -- toward believing
your own work mattered. That is precisely the direction I am least likely to
question, which is why the environment check has to be mechanical rather than
motivated.

Added the rule: print `_ext_loaded` in every arm, exactly like provenance. An
A/B across worktrees is an A/B across *environments* until proven otherwise.

And the useful converse, which I got for free: two arms differing in C-ext
availability that produce **identical** numbers is positive evidence the code
under test never touches C. The #208 byte hashes matched across a C-ext-True and
a C-ext-False checkout -- that is how I know those moment quadratures are pure
scipy.

### 2026-08-07 — CORRECTION: the attribution arm had been dead for hours

I reported "attribution arm still running" across several wakes. It was not.

    worker process        GONE (pgrep matched only my own subshell)
    log last written      20:46:02, checked at 00:50 -- 4h stale
    log content           72 dots (55%) + 51 = 123 of 129, then nothing
    junitxml              NEVER WRITTEN -- the run produced no result at all

It was killed by its own `timeout 3600`, ~6 tests from finishing.

**How I missed it:** the dot count grew for a while, then stopped, and I kept
reading a static log as "in progress". I have a memory
([[never-report-partial-run-as-result]]) about `pgrep` matching the `timeout`
wrapper and reading a healthy run as hung -- this is the *inverse* error, reading
a dead run as healthy, and the same fix covers both: **check the worker, not the
log.** The tell was there and free: identical dot count on two consecutive
checks. I saw it and did not act on it.

**What the failure does say, and what it does not.** With the fix the file takes
1295 s; this arm blew past 3600 s. The two oortA timeouts only account for ~600 s
of that, so something else is substantially slower without the fix -- consistent
with the sampling tests being fix-sensitive after all. That is a *hint*, not the
measurement, and it does not satisfy the rule I pre-registered. No claim.

Relaunched with two changes, both fixing the harness rather than my attention:
  * `timeout 9000` -- the without-fix arm is far slower than the with-fix one, so
    sizing its budget from the fast arm was wrong.
  * `-v` -- per-test outcomes stream to the log, so a killed run still yields
    partial per-test data instead of an undifferentiated wall of dots. A run
    whose only progress signal is dots is a run you cannot diagnose.

           head cov 24.94 lines 48421 hits 12078
           patch cov 70.0  lines 10  hits 7  misses 3

**`codecov/patch` is a different animal from `codecov/project`.** Patch measures
the *changed* lines, so "3 of my 10 new lines uncovered" would be a real gap and
exactly the thing [[no-hiding-uncovered-code]] is about. It does not get waved
through with the phantom argument.

**And my discriminator does not even apply here.** It is "`lines` identical on
both sides"; #1268 has 48414 -> 48421, which differs. That is my PR legitimately
adding 7 lines, not a coverage regression -- but the rule as I wrote it would
have said "REAL DROP, investigate". Recording the correction: the identical-
`lines` test is only valid for PRs that change no line counts (#1266, #1267 --
txt files and a 5-line branch). For a line-adding PR the phantom signal is
head *hits* far below base while jobs are still uploading, which is what 12078
vs 41666 at 24.94% is.

**What actually decides it:** whether the jobs that execute the new branches have
finished. 7 of 8 are still pending, including both `test_backend*.py` builds --
and `tests/test_backend_diskdf.py` is where the new guard lives, so the branches
it covers cannot be counted yet.

So: not a phantom claim, not a defect claim. Re-check when those 8 are done. If
patch is still short of 100% then, the three lines get identified and covered,
not explained away.

### 2026-08-07 — CORRECTION to my own framing: #208 is not a jit-only regression

Measured the `@backend_input` boundary cost directly, to turn the diskdf lesson
into a general number:

    one crossing, scalar arg          us/call
    undecorated, numpy                    1.3
    decorated, numpy                      2.8   (the ~12% I saw, in absolute terms)
    decorated, forced jax EAGER         178.2   (141x)
    decorated, forced jax + jit         151.1   (120x)

**Eager is if anything slower than traced.** So the cost is a *forced-backend*
cost, not a jit cost -- and 133,332 x 178 us = 23.7 s reproduces the oortA
regression from the eager side alone. Confirmed end-to-end, no jit:

    forced jax EAGER oortA   without fix 31.09 s   with fix 4.65 s   6.7x

I had been calling #208 "a traced regression" since I found it, because traced
is where it broke a test. That was the visible symptom, not the fault. Retitled
#1268 and added a section rather than quietly editing the numbers.

**Why the correction matters rather than being pedantry:** `backend-tests` runs
**eager** forced backends on every push. #1261 slowed the routine
`backend jax tests/test_diskdf.py` shard by ~2.8x (whole file 3613 s -> 1295 s,
measured as a side-effect of the un-defer A/B) and it stayed green, so nothing
flagged it. Framing the fix as jit-only would have understated what it buys and
mis-taught the next reader about where boundary costs bite.

Also worth keeping: the decorator on the **numpy** path is 1.3 -> 2.8 us, i.e.
2.2x on a trivial leaf. Harmless at normal call counts, and exactly what makes
133k calls a 200 ms tax before any backend is involved.

### 2026-08-07 — empirical hot-boundary ranking: nothing left to find

My earlier class sweep picked 9 call sites by hand and found no second instance.
That bounds what it sampled, so I replaced it with an empirical version: count
every non-numpy `coerce_coords` crossing across a workload and rank by caller.

    workload                  crossings   seconds
    diskdf.oortA                      0     3.64s     <- was 133,332
    diskdf.sigmaR2                    0     0.25s
    Potential.mass                    2     0.53s
    Potential.surfdens                4     1.51s
    isoHernq.vmomentdensity           4     3.25s

The ranking section printed nothing because there is nothing to rank -- the
maximum anywhere is **4**. At 178 us per crossing that is 0.7 ms, i.e. noise.

Two things this establishes that the hand-picked sweep could not:

1. **`diskdf.oortA` is now 0, not merely smaller.** The fix removes the hot
   boundary rather than trimming it. That is a stronger statement than the
   4.40 s / 4.09 s timings, which could in principle have come from a cheaper
   boundary rather than no boundary.
2. **The 133k site was singular.** Four orders of magnitude separate it from
   everything else measured. There is no second one hiding behind a call site I
   failed to guess, at least across these five workloads.

Still not a proof of absence -- five workloads, and the instrumentation only
sees `coerce_coords`, so a boundary that skips it would be invisible. But it is
evidence of a different kind than "I checked the places I thought of".

### 2026-08-07 — productized the boundary detector (appendices/boundary_census.py)

I had written the `coerce_coords` counter ad-hoc three times today, so it is now
a script with the reasoning attached. Verified end-to-end:

    diskdf.oortA                              0     3.95s
    diskdf.sigmaR2                            0     0.28s
    Potential.mass                            2     0.54s
    Potential.vesc                           10     0.22s
    isoHernquistdf.vmomentdensity             4     3.05s
    no workload reached 1000 crossings (max 22)     exit 0

Design choices worth stating:

* **Exit code 1 above 1000 crossings**, so it can gate rather than just inform.
  1000 is three orders below diskdf's 133,332 and two above the healthy max
  seen (22) -- a wide gap on both sides, which is what makes the threshold safe.
* **The docstring says the wall-clock column is not the finding.** Every time I
  ran this by hand the timings screamed (sub-ms numpy vs first-call jax compile)
  and meant nothing. A tool that prints a misleading number next to the real one
  needs to say which is which, or the next reader repeats my mistake.
* **Caller attribution walks out of `galpy/backend/` frames** so crossings are
  blamed on the code that caused them, not on the boundary itself. It currently
  lands on `util/conversion.py:wrapper` (the units decorator, one frame further
  out than ideal) -- honest but coarse; the workload column is the useful axis
  today.
* Caveats are in the module docstring, not just here: only `coerce_coords` is
  visible, the workloads are a sample, and without the C extension the timings
  are meaningless.

This is what task #200 ("boundary-count column in the census") was really
asking for, arrived at from the other direction -- I needed the detector to
diagnose my own regression, and the detector is the deliverable.

  a routine CI shard 2.8x while staying green, not just breaking traced tests.
  And I removed a "Pdf.3 will remove this pin" claim after checking: the
  quadrature is already migrated and differentiable.

  values), with provenance *and* a distinguishing grep in each -- because three

### 2026-08-07 — decomposing the forced-backend per-call cost (advances #79)

    numpy evaluateRforces           12.1 us/call
    forced-jax evaluateRforces    1031.8 us/call   (85x)
    boundary crossings per call        3
    x 178.2 us/crossing              534.6 us      (51.8% of the forced cost)
    remainder                        497.2 us      (48.2%)

**About half the per-call backend overhead is the `@backend_input` boundary**,
not the jax work. I would have guessed a few percent.

**Two honesty notes on this number.**

*It is an estimate, not a measurement.* 178.2 us/crossing was measured on
`surfaceSigmaProfile.surfacemass` (one scalar coord); `evaluateRforces` crosses
with R, z and possibly phi/t, so its crossings may not cost the same. The
**3 crossings** are counted directly; the 534.6 us is 3 x an imported constant.
Treat 52% as "boundary is roughly half", not as 51.8%.

*It does not refute task #79's "~5 ms".* That was a different potential under
different conditions; I measured MiyamotoNagai at 1.03 ms. Different setups,
both plausibly right -- I am adding structure to #79, not correcting it.

**The interesting number is 3.** One force evaluation crossing the boundary
three times is worth understanding before optimising anything: if two of those
are redundant re-coercions of already-coerced coords, that is ~35% of the
per-call overhead available without touching any jax code. `boundary_census.py`
already attributes crossings to callers, so the next step is a per-crossing
breakdown of a single force call rather than a whole-workload count.

### 2026-08-08 — the "3 crossings" lead: real, and NOT worth optimising

Traced where the 3 crossings in one `evaluateRforces` come from. All three are
the same site, once per coordinate:

    [1] coords=['float64']   from potential/Potential.py:wrapper:123
    [2] coords=['float64']   from potential/Potential.py:wrapper:123
    [3] coords=['float']     from potential/Potential.py:wrapper:123

R, z, and an injected scalar default. Mechanism confirmed in the source:
`galpy/backend/_input.py:93` does `(out,) = coerce_coords(xp, val)` -- **one call
per coordinate**, even though `coerce_coords` takes varargs and could take all
three at once.

That looks exactly like a free win, so I measured it before proposing it:

    3 separate coerce_coords calls : 262.5 us
    1 batched coerce_coords(a,b,c) : 251.6 us
    saving                         :  10.9 us  (4%)

**4%.** The per-call overhead is nearly nothing; the cost is the per-coord
`asarray_on_device` jax dispatch, which batching cannot remove -- three scalars
still become three device arrays. Refactoring the decorator's coercion loop
would buy 4% of half the per-call cost, i.e. ~2% of a force call, in exchange
for touching the boundary every migrated potential depends on. Not worth it.

Recording it as a **closed** avenue rather than an open TODO, because the shape
of it ("N redundant-looking calls where 1 would do") is exactly the kind of
thing I would rediscover in three weeks and spend a PR on. The real lever
remains what #79 already says: stop crossing per-scalar, i.e. vectorize at a
higher level.

    #1269  149 pending / 2 pass

### A. Tolerances (need a call, not a fix)

### B. Pre-existing numpy defects (predate the backend work, mine to fix only if you want them fixed)

3. **`AnyAxisym._R2deriv` at z=0** (task #203) — wrong by up to **3.3e-6** at

4. **`RazorThinExponentialDiskPotential.Rforce`** (task #206) — wrong by up to

### C. Design decisions

5. **AnyAxisym traced z-discontinuity** (task #207, from #1259). The fix is to
   **continuity, not accuracy**, and the quadrature change plus the test
   recalibration have to land together — which is why I did not do it solo.
6. **Slow-skip inheritance** (task #194). Tracing can make a slow test
   *runnable* (streamTrack is the counterexample), so `-jit` inheriting the
   eager slow-skip list is not always right.
7. **The 4 AnyAxisym / 2 units traced-ledger entries** are by-design, not
   defects: GL is used on the backend path so gradients exist, and it cannot
   resolve the a=R principal value or the z=0 Hadamard 2nd derivative; a
   units-based density strips a tracer to numpy by construction. They stay
   unless you want the design changed.
8. **[added 2026-08-08] Internals calling the DECORATED public evaluators —
   scope: three fixes or a convention?** A `@backend_input` entry point costs
   ~178 us per call under a forced backend. Harmless at a few calls, ruinous
   inside a loop. Found and measured three:

       planar adapter `_evaluate`          989 -> 5     (PR #1271, gates green)
       vertical adapter `_evaluate`       1708 -> 244   (held, gates green)
       actionAngleVertical `f` closure     238           (task #210, not started)

   An AST scan finds **96 internal call sites across 17 files** that use a
   decorated public evaluator where an undecorated inner already exists. But 96
   is a population, not a defect count — only *loop-resident* sites can hurt.
   Classifying them by syntactic context:

       inside a for/while/comprehension     27
       inside a nested def/lambda            7   (closures given to root-finders)
       straight-line, called once           62   <- harmless at ~178 us
       ------------------------------------------
       AT RISK                              34

   concentrated in exactly the modules whose consumers are loops:

       actionAngleVertical.py         16
       actionAngleVerticalInverse.py   5
       orbit/Orbits.py                 5
       potential/interpRZPotential.py  3
       constantbetadf / streamgapdf / streamspraydf / Potential.py   1 each

   **Caveat, stated: loop-residency is syntax, not measurement.** A call inside a
   `for` that runs twice costs nothing. So 34 is an upper bound on *candidates*;
   3 are measured hot, the other 31 are unmeasured. I am not claiming 34 defects.

   **RESOLVED BY MEASUREMENT, 2026-08-08 — my recommendation is now "four fixes,
   no sweep".** I stopped guessing and censused 27 previously-unmeasured
   workloads (potential root-finders, orbit derived quantities, two more AA
   families, five more DFs, streams), then a second pass over the module families
   the first sweep never reached (interpRZPotential, SCF, Ellipsoidal, Composite,
   ChandrasekharDynamicalFriction). Result: the cost is **concentrated**, and one
   more hot site exists:

       aAAdiabatic.actions   4166 -> 251 (#1271+#1272) -> 9 (#210)   never targeted, 460x
       interpRZPotential     30603 at galpy's DEFAULT 101x101 grid   <- 4th site (#211)
       all 38 other workloads              <= 153

   `interpRZPotential.__init__` builds grids with nested `for ii: for jj:` loops
   calling the decorated evaluator once per point; crossings are exactly linear
   in grid points (10.00/point over four grid sizes), which is why a toy 6x4 grid
   scores a harmless 240 and hides it. In wall-clock, for the default grid:

       numpy       0.19 s
       forced jax  7.76 s   (40.2x)
       of which    5.45 s   is boundary (30603 x 178 us) -- 70% of the total

   so #211 recovers about 70% of that slowdown.

   → **Question, now much narrower: land the four measured fixes and skip the
   sweep?** That is what I recommend — the candidates are mostly cold and the hot
   ones share a handful of root causes. Status as of 2026-08-08:

       #1271  planar adapters          MERGED  f1bb9f83
       #1272  vertical adapters        MERGED  7418aed5
       #1273  actionAngleVertical      OPEN, audited, CI running
       #211   interpRZPotential        patch written + measured, needs you

   **#211 needs less than I first said.** I originally flagged "add the 4 missing
   undecorated inners" as a decision. Measured afterwards: the **default** case
   needs none of them — `interpPot`/`interpRforce` go 30603 -> 0 using the
   already-existing `_evaluatePotentials`/`_evaluateRforces` (3 call sites,
   9.69 s -> 4.92 s, grid sha256 unchanged). Only `interpDens` / `interpR2deriv` /
   `interpvcirc` would need `_evaluateR2derivs` / `_evaluatez2derivs` /
   `_evaluateRzderivs` / `_evaluateDensities`, which do not exist. So it splits
   into a small no-decision part and an optional follow-up — and it must land
   **after** #212 (item 9), which touches the same call sites.

   **There is a second design I did not take, and you may prefer it.** Fixing
   #211 by *vectorizing* the grid build (evaluate the meshgrid in one call)
   keeps the **decorated** evaluator, so units behaviour is unchanged — which
   makes it strictly byte-identical, needing **no decision from you at all**,
   while taking crossings to O(1) and speeding the numpy path too. I did not
   start it because not every potential is array-safe on that path
   (`AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDisk`'s array opt-out is deliberate), so it needs a
   per-potential fallback — a larger design change than swapping three calls,
   and not one to land unilaterally while you are away. Flagging it because it
   is the better end state if you want the loop gone rather than just the
   coercion.

9. **[added 2026-08-08] `interpRZPotential` + units is a REAL pre-existing numpy
   bug — fix is written and tested, needs your target-branch call** (task #212).
   Verified on `origin/main` (cd81fbed), so not something feat/backends did.
   Building it from a potential with `ro`/`vo` set stores PHYSICAL values in the
   grids while the interpolator is queried in internal units:

       use_c=False  potential x48400 (vo^2)   Rforce x6.1874 (force_in_kmsMyr)
       use_c=True   potential ok, Rforce ok   (C path works internally)
       ANY use_c    dens x0.1758  R2deriv x790.99  epifreq/verticalfreq x28.12
                    (those grids have no C implementation -> always the Python loop)

   `interpRZPotential` exists for fast orbit integration, so this is wrong forces
   -> wrong orbits, silently. 284 test references, **none** passing `ro=`/`vo=`,
   which is why it survived.

   Fix is committed locally on `fix/interprz-units` (branch off main, `ff87e75e`,
   C ext built): `use_physical=False` at all 37 call sites, which restores the
   internal value bit-for-bit for all seven quantities. **It needs no
   byte-identity waiver** — on a unitless potential the flag is a no-op, verified
   bit-for-bit, so the only behaviour that changes is the path that was already
   wrong. New regression test fails without it, passes with it;
   `test_interp_potential.py` 41 passed.

   → **Question: land on `main` (it is a main bug) or on `feat/backends`?**
   Both branches carry the defect.

   **Now open as DRAFT PR #1274 against `main`** (2026-08-08, after #1273
   merged freed a slot). Draft, so I cannot merge it — it is there to be
   reviewable and CI-validated instead of sitting on a local branch you would
   have to reconstruct. Retarget to feat/backends if you prefer.

### 2026-08-08 — #125: the 1028.6 s entry is STALE. The test takes 21.9 s.

Profiled `test_king_sigmar` itself under forced jax, after four targeted probes

        backend/interpolate.eval_ppoly  7.01 s cum (666 calls)
        _sample_v                 3.26 s cum

**21.9 s, not 1028.6 s.** My probes were right and the *ledger entry* was wrong —
I spent the last few wakes hunting for a thousand seconds that no longer exist.

Two things worth separating:

*What I got right.* The probes said ~20 s and the truth is 21.9 s. Refusing to
nominate a suspect when the numbers did not add up was correct: there was no
suspect to find, and any story I invented would have been fiction fitted to a
stale premise.

*What I got wrong.* I never questioned the 1028.6 s itself. It came from the
ledger comment, I treated it as ground truth for four probes, and the whole
"where does the time go" investigation presupposed it. The same staleness I have
spent all session finding in slow-skip entries was sitting in the number driving
my search. **A measurement someone else recorded is evidence about the past, not
the present** -- exactly what [[ledger-staleness-sweep-from-artifacts]] exists
for, applied to everything except the number I was reasoning from.

**Consequence for #125:** its premise ("vectorize jeans/KingPotential" to make
this fast enough) is void. `jeans.sigmar` is already faster on jax than numpy
(0.038 s vs 0.099 s), and the test fits inside the 300 s cap with a 14x margin.

### 2026-08-08 — census blind spot closed; found a ~1000-crossing site in actionAngleSpherical

The detector I built for the #1261 class only sampled **df and potential**
workloads. So a hot-boundary site anywhere in actionAngle, qdf, or orbit was
invisible to it — the detector had the same shape of gap as the test suite it
was meant to compensate for. Added 7 workloads across those three areas.

The first run found one immediately:

    aAStaeckel.actionsFreqs        0 crossings     <- vectorized
    aASpherical.actions          989
    aASpherical.actionsFreqs    1023               <- above HOT
    qdf.density / sigmaR2      64 / 84
    Orbit.E / L                 4 / 0

980+ of them come from a single site, `planarPotential.py:_evaluate`:
`actionAngleSpherical` runs a scipy quadrature loop that evaluates the potential
~1000 times per call, one scalar boundary crossing each (~0.18 s of pure
boundary at the measured 178 us). **The Staeckel comparison is what makes this a
finding rather than a number** — same family, same job, vectorized, scores 0.

This confirms pending task **#88** ("unify actionAngleSpherical, drop the scipy
loop") which until now was justified on speed/DRY grounds without a measurement.

**Checked the environment before believing it.** The first run was in a worktree
with no C extension and jax x64 off; both can change dispatch, so the count could
have been a fallback artifact ([[worktree-missing-c-ext-fakes-passes]]). Re-ran
in a C-ext-loaded checkout with x64 on and got the same 989/1023. Also added the
x64 config to the script itself, since silently measuring float32 measures a
configuration nobody ships.

**Design choice: `KNOWN_HOT`.** Adding a genuinely-hot workload would make the
script exit 1 forever, and a permanently-red detector stops being a signal. So
known sites print and are labelled with their tracking item but do not fail the
run; only a *new* hot workload does. Deleting the entry is how a fix gets locked
in. Also fixed a summary line that compared unlike things — it reported the max
per-*caller* total ("max 1968") against a per-*workload* threshold, which read as

### 2026-08-08 — #88 re-diagnosed: it is the eager bisection, and it is backend-only

Decomposed the 989 crossings by sub-step:

    _setup_backend                4
    _calc_rperi_rap_backend     981     <- essentially all of it
    _calc_jr_backend              4
    _calc_or_op_backend           8

So the hot site is the **rperi/rap root-find**, not the quadrature. The shared
`bisect_root` runs a plain Python for-loop when eager — it only becomes a
`lax.fori_loop` under tracing ([[jit-trace-mode]], task #105) — and each
iteration re-enters the decorated potential, paying the ~178 us boundary again.

**This changes what task #88 is.** The task was filed as "drop the scipy loop,
vectorize numpy — relaxes byte-identity", and I had been treating it as blocked
on Jo for that reason. Reading the code says otherwise:

    elif xp is not numpy:  return self._actionsFreqs_backend(...)   <- forced jax
    else:                  ... numpy scalar loop ...                <- untouched

numpy and backend are already *separate branches*, and `_actionsFreqs_backend`
is already vectorised (`xp.where`, no Python loop over orbits). The measured
cost lives entirely in the backend branch, so a fix there **cannot** perturb
numpy and needs no byte-identity waiver. It is landable without a sign-off.

The shape of the fix is the #1268 lesson applied one level down: the leaf wants
its coercion done **once by its caller**, so the bisection should call an
undecorated inner evaluator with already-coerced arrays rather than re-crossing
per iteration ([[backend-kernel-decorator]]).

Two things I would have got wrong by reasoning instead of measuring: the
quadrature was the obvious suspect and is clean (4 and 8), and the task's own
framing pointed at numpy, which is not involved at all.

Not starting the implementation this wake — it wants tests and a free slot.

starts from the right line.

### 2026-08-08 — #88 design settled (implementation next wake)

Traced the crossing to its source. Per bisection iteration:

    _radicand -> _evaluateplanarPotentials -> <adapter>._evaluate
              -> Potential.__call__   @potential_physical_input
                                      @backend_input("R","phi","t")   <- crosses

**The trap I nearly walked into.** The obvious fix is "make `_radicand` use an
undecorated evaluator" — but `_radicand`'s own docstring says it is *shared by
the numpy integrands (xp=numpy, scalar r) and the backend panels*, and is
"byte-identical on numpy". Editing it would silently change the numpy path,
which is the one thing this whole branch must not do. The finding being
backend-only does not make every fix backend-only.

**Design that keeps both properties.** Parameterise rather than duplicate:

    _radicand(xp, r, E, L, pot, evaluate=_evaluateplanarPotentials)

* numpy callers pass nothing -> identical call, byte-identity preserved by
  construction (not by testing afterwards);
* `_calc_rperi_rap_backend` passes an evaluator that skips the decorator, with
  the coercion hoisted **once** outside the loop.

A second near-copy of `_radicand` would have been the easy route and exactly the
duplication the standing audit rule forbids — a general-purpose helper wants one
implementation, not a backend twin ([[audit-placement-and-duplication]]).

Expected effect: ~981 -> single digits for `_calc_rperi_rap_backend`, removing
~0.18 s of pure boundary per `actionsFreqs` call, eager only (traced already
rolls into `lax.fori_loop`). The census entry is the acceptance test — deleting
the `KNOWN_HOT` line is how the fix gets locked in.

Deliberately NOT implementing this wake: two jobs in flight, and this touches a
shared helper on a byte-identity-critical path. It wants its own slot, a
numpy-hash A/B across the touched calls, and forced-backend runs on both arms.

### 2026-08-08 — CORRECTION: the aASpherical cost is NOT eager-only, and 74% of it is plain floats

Went to verify the "eager only (traced already rolls into `lax.fori_loop`)" line
I wrote last entry. It is **wrong**, and the check that found it also found
something better.

First probe was itself invalid: I called `_calc_rperi_rap_backend` directly,
which bypasses the `@backend_input` boundary — and the boundary is exactly where
jit is applied ([[jit-trace-mode]]). Measuring an internal for a boundary
property measures nothing. Re-ran through the public `actionsFreqs`, and
confirmed tracing positively (by the appearance of tracer objects) rather than
trusting the mode flag:

    mode=off   crossings=1023   args: float 754, ArrayImpl 266, JVPTracer 2
    mode=jax   crossings=1023   args: float 754, ArrayImpl 248, DynamicJaxprTracer 18

Tracing IS active in the second row, and the crossing count is **identical**. So
this cost lands on the traced suite too, not just eager. The correction matters:
it widens who pays.

**The better finding: 754 of 1023 crossings (74%) carry a plain Python `float`,
not a backend array.** That is the same scalar-round-trip class as #208/#1261 —
a plain scalar resolving onto the forced backend, coerced in and cast back. The
`@backend_input("R","phi","t")` sites declare `t`, whose default is the literal
`0.0`, so a constant is being marshalled across the boundary on most calls.

That is potentially library-wide, not an actionAngleSpherical quirk — but I am
explicitly NOT generalising from one call site this time. "Every decorated
potential call coerces its default t" is a hypothesis with an obvious test
(census the arg types across all 15 workloads), and the last four times I
reasoned instead of measuring on this exact class of question I was wrong.

Method note worth keeping: `set_jit("jax")` returning without error does not
mean the call was traced. Positive evidence is a tracer object showing up in the
data. Same family of error as [[use-is-a-context-manager]] — the API call
succeeded and did nothing.

### 2026-08-08 — the plain-float hypothesis: ubiquitous, but NOT a general problem

Ran the test I said I would rather than generalising from one call site. Arg
types across all 15 census workloads under forced jax:

    Potential.mass                2 crossings   100% scalar
    isoHernquistdf.sigmar         4             100% scalar
    Potential.surfdens            4             100% scalar
    Potential.vesc               10              70% scalar
    aASpherical.actions         989              75% scalar
    aASpherical.actionsFreqs   1023              74% scalar
    qdf.density / sigmaR2     64 / 84         23% / 26% scalar
    Orbit.E                       4               0% scalar

**Refuted, in the way that matters.** Scalar-carrying crossings are everywhere —
several sites are 100% scalar — and they are harmless, because those sites cross
2-4 times total. The scalar *share* is not the discriminator; the crossing
*count* is. A 100%-scalar site at 4 crossings costs ~0.7 ms and nobody cares.

So "the decorator marshals a constant `t=0.0` across the boundary on most calls"
is a true description of the library and **not** a performance finding. Had I
written it up from the aASpherical numbers alone — which is exactly what the
74% invited — I would have opened a library-wide work item chasing something
that costs nothing at 4 crossings per call.

What survives: `actionAngleSpherical` is hot because it crosses ~1000 times, and
the 74% figure is useful only as a *hint for the fix* (the constant `t`/`phi` can
be hoisted out of the loop alongside the real coercion), not as a finding of its
own.

This is the third time today the same discipline paid: the ComplexWarnings were
main's, the "eager-only" claim was wrong, and now the scalar share is a
non-finding. In each case the cheap check was available and the plausible story
was wrong.

### 2026-08-08 — #88 scope correction #2: the leaf is a class-wide convention, not a one-liner

Started implementing the `_radicand(evaluate=...)` design and it is **aimed at
the wrong layer**. Following the chain properly:

    _radicand -> _evaluateplanarPotentials(pot, r)
                    -> Pot._call_nodecorator(...)     <- ALREADY undecorated
                 ...
    planarPotentialFromRZPotential._evaluate
                    -> self._Pot(R, 0.0, t=t, use_physical=False)   <- THE crossing

`_evaluateplanarPotentials` is already the no-decorator path, so parameterising
`_radicand` would have bought nothing. The crossing is one level deeper, where
the planar *adapter* calls the decorated 3D public API.

And it is not one call site. The whole adapter class does this:

    _evaluate  -> self._Pot(R, 0.0, t=t, use_physical=False)
    _Rforce    -> self._Pot.Rforce(R, 0.0, t=t, use_physical=False)
    _R2deriv   -> self._Pot.R2deriv(R, 0.0, t=t, use_physical=False)

So "call the undecorated inner" is a **class-wide convention change**, touching
the adapters that sit under essentially every planar consumer in the library —
high blast radius, on a path where numpy must stay byte-identical.

**Not starting that at the tail of a long session with #1270's CI mid-flight.**
This is the second scope correction on #88 today (first: no byte-identity waiver
needed; now: not a one-liner). Both came from reading the code instead of
trusting the previous note — including my own from an hour earlier.

The measurement stands and is what makes it worth doing: 1023 crossings/call on
jax, 1031 on torch, ~0.18 s of pure boundary, and `aAStaeckel` at 0 proving it

Both open gaps resolved, and the scope shrank again — in the good direction.

**Gap 2 (R2deriv) — resolved structurally.** There is no `_evaluateR2derivs`;
only `_evaluatePotentials`, `_evaluateRforces`, `_evaluatephitorques`,
`_evaluatezforces` have undecorated inners. But `_R2deriv` is not on the hot
path either (980 of the crossings are `_evaluate`, 52 `_Rforce`, R2deriv absent).

whole class. Third scope revision on #88 today, and the first that makes it
smaller.

**Gap 1 (composites) — resolved, on the second attempt.** `_evaluatePotentials`
rejects a raw list (`'list' object has no attribute '_call_nodecorator'`); lists
are converted to a composite by the decorator before reaching an adapter, and
`toPlanarPotential(MWPotential2014)` is a single `planarCompositePotential` whose
`_potlist` holds the real adapters. Descending into it:

    PowerSphericalPotentialwCutoff  __call__ / Rforce   BIT-IDENTICAL
    MiyamotoNagaiPotential          __call__ / Rforce   BIT-IDENTICAL
    NFWPotential                    __call__ / Rforce   BIT-IDENTICAL
    comparisons actually run: 6

**The thing worth recording is the mistake, which I made twice in a row.** First
the MW14 row compared the inner against itself via an `isinstance(P, list)`
fallback. Then the composite loop did `P = getattr(a, "_Pot", None); if P is
None: continue` on an object that has no `_Pot` — **zero iterations**, and `ok`
stayed `True` from its initialiser. Both printed a confident `True`. Neither
tested anything.

A boolean initialised to `True` and only ever ANDed reports success when the loop
body never runs. The fix is to **count the comparisons and assert the count**,
which is what the final run does (`comparisons actually run: 6`). Same family as
[[assertion-comparison-outside-reducer]]: the assertion passed while measuring
the wrong thing — here, nothing at all.

### 2026-08-08 — sizing the pattern: 96 internal sites, but that is NOT 96 bugs

Three instances in one day justified asking how large the class is. AST scan of
`galpy/` for calls to a **decorated public evaluator that has an undecorated
inner** (9 such pairs exist):

    96 internal call sites across 17 files

    19  actionAngle/actionAngleVertical.py         evaluatelinearPotentials
    15  actionAngle/actionAngleVerticalInverse.py  evaluatelinear{Potentials,Forces}
    13  potential/Potential.py                     evaluateplanar* / evaluate*
    12  orbit/Orbits.py                            evaluate{planar,,linear}Potentials
     9  potential/interpRZPotential.py             evaluate{Potentials,Rforces,zforces}
     6  snapshot/directnbody.py                    six different ones
     5  df/streamspraydf.py, 5 MovingObjectPotential, 4 streamgapdf, ...

**96 is a population, not a defect count, and I am not going to present it as
one.** A decorated call costs ~178 us; that is invisible at a handful of calls
and catastrophic inside a bisection. The discriminator is *called-in-a-loop*, not
*exists* — the same correction I had to make this morning when 74%-scalar looked
like a finding and turned out to be ubiquitous and harmless. Of these 96, exactly
three are measured hot so far (planar `_evaluate`, vertical `_evaluate`,
`actionAngleVertical:f`); the rest are unmeasured, and most are surely fine.

What the number is good for: it tells Jo the class is **structural**, not three
coincidences, and that a decision is needed on scope — three targeted fixes
versus a convention ("internals call the inner; the decorated entry is for
users"). That is a design call about the library's shape, so it goes in the
AWAITING JO list rather than getting decided here.

The concentration in the two `actionAngleVertical*` files (34 of 96) is also
suggestive: those are the modules whose consumers are loops by construction.

[[codecov-project-blocks-via-all-clear]]. Nothing is wrong with the PR.

**This is the case where "re-running will not help" inverts.** That rule applies
to a *real* coverage drop, where the fix is to cover lines. For an aggregator
that raced a heal, re-running IS the fix. The discriminator is codecov's
**current** state, which is why I read it before touching anything — had I
treated a failed all-clear as evidence of a broken PR, the next move would have
been rebasing or hunting a nonexistent coverage gap.

closure. That, plus censusing 40 workloads, is why my recommendation on item 8 is
**four targeted fixes, not a 34-site convention sweep**.

**Open / staged:** #1272 (vertical adapters, 1708 -> 244; gates green, guard
A/B-verified). #210 implemented behind it (-244 more, byte-identical, ordering
constraint proven).

### The arc that mattered

A regression I introduced yesterday (#1261) was **found by a tool I built for
exactly that purpose**, then closed within twelve hours. Chasing its residual
turned up a whole defect class: `@backend_input` costs ~178 us per crossing, and
internal loops were calling *decorated* entry points once per iteration.

    planar adapter   989 -> 5     merged
    vertical adapter 1708 -> 244  in review
    AA closure       -244         implemented

Each fix is numpy-byte-identical by sha256 A/B, each carries a regression guard
with a **negative control**, and each guard was proven to *fail without the fix*.

### What the day actually taught

Nearly every real finding came from measuring something I could have assumed:

* the `@backend_input` cost is **forced-backend**, not jit — so it degrades
  routine CI, not just the traced suite (I had it backwards and wrote it down);
* "74% of crossings are plain scalars" is **ubiquitous and harmless** — the
  crossing *count* is the discriminator, not the scalar share;
* the 96 decorated-entry call sites are **34 loop-resident candidates**, of which
  **3 are measured** — a population is not a defect count;
* `actionAngleVertical`'s guard proved an **ordering constraint git cannot see**:
  disjoint files, 0 merge conflicts, and still dependent *in measurement*.

And a run of self-caught tooling errors, each of which would have produced a
confident wrong number: two vacuous `ok &= ...` loops over empty iterations; a
diff parser counting PR-body text; `gh pr diff --patch` emitting the commit
series rather than the net diff; a mislabelled A/B whose "develop" arm was
another branch with a different C-ext state; and a C-ext probe that reported
`True` from outside the worktree and `False` from inside.

**The pattern worth keeping:** a number that matches expectation is not
self-validating. Every one of those was caught by checking *what was compared*,
not by doubting the result.

I was about to hand Jo "the defect is concentrated; three fixes cover it".
Before doing that I checked the claim's own scope, because a *workload* sweep
only covers sites its workloads reach. A static AST scan of every call to a
``@backend_input``-decorated entry point from inside a loop or nested closure
found **99** sites (54 decorated entry points) — and my 27-workload sweep had
touched **none** in `interpRZPotential`, `SCFPotential`, `EllipsoidalPotential`,
`CompositePotential`, or `ChandrasekharDynamicalFrictionForce`.

So I censused those families. Twelve of thirteen were cold (≤ 19). The
thirteenth was not, and the first measurement nearly hid it:

    grid      points   crossings   per-point
    6x4           24         240       10.00
    12x8          96         960       10.00
    24x16        384        3840       10.00
    48x32       1536       15360       10.00

Exactly linear. My toy 6x4 grid scored a harmless 240 — so I sized it by
galpy's own default instead (`rgrid=(log 0.01, log 20, 101)`,
`zgrid=(0,1,101)`):

    interpRZPotential(interpPot=True)   DEFAULT 101x101   30603 crossings
    ... plus interpDens=True                             ~102000

`__init__` builds its grids with nested `for ii: for jj:` loops calling the
**decorated** `evaluatePotentials` once per grid point (L270-272, same shape at
295/320/348/370/392/414, plus per-r comprehensions at 449/470/493/525). Same
defect as #1271/#1272/#210, at the second-largest scale measured anywhere —
behind only the diskdf case (133,332) that started this whole thread.

**The lesson is about parameter choice, not about interpRZPotential.** A
"measured" number is only as good as the size you measured it at; a linear-in-N
cost measured at toy N reads as clean. I only caught it because 168 crossings
for a grid build looked too cheap for what the code was obviously doing.

**four** fixes, not three. #211 filed; not started (two-PR limit — #1272 open,

### 2026-08-08 — chasing #211 uncovered a real numpy bug: interpRZPotential + units

Before writing the #211 fix I checked one risk: the grid loops call
`evaluatePotentials(...)` **without** `use_physical=False`, so swapping to the
undecorated inner might change behaviour. It does — and the reason is a
pre-existing bug, not a subtlety of my change.

    evaluatePotentials(mp_with_ro_vo, 1.1, 0.2)   -> -55040.799   (PHYSICAL)
    _evaluatePotentials(same)                     ->      -1.1372 (internal)

So when `_origPot` has ro/vo set, the grid stores **physical** values while the
interpolator is queried in internal units. End to end (ratio interp/direct,
both `use_physical=False`):

    use_c=False   potential  x48400.0169  == vo^2
                  Rforce     x6.1874      == conversion.force_in_kmsMyr(220,8)
    use_c=True    potential  x1.0000  ok  (C path works in internal units)
                  Rforce     x1.0000  ok

The C path is fine, which would make this look narrow — except the quantities
with **no C grid implementation** always take the Python loop and are wrong
regardless:

    use_c=True    dens x0.1758   R2deriv x790.99   epifreq/verticalfreq x28.12

`interpRZPotential` exists for fast orbit integration, so wrong forces mean
wrong orbits, silently. 284 test references, **none** passing `ro=`/`vo=` —
the units path is completely uncovered, which is why it survived.

Same root cause as #211 (loops call the decorated public API), so **one change
fixes both**: ~30603 crossings AND the units bug. That makes #211
**non-byte-identical on the numpy path** for units-set potentials — in the
direction of correctness, but the standing rule is to surface any such change,
so it needs Jo. Filed #212.

Worth noting how this surfaced: not by auditing units, but by asking "why does
this call site omit `use_physical=False` when #210's did not?" The
inconsistency was the tell.

**Verified pre-existing.** I had written "present on main" in #212 from reasoning,
having measured only on develop+#1272. Checked it properly against
`origin/main` (cd81fbed) — identical ratios to the digit:

    MAIN  potential(use_c=F)  x48400.016934
    MAIN  dens                x0.175847
    MAIN  R2deriv             x790.994398
    MAIN  epifreq             x28.124585

So it is genuinely a main bug, not something feat/backends introduced. Bonus
confirmation: that worktree has **no C extension**, yet its dens/R2deriv/epifreq
ratios match evdirect's `use_c=True` numbers exactly — independent evidence that
those three grids never use the C path, which is what makes them wrong
regardless of `use_c`.

### 2026-08-08 — #211 and #212 are separable, and #212 needs no byte-identity waiver

I had bundled these: "one change fixes both". Measuring the fix options split
them cleanly, and the split makes #212 much easier to approve.

**Only 3 of the 7 grid quantities have an undecorated inner.**
`_evaluatePotentials` / `_evaluateRforces` / `_evaluatezforces` exist;
`_evaluateR2derivs`, `_evaluatez2derivs`, `_evaluateRzderivs`,
`_evaluateDensities` do **not**. (Consistent with #1272, where `_force2deriv`
had to keep `.z2deriv` for exactly this reason and became the guard's negative
control.) So the undecorate-the-call fix cannot cover the grid build alone.

**But `use_physical=False` fixes the units bug for all seven, bit-for-bit.**
Checked each against the unitless potential as ground truth over 9 (R,z)
points: all seven return the exact internal value. And for a unitless potential
the flag is a no-op — verified bit-identical — so the change touches *nothing*
except the currently-wrong path.

That reframes the decision I sent Jo. It is not "accept a non-byte-identical
numpy change to get a perf win". It is:

  #212  units bugfix, byte-identical except where it repairs a bug,
        self-contained, belongs on main, lands independently
  #211  boundary crossings, needs 4 new undecorated inners, feat/backends,
        NOT blocked by #212

**Process note.** My first probe reported all seven inners "MISSING" — wrong.
`import galpy.potential.Potential as P` binds the re-exported **class**, because
`potential/__init__.py` does `from .Potential import Potential` and the
attribute shadows the submodule. I nearly logged "galpy has no undecorated
evaluators at all". The tell was that I had *already* imported
`_evaluatePotentials` from that module minutes earlier — a contradiction with my
own recent output, not with the docs. Fixed with `importlib.import_module`.

### 2026-08-08 — separability of #211/#212 CONFIRMED (and a hybrid-import trap)

I told Jo the two are separable. Verified rather than left asserted, from both
directions:

**1. `use_physical=False` does not bypass the boundary.** On feat/backends,
20 calls to `evaluatePotentials`:

    without use_physical      -> 60 crossings
    with use_physical=False   -> 60 crossings

The flag skips the *units* decorator, not `@backend_input`. So #212's fix leaves
the crossing count untouched and #211 is still needed in full.

**2. On main the question does not arise** — `galpy/backend/` does not exist
there, so there is no boundary to cross.

Point 2 arrived as a crash, and the crash is worth recording. Running the census
in the `main` worktree spliced two checkouts into one import graph:

    galpy         = /var/tmp/units212/galpy/__init__.py    <- correct worktree
    galpy.backend = /var/tmp/streamtorch/galpy/backend/    <- a DIFFERENT checkout
    ImportError: cannot import name '_ARRAY_API_COMPAT_LOADED' ...

`galpy.__file__` was right; a *subpackage* the branch lacks silently came from
the editable install. This is a sharper version of
[[galpy-editable-install-import-shadow]]: provenance on the top-level package is
not sufficient. It crashed here, which was lucky — two close-enough checkouts
would splice silently and I would have measured a chimera. Memory updated.

The right reading is not "work around the import": if a probe needs a package
the branch under test does not have, the measurement is **inapplicable to that
branch**, and that is the answer.

### 2026-08-08 — #211 and #212 overlap: sequence them, do not pick one

Both patches modify the *same three* grid-build calls in
`interpRZPotential.py` (they sit at different line numbers only because
feat/backends adds ~105 lines earlier in the file):

    #211 (feat/backends, 6905c0a8)  @@ 269, 294, 319   -> undecorated inners
    #212 (main, cd81fbed)           @@ 246, 271, 296 (+ 34 more sites)

They are **complementary, not alternatives**, and each is insufficient alone:

* #212 alone does not remove a single boundary crossing — measured, 60 crossings
  with and without `use_physical=False` on 20 calls. The flag skips the units
  decorator, not `@backend_input`.
* #211 alone covers only 3 of the 7 quantities and none of the 22 off-grid
  fallbacks or 4 per-r helpers, so the units bug would survive in
  dens/R2deriv/z2deriv/Rzderiv/vcirc/dvcircdR/epifreq/verticalfreq.

**Recommended order: #212 first** (it is the correctness fix and belongs on
main), then #211 rebases on top and swaps its three sites from
`evaluatePotentials(..., use_physical=False)` to `_evaluatePotentials(...)`,
dropping the flag as redundant at those sites.

Worth flagging because handing over two patches to the same file without saying
this invites a merge that silently drops one of them.

### 2026-08-08 — jit gap-check on #1273: "no regression" for a weaker reason than I expected

The backend suite runs **eager** ([[eager-only-potential-gaps]]), and #1273 swaps
to undecorated inners while jit is applied *at* the decorated boundary — so
"does the traced path still work?" is a fair question about my own PR. Ran it:

    tests/test_backend_actionAngle.py --backend jax --jit -k vertical
        15 passed   (same 15 as eager)

Pass counts do not prove tracing though ([[jit-coverage-not-pass-counts]]), so I
demanded positive evidence — arg types seen at the inner:

    set_jit(off) -> {'ArrayImpl': 122, 'JVPTracer': 1}
    set_jit(jax) -> {'ArrayImpl': 122, 'JVPTracer': 1}

**No `DynamicJaxprTracer` in either mode.** So the honest conclusion is not
"tracing still works through the inner" — it is "**this path is not traced at
all**, in either mode, so there was no tracing for my change to remove."
`actionAngleVertical`'s public methods carry `physical_conversion_actionAngle`,
not `@backend_input`, so they were never a jit boundary. That also explains why
the eager and --jit runs are identical at 15 passed.

Weaker claim, but the true one. Had I stopped at "15 passed under --jit, traced
path fine", I would have published a verification that never happened — the same
shape as the `set_jit` returning-without-error trap in
[[measure-boundary-properties-at-the-boundary]].

### 2026-08-08 — specced the AnyAxisym port (#207) instead of attempting it

Jo's rebase is days out and the cherry-pick of `cd81fbed` is deliberately not in
#1275, so the residual is a **port**. Rather than start numerical-method surgery
on a physics kernel unsupervised, I specified it precisely — measurement is the
part that does not need review.

`zforce(1.0, z)` / thin-disk limit, on feat/backends-develop:

    1e-04  1.0001727682     1e-07  0.0000001728  COLLAPSED
    1e-05  1.0000172803     1e-08  0.0000000173
    1e-06  1.0000017281     1e-09  0.0000000017
                            1e-10  nan
                            1e-11  0.0

A **cliff** between 1e-6 and 1e-7, then a fall that is **linear in z** — and that
linearity names the mechanism without needing to read the quadrature: the
integrand's 1/((a-R)^2+z^2) peak has width ~|z| and contributes 1/|z|, which must
cancel the -4z prefactor to leave a finite limit. Step over the peak and the
integral goes to 0, so zforce goes to -4z*(finite) -> 0 proportional to z. Exactly
the observed pattern, and exactly what main's a = R + |z|t substitution prevents.

So the port is now a one-line design statement rather than an exploration: carry
main's substitution into the backend-native path, keep `ellipkm1` for the exact
complement, then re-run this sweep + the R2deriv/FD screen + the AnyAxisym
jit/grad tests. Written into task #207 with the numbers.

Also recorded there: #207 (this cliff, main is correct) is **distinct** from #203
(R2deriv ~3e-6 vs mpmath), which is present on BOTH branches and NOT fixed by
cd81fbed. Two separate items in the same file; easy to conflate.

#### #206 was mischaracterised, and re-measuring before filing caught it

I had it recorded as "Rforce wrong by up to 2.8e-3 at small |z|". Filing a public
issue forced a re-measure, and the shape is different:

    R=0.5  z=1e-6   rel 5.2e-03    <- quadrature branch
    R=1.0  z=1e-3   rel 8.3e-04    <- quadrature branch
    R=1.0  z=1e-2   rel 1.5e-06
    R=1.0  z=1e-1   rel 5.8e-12
    R=1.0  z=1e-7   rel 1.3e-07    <- CLOSED-FORM branch, below the switch

It is a **band**, 1e-6 ≲ |z| ≲ 1e-2, not a small-|z| limit. The closed form
below the `|z| < 1e-6` switch is *accurate*; the quadrature above it degrades as
z → 0. So `Rforce(1., 1e-7)` is more accurate than `Rforce(1., 1e-6)` — **the
switch hands over in the wrong direction**, which is a different and more
reportable defect than "wrong at small z", and 5.2e-3 is ~2x the number I had.

The same threshold appears at **four** sites in the file, so other methods
plausibly share it. I said so in the issue *and* said I had not checked them.

Filed: **gh#1276** (band) and **gh#1277** (`R2deriv`, peak 9.9e-6 at R=0.2 —
also higher than the 3.3e-6 I had recorded).

Both were re-verified on a real `main` checkout, not inferred from the
byte-identity invariant — and they returned values identical to `feat/backends`
to every printed digit, which re-confirms that invariant as a side effect.

Arbiter discipline per [[mpmath-quadosc-final-arbiter]]: the mpmath Hankel
reference was validated *per quantity* before use — against galpy's own
closed form at z=0 for `Rforce` (3.5e-15), and against FD-of-Hankel-`Rforce` for
`R2deriv` (11 digits). An unvalidated arbiter would have been the third
plausible-but-wrong number in this pair.

#### #207: the K-sweep refuted the panel-reach hypothesis in one run

Before porting main's fix I checked my own explanation. `_bk_split_quad` grades
dyadic panels toward a=R with `dmin = min(4|z|, R/2)` and `K=24` levels, and
`R·2^-24 ≈ 6e-8` — so "24 levels cannot reach the peak once |z| is small" was
a clean, plausible story that predicted the observed 1e-7 onset almost exactly.

It is wrong. K=24 / 40 / 60 give **identical** values at every z:

     z        K=24          K=40          K=60
     1e-06    1.000001728   1.000001728   1.000001728
     1e-07    0.000000173   0.000000173   0.000000173
     1e-09    0.000000002   0.000000002   0.000000002

The panels reach the peak; the integrand *there* is garbage. main's commit
message names the mechanism — `(a-R)^2+z^2` formed by **subtraction** cancels
catastrophically — and its fix threads `u = a-R` and `d2` analytically through
an `f(a, u, d2)` signature.

Cost of not checking: I would have "fixed" #207 by raising K, measured no
change, and looked for a second bug.

**The backend port comes out cleaner than main's.** main needs the `|z| < 1e-4·R`
threshold because `integrate.quad` picks its own nodes and cannot know the
offset. `_bk_split_quad` *places* its nodes at `R ± dk` with `dk` in closed
form — so it can pass the offset through analytically at every |z|: no
threshold, hence **no data-dependent branch**, hence natively traceable with no
`xp.where` evaluating both arms, and uniformly more accurate than main rather
than only below a cutoff.

### 2026-08-08 — #207: the bug I set out to port was in the other code path

Jo cleared #207 ("fix the backend"), so I went to port main's `cd81fbed`
substitution into `_bk_split_quad`. There was no backend bug of that kind.

**`_bk_dispatch` routes CONCRETE backend input to the numpy function.** Only a
tracer or a `requires_grad` tensor reaches the GL path:

```python
try:    Rf, zf = float(R), float(z)   # concrete -> scipy quad
except Exception: pass                 # tracer  -> in-backend GL
else:   return ...numpy_fn(Rf, zf)...
```

My probe passed plain `jnp.asarray` scalars. So every number I reported for
"the backend at small |z|" was **scipy's**, and the collapse below |z|~1e-6 is
the numpy defect (#189 / `cd81fbed`) that the rebase supplies for free.

This is exactly [[value-checks-cannot-see-numpy-fallback]], and I had already
written that memory. What should have stopped me a step earlier: I monkeypatched
`_bk_split_quad` and swept K over 24/40/60, and the outputs were **identical to
the last digit**. I read that as "the panels reach the peak, so the integrand
must be wrong there" — a coherent story that even predicted the observed onset.
The other reading, that the function was never called, was the right one. A
patch that changes nothing is evidence about *reachability* before it is
evidence about *behaviour*.

#### Measured under jit, the real defect is two decades lower

    |z|      dyadic K=24   geometric K=24     (fraction of the sheet limit)
    1e-08    1.000000017   1.000000017
    1e-10    1.005054471   0.999999993
    1e-12    0.054         1.000003514

So the GL path was already fine down to 1e-8 — better than numpy, which is
`nan` by 1e-10. The genuine bug is that the dyadic ladder
`dk = max(R*2**-k, dmin)` bottoms out at `R*2**-K`, so below `R*2**-K/4` the
innermost panel never reaches the peak.

#### The fix is smaller than the port would have been

Span **geometrically** from `R/2` to `dmin` rather than dyadically. Same K, so
the jit graph does not grow, and it resolves the peak at any |z|. No threshold,
no substitution, no `f(a, u, d2)` signature change — main needs all three only
because `integrate.quad` chooses its own nodes and cannot be told the offset,
while `_bk_split_quad` already *places* its nodes at `R ± dk`.

It also deletes the `xp.maximum` kink where the two arms crossed, so panel edges
are now smooth in R. That is load-bearing: the file already carries a test
recording that an earlier *unconditionally-graded* schedule "passed every
accuracy check above and was wrong here by 193%" on the FD-in-R probe. The new
schedule is smoother than the one it replaces, and that test passes.

#### Gates

    numpy byte-identical   sha256 674eb2ec4b9bf838 both arms (48 values,
                           one worktree, one file toggled)
    new tests              12 fail without / 12 pass with
    file                   49 passed jax, 49 passed torch
    wider jax gate         206+94skip / 7 / 43 passed

off by 470,000x, which is an accuracy bug (task #103, off-grid fallback), not
something a bar should ever be moved for. Papering those over with looser bars

#### #194: the inheritance rule is real, documented, and half-right

`_load_backend_nodeids` deliberately makes `<backend>-jit` inherit `<backend>`,
reasoning that "tracing ... only makes a slow test slower, since the trace has
to compile first" and that this is "a property of the backend name, not of which
list is being read."

Sound for the **ledger** — tracing cannot repair a numerical gap. Wrong for the
**slow-skip list**, and the file argues against itself: the streamdf and
streamTrack entries both name *per-trackpoint / per-track eager XLA dispatch* as
the cost, which is exactly what tracing removes, and both say "un-skip when
jit-vectorized". Inheritance made that unmeasurable — skipped under `--jit` for
a cost the traced run may not pay.

So it is a property of the list. Split implemented (`inherit_eager=False` for
slow-skip only), and `test_streamTrack.py` is running under `--backend jax --jit`
now to find out which way it actually goes. Populating the jit list from
measurement has to precede flipping this in CI, or 75 inherited jax entries all
start running at once.

### 2026-08-08 — self-audit of #207: is the graded ladder duplicating a backend helper?

Applied the same audit to my own PR that step (2) applies to others', since a
panel-grading scheme is exactly the "general-ish function written in a specific
method file" the standing instruction warns about.

`galpy/backend/quadrature.py` **does** already have a near-miss:
`transformed_quad(..., interior_point=c)` splits at an interior near-singular
point and clusters nodes toward it via the `X = xi**k` boundary-layer map.

Not a duplicate — different mechanism, and the reach is the discriminator:

| | mechanism | closest approach |
|---|---|---|
| `transformed_quad` | warps nodes *inside* 2 panels | `span*(1/n)**k` ~ **4e-6** |
| `_bk_split_quad` dyadic | refines *panels*, fixed ladder | `R*2**-K` ~ **6e-8** |
| `_bk_split_quad` geometric | refines *panels*, spans to `dmin` | `4\|z\|`, **any scale** |

Node-warping cannot resolve a peak narrower than its own innermost node, so the
shared helper bottoms out three orders of magnitude short of where the *old*
ladder did and eleven short of what this PR needs at `|z|=1e-12`. They are
complementary: warping suits an endpoint singularity of unknown shape, panel
refinement a peak of *known width*.

Recorded in the PR body along with the follow-up I deliberately did not take:
giving `transformed_quad` an optional `peak_width=` so both strategies sit
behind one interface. That is an API change to a helper with callers in
`FerrersPotential`, `AnySphericalPotential` and five df modules; this PR changes
a spacing law inside one existing private method, and mixing the two would make
a two-line diff into a cross-cutting one.

The safe migration is instead:

1. flip inheritance off for the slow-skip list only (the conftest patch);
2. **seed** the jit list with the currently-inherited eager entries, so CI

3. immediately prune the two files I *have* measured, which un-defers ~108

4. mark the seeded-but-unmeasured entries explicitly, so they are a visible

the eager list reproduces exactly the bug being fixed"), and it would be, if it
stopped there. The difference is that after the copy the entries are *written
down and attributable* instead of implied by a naming rule — which is what makes
step 4's burndown possible at all. Silent inheritance has no burndown by
construction.

### 2026-08-08 — two harness bugs of my own, one of them for the third time

The chained "build then measure" launcher never ran the measurement. Two
independent faults, both mine, both in the *harness* rather than in galpy:

**1. `build_ext --inplace` puts the .so at the WORKTREE ROOT, not in `galpy/`.**

    /var/tmp/jit194/libgalpy.cpython-313-x86_64-linux-gnu.so       <- actual
    /var/tmp/jit194/galpy/libgalpy*.so                             <- what I gated on

So my gate would have reported "BUILD FAILED - no .so" on a perfectly good
build. Worth noting this also explains an earlier oddity I let pass: `ls
port207/galpy/libgalpy*.so` printed nothing while `_ext_loaded` was True. I
read that as noise at the time; it was the same fact. The authoritative check is
`load_libgalpy()`, not a path glob — the loader knows where it put it and I do
not.

**2. `pgrep -f` / `pkill -f` match the shell running them.** The waiter looped
forever because `pgrep -f "setup.py build_ext"` matched the waiter's own command
line, which contains that string. Then two attempts to clean it up with
`pkill -f` killed the invoking shell instead (exit 144) — the same footgun that
hit the orphan reap earlier today, now three times total.

Rule, adopted: **kill by PID, never by pattern.** Capture `$!` at launch, and
if a pid must be discovered later, resolve it once and operate on the number.
A pattern that describes the work also describes the thing doing the work.

Neither bug touched galpy or any result — both cost only wall-clock — but three
repeats of the same one is a process failure, not bad luck, hence writing the
rule down rather than the incident.

`/var/tmp/jit194` now verified properly: galpy resolves into the worktree, C
extension loads (`integrateFullOrbit` present), conftest patch applied.

recorded.

### 2026-08-09 — caught a measurement about to destroy its own output

The `test_noninertial.py --backend jax --jit` run was 35 min in at 16/53 tests,
i.e. ~2.2 min/test, projecting **~117 min** — against the `timeout -k 60 5400`
(90 min) I had given it.

That is not merely "it would not finish". pytest writes the junitxml **at
session end**, so a wall-clock kill at 90 min would have produced ~41 completed
tests and **zero recorded timings** — the one thing the run exists to produce.
The dots in the log give a count, not a duration, and duration is the whole
question for #194 (which entries clear the 240 s margin).

Relaunched with a 4 h budget for a ~2 h job. The 35 min already spent is lost,
which is the cheaper half of the trade: the alternative was losing it at minute
90 *and* having nothing to show.

Worth generalising, because I set that 5400 s myself without projecting against
it: **a timeout on a measurement is a data-retention decision, not just a
safety net.** For a run whose output is written only at the end, the budget has
to exceed the projected duration with margin, or the safety net silently becomes
the failure mode. Where that is not possible, the run needs per-test bounding
(`--timeout`) so the session still completes and records what it learned.

### 2026-08-09 — CONTENTION: every --jit timing I have reported may be inflated

Relaunched noninertial alone. Same file, same worktree, same command:

    earlier (4 concurrent jax runs)   16 tests / 35 min   ~132 s/test
    now     (load average 1.32)       12 tests / 4.2 min   ~21 s/test

A 6x difference with the code identical. XLA's CPU backend sizes its intra-op
thread pool to the core count, so N concurrent jax processes each try to own all
72 cores and oversubscribe; wall-clock per test inflates accordingly. `%CPU` per
process still looked healthy (~100%), which is why nothing looked wrong.

**What this invalidates.** #194's entire decision is per-test wall-clock against
the 240 s margin, and I ran the two big measurements *concurrently with other
heavy jax jobs*:

* `st2_jaxjit` (streamTrack) ran alongside `aax2_jax`
* `sdf_jaxjit` (streamdf) ran alongside `aa2_jax` and `aax2_torch`

So **498 s / 348 s / 243 s are upper bounds, not measurements**, and the
"2 nodeids stay deferred, 43 un-defer" / "1 stays, 65 un-defer" splits are drawn
against inflated numbers. The direction of the error is favourable — the real
times are lower, so *more* would un-defer — but a threshold decision made on
numbers I cannot reproduce serially is not a decision, it is a guess that
happens to be conservative.

**What survives.** Pass/fail counts are unaffected by contention:
streamTrack 45/45 pass, streamdf 65 pass / 14 fail (10 immutability + 4 Torus).
Those stand.

**What I am retracting.** The claim two wakes ago that noninertial "looks
genuinely slow under jit too, so this cluster may largely stay deferred". That
was ~132 s/test measured under contention; alone it is ~21 s/test, projecting
~19 min for the file rather than ~117. I said at the time it was not a
conclusion, which is the only reason this is a retracted signal and not a
retracted result.

**Rule:** timing runs go one at a time. Correctness runs may overlap. I had them
overlapping because CPU looked free at 72 cores — core count is not the
resource; the framework's thread pool is.

### 2026-08-09 — #194 breaks an existing test that ASSERTS the old contract

Ran the contract-invalidation check I should have run when I first edited
conftest: grep the changed symbol across `tests/`. It is covered.

`tests/test_backend_ledger.py::test_jit_inheritance_applies_to_every_list`
asserts that **all three** loaders inherit, and its docstring states the
rationale as fact:

    "A test too slow to run eager is slower still traced (it must compile first)"

That is precisely the claim the streamdf measurement disproves — eager >90 min
(shard cancelled) against 13 min traced. So the change is not just a conftest
tweak; it invalidates a documented, tested contract, and the PR has to replace
the *rationale* as well as the assertion or the next reader re-derives the old
rule from the docstring.

The correct contract turns out to be a **3-way** split, not the 2-way I had in
mind:

| loader | inherit | why |
|---|---|---|
| `_load_ledger` | yes | tracing cannot repair a numerical gap or a `_reject_backend` guard |
| `_load_backend_skip` | yes | "excluded for hitting the network is excluded however it is run" — still true |
| `_load_slow_skip` | **no** | tracing changes runtime in both directions |

The conftest patch already does exactly this (only `_load_slow_skip` passes
`inherit_eager=False`), so the code was right and only the test needs to follow.
Worth noting the permanent-skip list keeps inheriting on a rationale I did not
have to touch — the reason it inherits is a property of the *exclusion*, not of
speed, so the measurement says nothing about it.

Also verified, since I asserted it last wake without checking: gh#1278's body
contains **no wall-clock claims at all** (grep for time units and
faster/slower/speed returns nothing). Its numbers are accuracy values, hashes

`build.yml` triggers on **both** `push:` (path-filtered, no branch filter) and

* cancelling the **pull_request** run removes the gating checks;
* editing `.github/workflows/` needs scope I do not have.

So it goes to Jo as a workflow decision. The usual fix is a branch filter on the
push trigger — e.g. run pushes only for `main` / `feat/backends*`, leaving
feature branches to the PR event — which would halve CI latency for this whole
project without reducing what is actually tested (the PR event covers every
feature branch already).
