### 2026-08-09 — contention diagnosis corroborated from galpy's own code

Checked whether the suite already caps backend thread pools, which would have
falsified the contention explanation for the 6x timing inflation.

`galpy.backend.restrict_to_single_thread` exists but is called **only** from
`galpy.util.multi.parallel_map`'s forked children — not by the test suite. So
measurement runs get the full pool, and the diagnosis holds. Its docstring
argues the same point independently:

* "one process per core already saturates the machine" — i.e. N concurrent
  full-pool processes oversubscribe by construction;
* "jax has no equivalent knob" — so a jax run cannot be capped the way torch
  can, which is why my four concurrent jax runs each tried to own all 72 cores.

Useful for later, with a caveat: timing runs *could* be parallelised safely by
pinning each to a disjoint CPU set (`taskset`). That would arguably also be more
CI-representative, since CI runners have ~2-4 cores rather than 72. But it
changes the baseline, and I am mid-measurement on an unpinned run — so not now.
Introducing a second variable to fix the first is how the earlier retraction
happened.

### 2026-08-09 — #211(B) shape refined: 7 identical loops, so it is an EXTRACTION

Counted the actual sites rather than working from my earlier "3 call sites"
description. `interpRZPotential`'s no-C Python fallback contains **seven**
byte-identical double-loop grid builds:

    potGrid  rforceGrid  zforceGrid  r2derivGrid  z2derivGrid  rzderivGrid  densGrid

each of the form

    G = numpy.zeros((len(rgrid), len(zgrid)))
    for ii in range(len(rgrid)):
        for jj in range(len(zgrid)):
            G[ii, jj] = evaluateFOO(self._origPot, rgrid[ii], zgrid[jj])

So (B) is not "vectorize 3 places" — it is **extract one helper and call it
seven times**, which removes the duplication instead of multiplying it by seven.
That materially improves the diff and matches the standing instruction about
general-ish code living in one place.

Design, for when #1274 unblocks it:

* one module-level helper taking `(evalfn, pot, rgrid, zgrid)`;
* **capability probe, not try/except**: evaluate `evalfn` once on a 2-element
  array at construction and record the result, rather than catching `TypeError`
  per grid. Catching would work but can mask a genuine error inside a potential
  that *does* accept arrays;
* fall back to the scalar loop for the two array-rejecting potentials
  (`AnyAxisym`, `RotateAndTilt`); `DoubleExponentialDisk` opts in already;
* **byte-identity is the gate**: Jo chose (B) precisely because it keeps the
  decorated call, so the numpy grid must be bit-identical. sha256 over all
  seven grids, A/B on one worktree. That needs CPU, so it happens when the
  serial measurement is done -- not concurrently.

### 2026-08-09 — a codecov check can go green and then red again with no PR change

gh#1278's `codecov/project` passed at 86.05% (-0.01%), then failed at 86.05%
(-13.91%) two wakes later. The PR head never moved. What changed is the base:

    patch target   86.05%  ->  99.95%
    project        -0.01%  ->  -13.91%   (same 86.05% on this PR)

Codecov compares against an **adjusted base** when the base commit's own
coverage is incomplete. develop's push run (from #1275's merge) was still
uploading, so the adjusted base was 86.05% and #1278 matched it exactly. Once
develop finished uploading, the real base became 99.95% and the same #1278
number became a 13.91-point drop.

So a green `codecov/project` is not durable while either side is still
uploading. It is not evidence the PR is fine; it can be evidence that both sides
are equally incomplete. The stable signal is still the one identified earlier:
**has the shard that covers the diff reported?** For #1278 that is
`tests/test_backend*.py`, and it has not — which is why `patch` has sat at
exactly 0.00% through both the green phase and the red phase.

Practical consequence: do not treat an early `codecov/project` pass as a reason
to stop watching, and do not treat its later failure as a regression. Both
states are the same fact -- incomplete uploads -- read against different bases.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — sweep design flaw caught before it cost the data

`test_dynamfric` sat 21 min on its 5th test. Identified it: **`test_dynamfric_c`
-- which is exactly the file's one eager `jax` slow-skip entry.** So the very
first file of the sweep already confirms the gap: #1279 un-defers it traced, and
it is genuinely slow traced too, so it needs a `jax-jit` line.

But finding that exposed a flaw in how I'd built the sweep. There was only a
per-FILE timeout, and **pytest writes junitxml only at session end** -- so one
very slow test eats the file budget and the whole file's data is lost at the
kill. That is the same timeout-as-data-retention trap that cost the noninertial
run earlier in this mission, rebuilt from scratch in a new place.

Also confirmed while checking: there is **no timeout in the repo config**. The
300 s cap is passed on the CI command line, so local runs are uncapped -- which
is why a 21-minute test was possible at all.

Rebuilt with a **per-test** cap and restarted (pid 665925):

    --timeout=300 --timeout-method=thread

300 s matches CI's cap and sits above the 240 s slow-skip margin, so anything
hitting it is a slow-skip candidate whether it wanted 301 s or 3000 s -- which
is the only bit the sweep needs. Failures at the cap ARE the result, not an
error. It also bounds the whole sweep: 245-test `test_orbit.py` can no longer be
held hostage by one test.

Cost: the 21 min already spent. Worth it -- uncapped, `test_orbit.py` would very
likely have produced nothing at all after many hours.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — CORRECTION: the per-test cap did NOT fix the data loss

Checked the sweep's output instead of trusting the flag, and the fix from the
previous entry **did not work**. `test_dynamfric` ended `rc=1` after 5m40s and
the sweep moved on, which looked right -- but:

    ls /var/tmp/jitsweep/*.xml   -> nothing
    grep -c "passed|failed" log  -> 0

**No junitxml, no session summary.** `--timeout-method=thread` does not fail the
test and continue; it dumps stacks and **hard-exits the process**. So it turned
one slow test into total data loss for that file -- precisely the failure the
per-test cap was added to prevent. I swapped a slow total loss for a fast one.

Rebuilt properly, and this time verified against the running process rather than
the script:

    --timeout=300 --timeout-method=signal      raises INSIDE the test, so the
                                               session finishes and writes xml
    python3 -u -m pytest ... -v | stamp.py     one timestamped line per test as
                                               it completes

Belt and braces, because neither survives every case alone: `signal` cannot
interrupt a call stuck in C/XLA, and streaming has no session summary. Together,
per-test durations are recoverable by differencing **even on a hard kill**.

Verified live, not assumed:

    1786254507.729 ...::test_..._constLambda PASSED [ 14%]
    1786254519.628 ...::test_..._varLambda   PASSED [ 28%]     -> 11.9 s

and the process really carries `--timeout-method=signal`.

The memory note I wrote one wake earlier recommended `thread`. That was wrong
advice about to be recalled in future sessions, so it is corrected in place.

Three data losses now from the same root (`test_noninertial` 90-min cap, sweep
v1 file-caps-only, sweep v2 thread-method). The durable lesson is not a flag, it
is: **check that the artifact exists, rather than that the option was passed.**

**9 of ~27 uploads have landed.** 70.83% is simply what two-thirds of the shards

So: no action, and specifically **do not** "fix" coverage. The correct handling
is to let the remaining ~18 uploads land and, if `project` is still red once

Worth keeping as a technique: `api.codecov.io/api/v2/github/jobovy/repos/galpy/
pulls/<N>` returns `sessions` for base and head. **The session count is the
discriminator between a real coverage drop and an incomplete upload** -- far
faster than reading shard logs, and it turns "probably a phantom" into a number.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — sweep→entries classifier, and the split it enforces

codecov is now *confirming* the phantom prediction rather than merely being
consistent with it: sessions 9 -> 12, coverage 70.83% -> 76.12%, climbing in
step. No action.

Built `/var/tmp/sweep_to_entries.py` so turning 10 files of sweep junitxml into
list entries is mechanical rather than a judgement call each time. The point of
it is one distinction:

    over the 240 s margin / hit the 300 s cap  ->  backend_slow_skip.txt
    failed for any other reason                ->  backend_xfail.txt

**These must not be conflated, and a script is how I stop myself doing it.** A
traced run surfaces both at once, and filing a defect as "slow" hides it behind
a performance deferral -- which is precisely how the 10-test streamdf
immutability bug stayed invisible, and the reason gh#1279 exists. So the script
auto-drafts only the SLOW lines; defect candidates are printed with their
message to be **read**, never auto-filed.

Guarded the junitxml truthiness trap explicitly while writing it:

    bad = fail if fail is not None else err     # NOT `fail or err`

an empty `<failure/>` element is falsy, so the `or` form silently reports
failures as passes -- a bug that has already cost me one wrong verdict in this
mission.

### 2026-08-09 — streamgapdf follow-up: there is nothing to fix (and my PR text was wrong twice)

Closed out the piece I deliberately deferred from gh#1280, compute-free. Two
corrections to what that PR said:

**Count was wrong.** I wrote "four sites" from a grep. An AST scan finds **10**,
across 5 functions.

**Verdict was wrong in the safe direction.** I framed them as a deferred fix on
the grounds that "no failing test reaches them" -- true, but that is an absence
of evidence. The actual mechanism:

* `impulse_deltav_general` -- the public impulse kernel, the most exposed of the
  ten -- returns early **above** the in-place line:

      if is_backend_array(v) or is_backend_array(y) or is_backend_array(w):
          return _impulse_deltav_general_backend(v, y, b, w, pot)
      ...
      tilew[:, 1] -= numpy.sqrt(...)        # numpy-only side of the guard

  the standard leaf data-guard, with the backend path in a separate function.
* The other four functions write into arrays born from `numpy.dot` /
  `numpy.tile` / scipy interpolators -- numpy by construction.

So a backend array cannot reach any of them, and `test_streamgapdf.py` passing
31/31 traced and 31/31 on torch is a *consequence*, not a coincidence. **There
is no follow-up here.** PR body corrected on both counts.

This is also the general answer to the 98-site AST watchlist: the interesting
question is never "is there an in-place write" but "can a backend array reach
it", and that is answered by reading the dispatch above it. coords.py (dual
path), backend/interpolate.py (numpy-constructed weights) and now streamgapdf
(early return) have all cleared for three different structural reasons.

### 2026-08-09 — the 4 orbit ledger entries: the blocker is GRANULARITY, not difficulty

Characterised the uncharacterised group compute-free, by reading what the tests
actually assert rather than running anything (the ledger header explicitly warns
these must not be re-measured on the dev box -- one of them passes locally and
xfails in CI group g3).

`test_analytic_ecc_rperi_rap` and `test_analytic_zmax` are **monolithic matrix
tests**: a nested `for p in pots:` x `for integrator in integrators:` over the
*entire* potential list and 11 integrators, all inside a single test function.

That is why these entries are opaque. One ledger line covers hundreds of
potential/integrator combinations, and it cannot say **which** combination
fails -- so it cannot be burned down by inspection, only by pulling the failure
detail out of a CI artifact. The entry hides its own cause by construction.

**And the fix is already an accepted pattern in this repo.** `test_potential.py`
carries `@pytest.mark.parametrize("potname", _XXX_POTS)` in **14** places,
introduced for precisely this reason. Applying the same treatment to
test_orbit's analytic loop tests would turn 3 opaque entries
(`analytic_ecc_rperi_rap` jax + torch, `analytic_zmax` jax) into per-potential
entries, of which the large majority would pass immediately -- the same shape as
the earlier test_potential.py work, which is recorded as done.

Not started: it is a `main`-targeting test refactor (that is where the
test_potential.py precedent landed), there is no free PR slot, and it wants the
CI failure detail first to confirm the expected per-potential split. Recorded as
a scoped, precedented proposal rather than begun.

Net effect on the burndown map: of the 14 entries after gh#1280, the "orbit,
uncharacterised" group of 4 is really **3 granularity + 1 traced** -- and the
granularity three have a known, already-blessed remedy.

### 2026-08-09 — the slow shard was a RUNNER EVICTION, re-run dispatched

The anomalous shard failed at **08:19:13Z** -- *before* the 08:56Z timeout
deadline I had computed, so my "it will hit the 90-min backstop" expectation was
wrong about the mechanism. Read the failure instead of assuming, and it is
infrastructure, on four independent signatures:

    conclusion=failure   but step 16 "Test with pytest" frozen at IN_PROGRESS
    steps 17-20          all PENDING -- including "Upload shard JUnit XML",
                         so the job produced no artifact at all
    job log              BlobNotFound -- logs never uploaded
    duration             53m03s, well under timeout-minutes: 90

A real test failure completes the pytest step and uploads its junitxml. A job
whose step is frozen mid-run, with no artifact and no log blob, was killed under
it. Same class as the eviction recorded earlier in this project ("The runner has
received a shutdown signal" after 36 min against 59 min of honest runtime).

So the 3x-normal duration was the *symptom* of a sick runner, not a slow test --
which also explains why it never reached the timeout.

**Response: targeted re-run of the failed jobs only** (`gh run rerun 31294400216
--failed`). Not a blanket re-run, and not a polling loop -- that cancels
in-progress jobs. The shard is running again.

`all-clear` went red purely as a consequence (it fails if any job fails). It
needs its own re-run **after** the shard goes green, not now -- re-running it
while its dependency is still running would just re-fail it.

Worth recording as a rule: **a stuck-looking shard is not necessarily slow.**
The discriminator is whether the step completed and the artifact exists, not the
elapsed time. Elapsed time only told me something was wrong; it did not tell me
what, and I guessed the wrong mechanism from it.

meant to reject. Needs a decision, not a fix-by-reflex.

### 2026-08-09 — AnyAxisym forceAsDeriv ATTRIBUTED: pre-existing, NOT gh#1278

Reproduced the failure exactly, then A/B'd it. Two wrong assumptions in the
first probe, both fixed:

* the test does `tclass()` -- **default** surfdens, not one I choose;
* the derivative is **ONE-SIDED**, `(Phi(z) - Phi(z+dz))/dz`. A centred
  difference across z=0 cancels by symmetry, which is exactly why the first
  probe read `diff = 0` and reproduced nothing.

Faithful probe, current develop:

    eager  Phi(z=0)   = -1.7599930722150277   Phi(z=1e-8) = -1.7599930722110944
           one-sided dPhi/dz = -3.93e-04            <- fine
    jit    Phi(z=0)   = -1.7599195947859025   Phi(z=1e-8) = -1.7599930535685753
           one-sided dPhi/dz = +7.345878e+03        <- matches the test's 7.345999e+03

**Mechanism**: under tracing, `Phi` at **exactly z=0** is wrong by ~7.3e-5
relative to `Phi` at z=1e-8. Eager has the two agreeing to 11 digits. Dividing
that inconsistency by dz=1e-8 is what manufactures 7346.

**A/B, same probe, pre-gh#1278 file swapped in (it touches only 2 files):**

    pre-#1278  jit Phi(z=0) = -1.7599195947859025   dPhi/dz = 7.345878e+03
    post-#1278 jit Phi(z=0) = -1.7599195947859025   dPhi/dz = 7.345878e+03

**Identical. gh#1278 did NOT cause this -- it is pre-existing and traced-only.**
The only difference gh#1278 makes anywhere in the probe is the last digit of the
traced `Phi(z=1e-8)` (`...5753` vs `...5750`), ~2e-16 relative: noise.

So my merged change is cleared -- and cleared by a probe that **reproduces** the
failure, which is the only kind of clearance worth anything. The previous
wake's probe returned `diff = 0` and I explicitly refused to read that as
exoneration; that refusal was right.

### 2026-08-09 — RotateAndTilt: the trigger is a missing FLAG, not the guard (`532f251f`)

Read the guard instead of leaving my own diagnosis at "it fires". It is not a
blanket array refusal:

    if arrays and not (getattr(self, "_backend_accepts_arrays", False)
                       and all(is_backend_array(x) for x in arrays)):
        raise TypeError(...)

Under tracing the `is_backend_array` half is **satisfied** -- traced arrays are
backend arrays. So what actually trips is that **RotateAndTiltWrapperPotential
never sets `_backend_accepts_arrays`**.

That changes the shape of the work: it is a **one-flag opt-in**, not a guard
rewrite. It does *not* make it a safe one-line fix -- the gate exists precisely
to keep arrays out of potentials whose internals dispatch to bare numpy/scipy,
so the flag must not be flipped before verifying the wrapper is actually correct
on array input. (The AnyAxisym opt-out is deliberate for that reason; this one
reads as unverified rather than intentional, which is why all 5 stay **xfail**
-- a burndown item -- rather than becoming a permanent skip.)

Did not start the fix: it would be a third open PR against a two-PR cap, and it
needs array-correctness verification I cannot run while the sweep owns the
machine. Recorded in the ledger entry itself so the next person starts from the
mechanism rather than the symptom.

and quotes in a heredoc-less `-m` got word-split by the shell and git tried to

The sweep's junitxml carries full tracebacks, so this cost nothing to extract --
and it collapsed "a gap in two composite MW potentials" into a single cause:

potential cannot even be *constructed* under a trace, so no amount of fixing its

### 2026-08-09 — RotateAndTilt: this is a DESIGN CALL, not a fix. Not making it.

Took the 5-entry RotateAndTilt burndown with the machine finally free, and
stopped short of the change. What the code actually says:

    # Opt-in escape hatch: a potential whose BACKEND evaluation broadcasts
    # over a trailing node axis (``_backend_accepts_arrays``) may be handed
    # the whole Gauss-Legendre node array ... Gated on every array argument
    # being a BACKEND array, so the documented numpy contract -- these
    # methods take scalars -- is unchanged

Three things follow, and together they change the task:

1. The flag does **not** mean "tolerates arrays". It means the backend
   evaluation **broadcasts over a trailing node axis**, so the traced
   surfdens/mass quadrature may hand it the whole GL node array at once. That
   is a property to demonstrate, not a switch to flip.
2. **Only `DoubleExponentialDiskPotential` sets it** -- one potential in the
   whole tree, added for exactly that quadrature purpose.
3. "These methods take scalars" is called **documented** in the comment. The
   scalar-only contract is deliberate, not an oversight.

Tried to measure the broadcasting property anyway -- array call vs scalar loop,
element by element -- and the guard also wraps the private methods, so it cannot
be probed from outside without editing the guard itself.

So the honest position: **the fix is one of two designs, and choosing is Jo's.**
Either opt the wrapper in (after demonstrating the trailing-axis property), or
have the quadrature *fall back* to per-node evaluation when a potential is not
opted in, instead of the guard raising. The second is arguably the better shape
-- a missing opt-in should cost speed, not correctness -- but it changes a
quadrature contract, which is not mine to redefine while Jo is away.

Did not flip the flag. The ledger entry already carries the mechanism and the
"do not flip before verifying" caveat, and gh#1281 is in CI, so I am not adding
a commit to refine a comment at the price of restarting ~151 checks.

### 2026-08-09 — RotateAndTilt: measured, half-fixable, REVERTED. Not a one-liner.

Last wake I said the empirical question could not be probed from outside the
guard. Wrong: the guard reads `getattr(self, "_backend_accepts_arrays", False)`,
so setting it on a **throwaway instance** admits backend arrays without touching
any code. Did that, and got the measurement.

**It does not broadcast.** `RotateAndTiltWrapperPotential.py:180`:

    xyzp = xp.stack([x, y, z])
    ValueError: Cannot stack arrays with different numbers of dimensions:
                got (), (), (3,)

With a trailing node axis only `z` carries it, so the stack mixes rank 0 and 1.
One line fixes that — `x, y, z = xp.broadcast_arrays(x, y, z)` — and the rotation
then works for free, because `(3,3) @ (3,N)` is the same matmul as `(3,3) @ (3,)`.
Measured, not assumed: `_evaluate/_Rforce/_zforce/_dens`, two geometries, array
call vs scalar loop → **max rel 0.000e+00** (bit-identical), result is a real
backend array (`ArrayImpl`, not a numpy fallback), `jax.grad` through it works,
and numpy `_Rforce` is byte-identical (sha `04e57c75…` both sides).

**But that is not the failing path.** The 5 ledgered tests are
`test_poisson_surfdens_potential`, which drives the **second derivatives**:

    deriv2p = stack([stack([x2,xy,xz]), ...])        # (3,3), or (3,3,N)
    return inv_rot @ (deriv2p @ inv_rot_T)
    TypeError: dot_general requires contracting dimensions to have the same
               shape, got (50,) and (3,)

`(3,3,N) @ (3,3)` contracts the node axis against 3. So the Hessian rotation has
to be restructured too. I tried the obvious `xp.einsum("ia,ab...,jb->ij...")` —
it broadcasts perfectly (`_R2deriv/_z2deriv/_Rzderiv` all 0.000e+00) but it is
**not numpy byte-identical**: `507263c4…` vs stock `433a5731…`. einsum picks a
different contraction order than two chained matmuls.

So I **reverted the whole RotateAndTilt change.** Byte-identity is the standing
constraint and I will not trade it for a ledger entry. The KD `_mass` fix
(`56e179e5`) is untouched and still committed.

**What it would actually take** (for whoever picks this up, likely me): build
`deriv2p` with the node axis **leading** — `(N,3,3)` instead of `(3,3,N)` — so
`inv_rot @ deriv2p @ inv_rot_T` stays a plain chained matmul and the scalar case
executes the identical operations, preserving the bits, while the array case
rides numpy/jax batched-matmul semantics. That changes the returned shape, so
the call sites need checking. Bounded, but not a one-liner, and not something to
half-land while CI is starved.

**Two counting corrections, both mine.** Mid-wake I "corrected" the count to 3
RotateAndTilt entries; that was itself wrong. There are **5**, and my `-k
"RotatedAndTilted or RotateAndTilt"` filter only selected 3 of them because two
are named `mockRotatedTiltedOffsetMWP14WrapperPotential` and
`mockOffsetMWP14WrapperPotential` — no matching substring. The original 5 stands.

### 2026-08-09 — RotateAndTilt FIXED via axis order. numpy bits held.

Picked the write-up from the previous entry back up and finished it. The
axis-order idea works, and it clears the constraint the einsum could not.

**Three rank assumptions, not one.** The first-order stack was only the first:

1. `_rect_transformed` stacked `[x, y, z]` where only `z` carries the node axis
   → `broadcast_arrays` first. The rotation then needs nothing, since
   `(3,3) @ (3,N)` is the same matmul as `(3,3) @ (3,)`.
2. the **offset** add assumed `(3,)` against a `(3,N)` stack → reshape to
   `(3,1,…)`. Found only because I added an `offset` geometry to the probe;
   the first three geometries all passed without it.
3. `_2ndderiv_xyz` built the Hessian as `(3,3,N)`, so `deriv2p @ inv_rot.T`
   contracted the node axis against 3 → rebuilt as `(...,3,3)`, tensor axes
   **last**, so a node axis becomes a leading batch axis that matmul carries.
   Consumers index `[..., i, j]`.

**Why axis order and not einsum.** `xp.einsum("ia,ab...,jb->ij...")` broadcasts
perfectly too, but picks a different contraction order and is **not numpy
byte-identical** (`507263c4…` vs stock `433a5731…`). Chained matmul on a plain
`(3,3)` executes exactly the operations it did before, so the bits survive.
That is the whole reason the first attempt was reverted and this one lands.

**Verified before claiming it:**

### 2026-08-09 — gh#1281 was starved by its OWN pre-rebase runs. Cancelled them.

Two hours at 2/151 was not ordinary slowness. Job-level detail showed the head
SHA's 26 jobs **all queued, none started**, while runners were busy — with runs
for a *different* SHA:

    31309341573  sha=915ccb57  pull_request  in_progress
    31309338114  sha=915ccb57  push          in_progress
    31311623779  sha=1be681c3  pull_request  queued      <- the actual PR head
    31311622068  sha=1be681c3  push          queued

`915ccb57` is **my own pre-rebase commit** ("slow-skip: test_orbit's 7 measured
jax-jit entries"), and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` says it is **not an
ancestor** of the head — the rebase orphaned it. Its 52 jobs (2 duplicate sets ×
26) were holding the runners while the real head waited behind them.

Cancelled all 3 active runs on the stale SHA. Safe, and checked rather than
assumed: the merge gate evaluates check runs on the **head** SHA, and this is
not it — so the "never cancel a same-SHA push run, it blocks the merge" rule
does not apply here. That rule is about the head; this is its orphan.

**This sharpens the `build.yml` item for Jo, and makes it worse than I said.**
I had reported the double-run as roughly a 2× CI *bill*. On a runner-constrained
account it is also a 2× *wall-clock* cost, and today it compounded: **four**
complete job sets were live for one PR — duplicate × {stale SHA, head SHA} —
so the head was fourth in line behind three sets nobody needed.

Two independent workflow gaps, both needing scope I do not have:

1. **no `concurrency:` group** — after a rebase or force-push, the superseded
   SHA's runs keep going. A `concurrency: {group: <workflow>-<ref>,
   cancel-in-progress: true}` would auto-cancel them, which is exactly what I
   just did by hand.
2. **`build.yml` triggers on both `push:` (no branch filter) and
   `pull_request:`** — every in-repo PR runs ~52 build jobs where 26 would do.

Fix (1) and this stops needing a human. Until then I will check for orphaned
SHAs whenever a PR sits queued after a rebase — it is not obvious from
`gh pr checks`, which only ever shows the head.

**Confirmed within 5 minutes.** Before the cancellation gh#1281 was
`{QUEUED: 149, SUCCESS: 2}` and had been for two hours; after, it is
`{IN_PROGRESS: 5, QUEUED: 144, SUCCESS: 2}`. The head's jobs picked up the
runners as soon as the orphans released them, so the diagnosis was right and the
fix was the cancellation, not waiting.

Also swept the rest of the repo for the same waste — compared every
`in_progress` run's SHA against its branch tip — and found **no other stale-SHA
runs**. The only one left is develop's `all-clear` on the current tip. So this
was a one-off caused by my rebase, not an accumulating leak.

### 2026-08-09 — PASS does not mean "under the cap". My torch delta was wrong.

The clean `test_FDMdynamfric` re-run was supposed to settle one contaminated
row. It exposed a hole in the classification rule instead:

    const_FDMfactor   contaminated: 300.0s FAIL(cap)
                      clean:        534.0s **PASS**

534 s **passing** with `--timeout=300`. The timeout did not fire, and the reason
is mechanical: `--timeout-method=signal` delivers SIGALRM, and the handler
cannot run while the interpreter is inside a C extension call that does not
return to bytecode. The alarm is pending, the test finishes, nobody notices.

**So "PASSED" does not imply "under the cap"** — and my torch delta table
classified slow-vs-not by *timeout failure*, which silently drops every such
test. Audited both sweeps for passing tests over the 240 s margin:

| sweep | passing-over-margin |
|---|---|
| jax (gh#1281) | 5 |
| torch (mine, this session) | 8 |

**gh#1281 is safe** — I checked all 5 against its added entries and every one is
already there, because the jax classification went by *duration*. The merge
stands.

**The torch delta was not.** Recomputed by duration:

| | old (failure-based) | corrected |
|---|---|---|
| slow additions | 2 | **9** |
| defects | 2 | 2 |
| keep | 1 | 1 |
| reclassify | 1 | 1 |
| deletes | 14 | **13** |

The four `poisson_surfdens[RotateAndTilt…]` variants are the clearest case: I
reported "4 pass, 1 slow", but three of those "passes" took **313–398 s**. They
are all slow. Also newly caught: `test_interprz_dxdv_3d` (295 s),
`test_liouville_planar` (250 s), `test_analytic_zmax` (269 s).

Corrected net: **delete 13, add 11, keep 1, reclassify 1** — against the
"delete 14, add 4, reclassify 1" I had drafted into the PR body an hour ago.

Caught only because I re-measured a row I had flagged as contaminated. The
contamination turned out not to matter for that row's *verdict*; chasing it is
what surfaced the rule error, which mattered a great deal more.

**Arithmetic correction on that correction.** I wrote "9 slow additions / add 11"
into the PR body; the table under it lists **8**. Counted the rows
programmatically rather than trusting the sentence, and the computed classifier
agrees: 1 `const_FDMfactor` + 4 `poisson_surfdens` + `interprz_dxdv_3d` +
`analytic_zmax` + `liouville_planar` = **8 slow**, plus 2 defects = **10
additions**.

Corrected net: **delete 13, add 10, keep 1, reclassify 1.** `test_dynamfric_c`
is a *keep*, not an add, and `test_analytic_ecc_rperi_rap` is already an xfail
entry — those two are what I double-counted.

Two consecutive arithmetic slips in one summary is a signal about the format,
not just the instance: prose totals sitting next to a table drift from it. The
fix I will actually use is to derive the totals from the table
programmatically before writing them down, which is how both were caught.

### 2026-08-09 — THE GATE FAILED, and it was right to. RotateAndTilt reverted.

    4 failed, 164 passed, 45 skipped, 2 xfailed in 457.27s

Four of the five `poisson_surfdens[RotateAndTilt…]` tests **still fail** on the
fixed tree. My fix does what I measured it to do — the array-input guard is
gone — but what it uncovers is worse than what it removed:

    (R,Z,phi) = (0.500, 10.000, 0.000)
    tpoissondens = 0.07701375   vs   tdens = 0.07209774
    rel. diff = 6.8e-02   against a 1e-8 bar

**The opt-in trades a hard `TypeError` for a silent 6.8% wrong answer.** Once
the wrapper accepts the node array, the traced path evaluates the Poisson
surfdens with fixed-order Gauss-Legendre where scipy's adaptive `quad` had been
coping, and at |Z|=10 that is not nearly enough. An exception is a bad outcome;
a plausible-looking number that is 6.8% off is a worse one.

So I **reverted the RotateAndTilt commit** and restored its 5 ledger entries.
Verified by set difference rather than by reading the diff: exactly
`test_McMillan17` and `test_Cautun20` removed, **0 added**.

**What I claimed and what is true.** I had this branch described — in STATUS, in
the log, and in a drafted PR body — as *"fixes 7 of gh#1281's 8 traced
defects"*. It fixes **2**. The 40/40 bit-identical broadcast measurement was
real and is still real; I over-read it as evidence the *tests* would pass, when
all it showed was that the wrapper computes the same values array-wise as
scalar-wise. It does — and the quadrature built on it is still wrong at large
|Z|.

That is exactly the gap the pytest gate exists to close, which is why it was
owed before opening rather than after. Every prior wake that deferred the PR for
"the gate is still owed" was the right call.

**RotateAndTilt goes back to the follow-up list** with what is now known:
opting it in requires the traced surfdens quadrature to be range-aware (there is
already a `surfdens` range-aware mechanism in the tree from earlier work — that
is the thread to pull), not merely rank-correct.

### 2026-08-09 — KD-only branch passes its gate; and I tripped the `cd`-and-`&` trap

**Gate 2 (reverted branch): `163 passed, 45 skipped, 7 xfailed, 0 failed`.**
Cross-checked against gate 1 (`164 passed, 4 failed, 2 xfailed`): both total 170
non-skipped, and xfails go 2 → 7, i.e. exactly the 5 RotateAndTilt entries moved
back under deferral. The count reconciles, so the revert did precisely what was
intended and nothing else.

Committed the 2-entry ledger drop (`5c1b9264`).

**Mistake worth recording.** I ran

    cd /var/tmp/defects-edit && nohup pytest ... > log 2>&1 & echo ...; git add -A && git commit ...

`&` backgrounds the **whole** `cd && nohup` compound, so the `cd` happened in a
subshell and `git add -A` ran in the **main repo** — staging `.claude/`, a stray
`.nfs*` file, notebooks, and an *embedded git repository*
(`actionAngleTorus_c_ext/torus`). git warned about the embedded repo, which is
what made me look.

Nothing was committed (the pre-commit `ruff format` hook rejected it, and the
`git log` I printed showed the *main* repo's HEAD `dbb09ffc` — a second tell).
`git reset -q HEAD -- .` restored the main worktree to exactly its prior state.

I have this in memory as *"cd does not survive &"* and still walked into it. The
durable fix is not vigilance: use **`git -C <path>`** for every git call against
a worktree, which is what the redone commit does, and stage the **named file**
rather than `-A`. Both of those make the failure impossible rather than
unlikely.

### 2026-08-09 — gh#1282 contained the WRONG commits. Closed; gh#1283 is correct.

Caught by checking what the PR actually contained rather than what I believed I
had pushed. `gh pr view 1282 --json headRefOid` came back **`e1fa8bf9`** — the
*old* tip, with the RotateAndTilt code that **fails its own gate** — not the
`5c1b9264` I had gated.

**Mechanism.** The branch `backend-jit/kd-mass-quadrature` was already checked
out in `port207` at `e1fa8bf9`. So in `defects-edit`:

* `git checkout -b <name>` failed (branch exists),
* `git branch -f <name> HEAD` failed (checked out in another worktree),
* both were `2>/dev/null`-suppressed, and
* `git push -u origin <name>` then pushed **that other worktree's branch**.

Three silent failures composing into a confidently wrong result. The `rev-parse
--abbrev-ref HEAD` in my own command printed `HEAD` (detached) — I read past it.

**Fix, without force-pushing an open PR** (my own standing rule): closed gh#1282
with an explanatory comment, pushed the gated commits to a *new* branch
`…-v2`, opened **gh#1283**, and then **verified the PR's content** rather than
its existence:

    head=5c1b9264 -> 07deb9c1  base=feat/backends-develop
    files: KuijkenDubinskiDiskExpansionPotential.py, tests/backend_xfail.txt
    ledger diff: -test_McMillan17, -test_Cautun20      (2 removals, 0 additions)

**Also cleaned the ledger diff.** Restoring the reverted entries had put them
back at a different position, so the diff read as *7 removals + 5 re-additions*
— net −2, but a reviewer would reasonably see "7 entries un-deferred" and stop.
Rebuilt the file from the base minus exactly the 2 fixed entries. A diff should
say what it does.

**The lesson is not "be careful with branches".** It is that `git push`
succeeding tells you a push happened, not that it pushed *your work* — and every
step that could have caught it was suppressed or skimmed. The check that works
is reading the PR's own head SHA and diff back from the API afterwards, which is
now what I do.

### 2026-08-09 — "needs range-aware quadrature" was wrong; the real lead is the SPLIT POINT

Sized the deferred RotateAndTilt follow-up by reading the code rather than
guessing, and it corrected what I had written into gh#1283's body.

The traced surfdens Poisson path is **already range-aware**:

    # Fixed-order GL over the whole [-z, z] needs an order that grows with the
    # range (n=100 is only 3.7e-4 at |z|=10). Splitting at z=0 and clustering
    # nodes toward the split ... so one node count holds at every |z|.
    inner = _bquad.symmetric_quad(..., absz, n=50)

So "opting it in first requires the quadrature to be range-aware" was false —
that work is done, from an earlier task of mine. And the observed error is
**6.8e-2**, two orders worse than the 3.7e-4 that comment quotes for the naive
case, so the *range* is not the problem.

**The lead, as a hypothesis:** `symmetric_quad` takes `interior_point=0.0` — it
assumes the integrand's structure sits at z=0 and clusters nodes there. For a
**tilted** potential the disk plane is inclined, so in the evaluation frame the
density peak is *not* at z=0: the nodes cluster where the integrand is smooth
and sample the peak sparsely. That would explain why this family fails where
others pass, and why it worsens with |Z|.

Marked a hypothesis, not a finding: it follows from the code and fits the
numbers, but I have not measured it. The test is to pass the wrapper's rotated
mid-plane as `interior_point` and see whether 6.8e-2 collapses.

Updated gh#1283's body with the correction. A PR body that sends the next reader
to "make the quadrature range-aware" would have cost them the time it took me to
find that it already is.

### 2026-08-09 — split-point hypothesis MEASURED and REFUTED; fault is the array path

    scipy adaptive reference : 3.5452228457e+00
    GL(n=50) split at 0      : 3.5452228457e+00   rel.err 1.729e-14

The tilted potential's Poisson integrand peaks **at** z=0, not away from it, and
the existing split-at-0 quadrature is exact to 1.7e-14 at the exact failing
point. So both of my quadrature explanations are dead: it is neither the range
nor the split location.

**What that leaves.** The probe is *eager scalar*; the 6.8e-2 appears only under
tracing with array input. Since the quadrature and integrand are exact in eager
scalar, the error has to enter on the **traced/array path of the wrapper
itself** — i.e. my broadcast change makes the wrapper *run* on node arrays but
apparently not compute the same thing it computes scalar-wise in that regime.

That is worth stating carefully: the 40/40 bit-identical check I ran earlier
used a 5-element z at R=1.1, **not** the quadrature's node distribution over
[-10, 10]. Agreement on one small array is not agreement on all arrays, and I
treated it as if it were. The next attempt should start by comparing
array-vs-scalar **at the quadrature's actual nodes**, which is the comparison
that would have caught this before the PR.

### 2026-08-09 (final) — DIAGNOSED, with a bit-exact reproduction of the failure

Ran the real nodeid traced with `--runxfail` (the ledger was xfailing it, which is
why the first attempt printed nothing). Its own assertion:

    (R,Z,phi) = (0.500,10.000,0.000)
    tpoissondens = 0.07701375
    tdens        = 0.07209774
    rel. diff    = 6.818545e-02

That immediately reframes the problem. **`tpoissondens` is the side that is
nearly right** (scipy says 0.07699991, so it is off by 1.8e-04 — exactly the
split-point error I had measured). The 6.8% lives in **`tdens`**, i.e.
`evaluateSurfaceDensities(..., forcepoisson=False)`, the *direct* `_surfdens`
path — the **other** `symmetric_quad` call site (Potential.py:873), which
integrates the density rather than the Poisson force combination.

Reproducing that site alone in numpy:

    scipy (numpy path)      : 0.07699991
    GL n=50  split   0.0    : 0.07209774   rel.err 6.366e-02   <-- test's tdens, to all 8 digits
    GL n=200 split   0.0    : 0.07747929   rel.err 6.226e-03
    GL n=50  split  -1.0    : 0.07699991   rel.err 1.176e-10
    GL n=200 split  -1.0    : 0.07699991   rel.err 6.231e-13

**Bit-exact.** So the mechanism was right the whole time — the split point — and
my error each round was probing the wrong *integrand*: the force combination,
which is smooth and only loses 1.8e-04, instead of the density, which for a disk
displaced to z=-1 is sharply peaked exactly where the rule puts fewest nodes.

Two things this settles:

- **Node count is not the lever.** n=200 with the wrong split is still 6.2e-03;
  n=50 with the right split is 1.2e-10. Quadrupling work buys one order;
  moving the split buys nine. The PR body's earlier "node count or placement
  needs work too" was wrong and is corrected.
- **Both call sites are affected**, at very different magnitudes (1.8e-04 and
  6.4e-02) for the same root cause, which is why measuring only one of them was
  so misleading.

**Fix design for the follow-up** (not for gh#1283, which is scoped and in CI):
`interior_point` must be the z at which the *wrapped* potential's own mid-plane
crosses the vertical line at (R, phi) — for a pure offset that is the offset's
z; for the tilted cases it is a one-line linear solve from the rotation matrix.
That generalises to all 5 ledgered entries rather than special-casing the offset
one. It needs `RotateAndTiltWrapperPotential`, which gh#1283 deliberately
reverted, so it lands **after** gh#1283 merges to keep files disjoint.

**Method note.** Three probes, three wrong answers, then the real test settled it
in 15 seconds. The reproduction was cheap and available the whole time; what it
needed was `--runxfail`, because the ledger entry silently converts the failure

### 2026-08-09 (later still) — split fix built and verified, but it does NOT clear the 5 entries

Built the fix the diagnosis called for, on `backend-jit/rt-vertical-split`
(local, unpushed): a `Potential._vertical_quad_split(R, phi, t)` hook (0.0 by
default) that `surfdens`/`_surfdens` clamp into `[-|z|,|z|]` and pass as
`symmetric_quad`'s `interior_point`, overridden in
`RotateAndTiltWrapperPotential` with the plane-crossing solve

    z = -(rot[2,0] x + rot[2,1] y + offset[2]) / rot[2,2]

plus the array-broadcast fix gh#1283 reverted (that one is a prerequisite: the
wrapper rejects the node array outright without it).

**It works, and it does not fix the tests.** Both halves verified:

- bare wrapper, `offset=[1,1,1]`: hook returns **-1.0**, and the wrapped `z'`
  really vanishes there (checked against `_rect_transformed`, 0.0e+00);
  clamps to -0.3 when `|z|=0.3`; ordinary potentials keep a literal `0.0`.
- earlier numpy measurement: that split turns 6.4e-02 into **1.2e-10**.

But an A/B over the 5 ledgered entries -- broadcast-only vs broadcast+split --
gives **byte-identical results**: 4 failed / 1 passed both ways, same four
rel. diffs (6.818545e-02, 1.482317e-02, 9.244103e-04, 3.596995e-04). The one
that passes was already passing on broadcast alone.

**Why:** every one of the 5 is a `testMWPotential`, a `Potential` subclass whose
`_dens` delegates to a `CompositePotential`. So `Potential._surfdens` integrates
at the **composite** level, where `self` is the mock and the hook returns the
base 0.0 -- it never reaches the wrapper that knows where its plane is. The hook
is at the wrong level for a summed density.

The fix is still correct for the path users actually take (a bare wrapper, or a
list of potentials, where `evaluateSurfaceDensities` sums each potential's own
`surfdens`). It is simply not what these tests exercise.

**Options for finishing it**, none started:
1. make the split resolvable through composition (a composite returns its
   components' common split, or refuses when they disagree);
2. integrate a composite's surfdens **per component** rather than as one summed
   density -- arguably the real bug, since a sum of displaced disks has no
   single mid-plane;
3. drop the declared-plane approach for a structure-agnostic panel rule; gh#1278
   already did geometric panel grading for AnyAxisym, so there may be a helper
   to reuse rather than invent.

(2) is the most principled and (3) the most reusable. Not guessing between them
on a Sunday; the branch stays unpushed and the 5 entries stay ledgered.

**Method note.** I nearly reported "1 of 5 now passes" off the post-fix run
alone. The A/B is what showed that pass was pre-existing and the fix contributed
nothing -- [[verify-burndown-flips-stash-rerun]] earning its keep.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — measured the three options; my preferred one was the worst

Last entry listed three ways to finish the split-point fix and said I would not
guess between them. Measured, on the failing offset wrapper and on a no-offset
control that must not regress (numpy, pointwise, vs adaptive scipy):

| rule | offset case | no-offset control | nodes |
|---|---|---|---|
| current (split at 0, clustered)          | 6.366e-02 | 2.501e-09 | 100 |
| geometric panels K=4 n=50                | 1.664e-06 | **9.815e-03** | 450 |
| hybrid: clustered inner + geometric shells, K=4 n=50 | **1.664e-06** | **1.330e-15** | 500 |

Test bar is rel diff < 1e-4 (the assertion squares it against 1e-8).

**Option 3 as I first wrote it is refuted.** Plain geometric grading fixes the
offset case but regresses the ordinary z=0 case by **six orders** (2.5e-09 ->
9.8e-03), because my panels threw away the clustering-toward-zero that makes the
current rule so good for a disk at the origin. I had called (3) "the most
reusable" -- it was the worst.

**The hybrid works and is strictly better on both.** Keep the current clustered
split-at-0 rule for the innermost panel, add geometric shells outside it: the
offset case reaches 1.664e-06 and the control *improves* to 1.330e-15. It needs
no per-potential knowledge, so unlike the `_vertical_quad_split` hook it also
reaches the composite path these tests exercise. K=4 saturates; n=50 is required
(K=4 n=30 gives 5.8e-04, just over the bar).

**The catch is cost: 5x the density evaluations** (500 vs 100 nodes) on a path
whose tests already run 300-400 s traced. That is exactly the
[[migration-flips-numpy-fallthrough-to-eager-slow]] shape, so it is not a free
win.

So the real choice is now a measured trade-off, not a guess:

- **(2) per-component composite surfdens** -- exact (1.2e-10 measured earlier via
  the hook) at **no** extra cost, but needs composites to integrate component-wise
  and only works where each component can declare its plane.
- **(3-hybrid)** -- works everywhere with no declarations, **5x cost**.

They compose well: (2) as the cheap default, hybrid as the fallback for
potentials that cannot declare a plane. I am not committing a 5x slowdown on a
shared hot path unilaterally while Jo is away -- recording it in STATUS for a
decision, and the cheap half (2) is buildable meanwhile.

it now guarantees a rebase conflict". Actually testing that:

    git merge-tree --write-tree <gh#1283 head> <torch head>   ->  no conflict

It merges **cleanly**: gh#1283's two xfail deletions are mid-file, the torch
additions are appended at the end. Same file is not the same hunk, and I never
checked. `merge-tree` answers this in one second and costs nothing.

The second reason for holding -- runner starvation -- was also weaker than I
thought: **queued jobs keep their place**, so a new PR's jobs enter the queue
*behind* gh#1283's 57 already-queued ones rather than competing with them. The
cost to gh#1283 is close to nil.

Also corrected a real inaccuracy in the PR body before opening: it reconciled the
counts against a raw diff of "-14/+8 slow-skip, +2 xfail", but the raw diff is
**-14/+11 and +5** -- the difference being 3 comment lines in each file. The
entry counts (8 slow, 2 defects) were right; the diff line counts were not, which
is exactly the sort of thing that makes a reviewer distrust the rest of a table.

**Lesson.** "These touch the same file" is a hypothesis about a *merge*, and
merges are cheap to simulate. I let a plausible-sounding blocker sit unexamined
across two wakes while the work it gated was finished and waiting. Sibling of
[[reproduce-the-assertion-not-a-proxy]]: I reasoned about the artifact instead of
running the operation on it.

green / 57 queued, only the codecov/project phantom red) and **gh#1284**.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — composite delegation: the density route is SOLVED, the Poisson route is not

Found why the `_vertical_quad_split` hook was inert, and it is in galpy source,
not the test mock: **`CompositePotential` defines `_dens` but inherits
`_surfdens` from `Potential`**, so the quadrature ran once over the summed
density with `self` = the composite, whose mid-plane is 0.

Fixed by delegating per component on backends (numpy keeps the inherited scipy
path, byte-identical -- 19 passed / 0 failed on the numpy surfdens tests). With
that, the hook finally fires, and it is very good. Measured at the failing point:

| mock | split | true density peak | err(split 0) | err(split c) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RotatedAndTilted   | -0.5000 | -0.4950 | 1.383e-02 | **1.070e-10** |
| ...wInclination    | -1.0925 | -1.0850 | 4.736e-03 | **1.450e-06** |
| Offset             | -1.0000 | -1.0000 | 6.366e-02 | **1.176e-10** |

The plane-crossing solve lands within ~1% of the true density peak in every
case, including the tilted ones, and buys 8 orders.

**The 5 tests still fail.** The roles simply swapped: mockOffset's residual is
now **1.797e-04**, which is exactly the *Poisson*-branch split error measured
hours ago. So I split `Potential.surfdens`'s Poisson branch into
`_surfdens_poisson` and delegated that per component too -- and it changed
**nothing**, byte-identical numbers.

Reason, one level up from the last one: the test calls
`surfdens(..., forcepoisson=True)` on **`testMWPotential`**, which defines
`_surfdens` (so the composite fix reached it) but **not** `_surfdens_poisson`,
so that route falls through to `Potential`'s with `self` = the mock and the
quadrature happens there, at split 0. My `CompositePotential` override sits
below it, unreached.

**What this settles for the pending decision.** The declared-plane approach
works exactly where the delegation chain is complete, and is essentially exact
when it does (1e-10). It cannot help a `Potential` subclass that sums displaced
components internally without delegating -- which is precisely what a user's own
composite-like class would look like. The hybrid panel rule needs no delegation
from anyone. That is a real argument for paying its 5x, and it belongs in the
decision I left for Jo in STATUS.

Two hypotheses tested and refuted along the way: that clamping the split to the
interval edge caused the tilted regressions (fallback-to-0 gave byte-identical
results), and that the tilted splits were bad (they match the peak to ~1%).
Branch `backend-jit/rt-vertical-split`, local, unpushed.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — regression tests for the split fix, A/B'd

`backend-jit/rt-vertical-split` had a real 8-order accuracy fix with nothing
pinning it. Added 6 tests to `test_backend_wrappers.py`: **6 pass with the fix,
6 fail without it.**

Design notes worth keeping:

- the split is checked against `_rect_transformed` (does the wrapped z' actually
  vanish there, <1e-12?) rather than against a re-derivation of my own formula --
  a self-consistent re-derivation would not catch a sign error or a transposed
  rotation;
- the quadrature test asserts **both** arms: accurate at the mid-plane (<1e-8)
  *and* visibly wrong at 0 (>1e-2). One-sided, it could pass on an integrand
  that happened to be easy;
- the composite test is structural. My **first draft compared values and passed
  vacuously on jax without the fix** -- untraced, both routes go through the same
  adaptive scipy quadrature and agree no matter what. Its torch arm "failed"
  only on an incidental pre-existing TypeError, i.e. for the wrong reason. Caught
  by running the A/B rather than trusting 7 green.

That is [[value-checks-cannot-see-numpy-fallback]] wearing a different hat: a
test that exercises the fallback measures the fallback, and passes whether or
not the code under test is right.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — the final gate HUNG; investigating before claiming the clearance

The re-dispatched whole-file traced sweep (on the final commit cf8828e7, with the
5 entries un-ledgered so they actually execute) **hung**. Not slow -- hung:

* stalled at 10%, log mtime frozen for >50 min;
* every xdist worker at **0.0% CPU**, cputime 1:17 total.

The identical command on the *pre-mock* tree finished in **586 s**. The only
difference is that those 5 tests now run instead of xfailing. So either they
deadlock under `-n 8`, or they interact badly with xdist + jax.

This matters more than the ledger drop: **CI runs `test_potential.py` under
`pytest-split` (`--splits 5 --group N`), not xdist**, so a pure xdist artifact
would not affect the PR -- but I am not going to assert that from the shape of
the failure. Re-running the whole file **serially** (no xdist) to discriminate:

* completes -> the hang is an xdist interaction, local-only, PR unaffected;
* hangs at the same place -> a real deadlock in the newly-executing tests, which
  must be fixed before this branch becomes a PR.

Caveat on the serial run: at ~8x the parallel wall-clock it may exceed its own
`timeout 3300`, and **a killed pytest writes no junitxml at all**
([[per-test-cap-not-per-file-timeout]]), so a timeout yields zero data rather
than partial data. If that happens, next attempt is `-n 4`.

**The 5-entry clearance therefore stands on: the 5 nodeids passing in isolation
(5 passed, 40 s), the numpy whole-file run (1283 passed / 0 failures), and the
pre-mock traced whole-file run (1271 passed / 0 failures / 1 xpass).** What is
NOT yet established is a clean whole-file traced run on the final tree. Not
claiming it until I have it.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — RETRACTION: there was no hang. I killed a healthy run.

The previous entry reports the final traced gate deadlocking. **It did not.**
Reconstructed from file timestamps and a clock I should have read the first time:

    15:00:13  pre-mock jax sweep finishes
    15:00:21  numpy subset check finishes
    ~15:01    final_jax sweep launched
    15:02     I observe it at 10% and call it hung
    15:03:03  its log's LAST write -- the teardown errors from my kill
    15:03:21  serial re-run launched

So at the moment I diagnosed a 50-minute stall, the run was **~2 minutes old and
its log had been written seconds earlier.** Both pieces of evidence were bad:

1. **"log mtime frozen for >50 min"** -- I never ran `date`. I inferred the
   current time from how long the *wake* felt, and wakes are not wall-clock
   hours. The elapsed time was invented.
2. **"every xdist worker at 0.0% CPU"** -- I read
   `ps aux | grep '[p]ytest' | head -3`, which matched the **bash wrappers**
   whose command strings contain "pytest", not the python workers. The real
   process was the 4th line and I never printed it. Minutes later I hit exactly
   this trap again (`pkill -f "pytest ..."` matched its own launcher) and
   *still* did not go back and revise the conclusion.

Cost: a healthy ~10-minute run destroyed, a wake spent on a fictitious deadlock,
and a log entry asserting a defect that never existed. The
`pytest-split`-vs-xdist reasoning in that entry is still true but was answering a
question nobody had asked.

**The fix is mechanical, which is what makes it worth writing down:** `etimes`
from `ps` is authoritative for "how long has this been running", and `date` is
authoritative for "what time is it". Neither costs anything. Recorded as
[[measure-elapsed-time-never-assume-it]].

The serial re-run is healthy and progressing (194% CPU, `etimes` confirms it,
5-10%), so the gate is coming from it regardless. No conclusions about the
5-entry clearance change: what is established is still the 5 nodeids in
isolation, numpy whole-file, and the pre-mock traced whole-file.

Set out to check the speedup I flagged last wake. It was not a speedup, and

**Which makes the sweep's 300-400 s numbers impossible on develop.** Checked the
worktree they came from: `/var/tmp/port207` is at **`e1fa8bf9` = "RotateAndTilt:
broadcast over a trailing node axis"**. The sweep measured a tree carrying an
unmerged fix.

Re-measured on clean develop source, `torch --jit`: **4 failed in 35.6 s total**,
plus a 5th (`...TriaxialLogHalo...`, 28.3 s) that fails identically and was never
ledgered at all.

**So gh#1284 as filed classified 4 defects as `slow-skip` — which SKIPS them.**
It would have silently masked four real failures in exactly the traced runs meant
to surface them, and left a fifth unrecorded. Pushed `19832bb1` moving all five
into `backend_xfail.txt` with the mechanism, and corrected the PR body's

Per-PR CI is unaffected: `JIT_FLAG` is only set by a `workflow_dispatch` with

**The lesson is precise.** That PR body *already* carried a provenance warning —
"the tree under test carried the unmerged KD `_mass` fix" — and I wrote it. I
checked that worktree for **one** contaminant and treated it as cleared.
`git log --oneline -1` on the tree you measured is one command; a provenance note
that names one fix is not a provenance check. Recorded as
[[verify-sweep-tree-provenance-completely]].

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — gh#1283 merge audit done ahead of green (131/153, 0 red)

identical on floats, consistent with the sha256 byte-identity check already run.

until I checked the convention: **both** forms exist in the tree — module-level
in 5 files, function-local in 3 sites — and `Potential.py:938` and
`AnySphericalPotential.py:185` already use *literally* `from ..backend.quadrature
import quad as _bk_quad` inside a function. Same alias, same shape. This PR
matches the nearer idiom rather than inventing one.

(Non-blocking observation for later: `Potential.py` carries *both* idioms, a
module-level `_bquad` and a function-local `_bk_quad`. Pre-existing, not
introduced here, not worth churning a shared file over mid-flight.)

difference.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — the 900 s cap is unenforceable here, as designed; classification survives it

`test_orbit` eager has sat at 86 % for **921 s** — past its own per-test cap.
That is not a hang and not a surprise: `--timeout-method=signal` delivers
SIGALRM, whose handler only runs when control returns to bytecode, so a test
inside a C-extension call **cannot be interrupted**
([[signal-timeout-misses-c-extension]]). Measured earlier today on
`const_FDMfactor`: 534 s under a 300 s cap, reported as PASS.

So the cap does not bound this run's wall clock. Two consequences, one of which
is reassuring:

* **the run may take substantially longer than 8 x 900 s of slack suggests**, and
  in the worst case a C-bound test never yields and the run never writes its
  junitxml at all (written at session end — [[per-test-cap-not-per-file-timeout]]);
* **but the classification is already determined for the half I care about.**
  The question is which of the 25 are *fast enough to drop*; every one of those
  completed early and is in the junitxml-to-be. Anything still running past 900 s
  is "slow, keep" by definition — its exact duration changes nothing.

So the downside is precision on entries I would keep regardless, not the verdict
itself. Letting it run rather than killing it: switching to
`--timeout-method=thread` would `os._exit()` the whole pytest process and lose
every result, which is strictly worse than an imprecise number on a keeper.

Watching it. If it is still at 86 % after a substantially longer window I will
harvest what completed and classify the remainder as keepers on the >900 s
evidence, which is sound and does not require the run to finish.

### 2026-08-09 (cont.) — the dissipative-composite defect, characterised

Ran the discriminator rather than reasoning about it. Under forced torch:

    CompositePotential([MN, Hernquist])                    _backend_ready = True
    CompositePotential([MN, Hernquist, ChandrasekharDF])   _backend_ready = False
    get_namespace(0.5, 2.0)                             -> torch  in BOTH cases

So `@backend_input`'s gate is `xp is not numpy and _backend_ready(args[0])`,
while the method body resolves its **own** `xp = get_namespace(...)`, which
under a forced backend ignores `_backend_ready` entirely. When the gate says
"not ready" the coordinates stay Python floats and the body still takes the
backend branch — `xp.abs(z)` on a float, and torch raises.

The sharp part: `surfdens` **filters dissipative members out** and never touches
the friction term, yet its presence flips the whole composite. **The gate is
per-object; the coercion need is per-call-path.**

Deliberately NOT fixing it in this wait. It is not a local patch — the two
notions of "are we on the backend" have to be made to agree, either by teaching
the body to respect `_backend_ready` or by making the gate stop being
per-object, and `_backend_ready` is already marked TEMPORARY with a documented
history of a removal that was tried, measured and reverted (#1196, four
independent breakages). Patching the `xp.abs` site would hide it. Recorded in
the existing gate memory with the measurement, as its own follow-up.

0 conflicts each). Both delete lines from `backend_slow_skip.txt`, which looks

### 2026-08-09 — boundary census on the surfdens path: the eager lever is scipy's scalar quadrature

CI is starved (1 in-progress run repo-wide), so I took the vectorisation
prerequisite: found the existing tool, `appendices/boundary_census.py`, rather
than writing one. Its docstring already records the last sweep — *"residual:
interpRZPotential only (task #211)"* — but its workload list does **not** cover
the surfdens/SCF tests that dominate the remaining jax ledger. So I censused
those directly, reusing its spy.

**Result 1 — the 1440-2641 s test_potential entries are NOT one problem, they
are two.** Same hot caller, wildly different economics:

    MWP14 surfdens        2779 crossings    2.23 s     ~0.8 ms/crossing
    McMillan17 surfdens   3703 crossings   56.91 s    ~15   ms/crossing

Same `CompositePotential.py:<genexpr>` at x2772 in both. MWP14 is
**boundary-bound**; McMillan17 is **compute-bound** — its SCF/DiskSCF components
cost ~20x more per evaluation, and no amount of crossing elimination touches
that. Treating "the slow potential tests" as one vectorisation target would have
been wrong.

**Result 2 — gh#1285 already removes that hot spot, and I had not noticed.**
Censused the same workload on the fix branch:

    develop  9dc31569   MWP14 surfdens (density)   2779 crossings
    gh#1285  a2d24422   MWP14 surfdens (density)     19 crossings

**146x fewer.** The mechanism is the delegation itself: instead of scipy's
scalar quadrature calling a summed integrand ~924 times (3 components x 924),
each component runs **one vectorized `symmetric_quad`** over a node array.

**What I am NOT claiming:** a speedup. Wall time went 2.23 s -> 3.62 s in this
micro-measurement, and the two numbers come from *different trees*, one call
each, with jax dispatch warmup included. The crossing count is the robust
signal; the timing is not, and I am not going to dress a 146x crossing
reduction up as a performance win it did not demonstrate.

**Result 3 — the actionable lever, stated as a hypothesis not a plan.** The
poisson route on the fix branch still shows **2299 crossings**, attributed to
`Potential.py:<lambda>:810/811` — the poisson integrand, called scalar-wise by
`scipy.integrate.quad`. That path is taken because `_quad_needs_backend`
returns False under a **forced-but-untraced** backend, so eager forced-jax gets
scipy's scalar loop while traced jax gets the vectorized backend quadrature.
That is precisely the shape of the eager-jax slowness in these tests.

So the candidate next PR is: let the backend quadrature serve the eager forced
path too, leaving numpy on scipy. It would be numpy-byte-identical by
construction. **Unverified** — I have not checked whether accuracy holds at the
extremes (the GL-vs-adaptive floor is a known trap here), nor what it does to
the 12 ledgered entries. That is the next wake's measurement, not a conclusion.

### 2026-08-09 — tested last wake's hypothesis: GL-for-eager is viable but NOT unconditional

The candidate lever was "let the backend quadrature serve the eager forced path
too". Tested it the only way that settles it: ran both arms on the **real**
poisson integrand (MWPotential2014) over a 4x4 grid of (R, |z|) spanning the
extremes, GL n=50 with mid-plane clustering vs `scipy.integrate.quad` adaptive.

    R\|z|      0.01      0.5        5         50
    0.01     5.8e-14   2.6e-13   5.9e-10   2.6e-05   <-- 
    0.1      4.4e-15   4.3e-13   1.9e-13   1.8e-09
    1.0      2.2e-16   7.5e-13   5.0e-16   2.1e-11
    8.0      1.5e-15   1.2e-12   1.4e-10   4.8e-11

**Verdict: agrees to ~1e-12 across the useful domain, and loses five digits at
extreme aspect ratio** — 2.6e-05 at (R=0.01, |z|=50), where the integrand has
structure on scale ~R across a 5000:1 range. This is the
[[match-numpy-quadrature-floor]] trap arriving exactly where that note says to
look, which is why I tested the corners rather than a mid-range point.

**But the framing changes on inspection.** The **traced** path *already* uses
this GL rule — that is what `_quad_needs_backend` selects when tracing. So the
2.6e-05 is not a new error the swap would introduce; it is an error that
**already exists in traced jax today**, and eager currently disagrees with
traced at the extremes. Making eager use GL would make the two *consistent*,
not less accurate in aggregate.

So the honest statement is: the lever is real (2299 crossings on the poisson
route), the accuracy cost is bounded and quantified, and the decision is a
**design question, not a mechanical change** — either let eager match traced and
accept 1e-5 at extreme aspect ratio, or make the node count adapt to |z|/R so
both paths improve. I am not making that call unilaterally inside a CI wait; it
changes numerical behaviour on a path users can hit.

Recorded with the numbers so it can be decided rather than re-derived. numpy is
untouched either way — it keeps scipy.

Note also what the grid shows about the SPLIT fix itself: at R>=0.1 the
agreement is 1e-12 to 1e-16 across four decades of |z|, i.e. the clustered-node
rule is sound where it is used; the failure is specific to R much smaller than
|z|, not general.

### 2026-08-09 — the quadrature trade-off DISSOLVES at n=100 (and traced jax has a latent accuracy bug)

Last wake I left the GL-for-eager question as a design trade-off: accept 2.6e-05
at extreme aspect ratio, or make the node count adapt. Before handing that to Jo
as a judgement call, I checked whether the second option is hard. **It is not.**

    (R,|z|)          n=50      n=100      n=200      n=400
    (0.01, 50)   2.57e-05   1.24e-10   2.04e-14   2.84e-14
    (0.01,  5)   5.88e-10   8.79e-15   2.46e-14   1.48e-14
    (0.1,  50)   1.81e-09   1.04e-14   3.87e-15   1.60e-14
    (1.0,  50)   2.12e-11   1.04e-15   6.42e-15   2.77e-14

**n=50 -> n=100 buys five orders at the worst corner; n=200 reaches ~1e-14
everywhere.** There is no accuracy-vs-speed trade to adjudicate — the rule
simply converges, and one extra *vectorized* node batch is nothing against
scipy's ~900 scalar integrand calls.

**The more important consequence, stated plainly: this is a latent accuracy
defect in the TRACED path that ships today.** Traced jax uses this GL rule at
n=50 right now, so `surfdens(forcepoisson=True)` on a traced backend is carrying
**2.6e-05 relative error at (R=0.01, |z|=50)** — not a hypothetical of some
future change. Eager gets scipy and is right; traced is wrong at that corner and
nothing tests it. That reframes the work from "an optimisation with a cost" to
"a correctness fix that also removes 2299-5307 boundary crossings".

**Not acting on it unilaterally, for two reasons that are about scope, not
nerve:** raising the order changes shipped traced values (tests with tolerances
near 1e-5 could move, and the 12 jax `test_potential` ledger entries all live on
this path), and two PRs are already in flight. It is a third PR's worth of work
with its own gate: numpy byte-identity is free (numpy keeps scipy), but the
traced-value shift needs the full traced `test_potential.py` before and after.

Queued as the concrete proposal, replacing last wake's open question:
**raise the surfdens/poisson GL order to 100 (or 200), then route eager through
it** — one change, fixes a shipped traced inaccuracy, makes eager and traced
agree, and removes the last big eager boundary hot spot. Numbers above are the
justification; the gate is a traced before/after.

### 2026-08-09 — searched before writing, and it changed the GL-order design

Went to prepare the GL-order branch and found `/var/tmp/glorder` **already
exists**, on `98c2d5c7 actionAngle: one shared _BACKEND_GL_ORDER, and correct
its documented floor`. So a named GL-order constant already exists in this
codebase — exactly the "check existing utilities before creating one" case, and
I only found it because the worktree name collided.

Confirmed on **current develop** (not just that stale branch):

    galpy/actionAngle/actionAngle.py:26      _BACKEND_GL_ORDER = 50
    used by actionAngleSpherical (2 sites) and actionAngleVertical (3 sites)

**And the right conclusion is NOT to reuse it.** Two reasons, both checked:

1. **Direction.** It lives in `galpy/actionAngle/`. `Potential.py` imports
   nothing from `actionAngle` (verified — no such import), and it should not
   start: potentials are the lower layer. Importing upward to share a number
   would invert the dependency for no benefit.
2. **It is a different quadrature.** The AA constant orders a `fixed_quad` over
   `[0, 1]` on the action radicand; the surfdens rule is a *split, clustered*
   `symmetric_quad` over `[-|z|, |z|]` on a density/Poisson integrand. They
   share only the letter `n`. Folding them into one symbol would silently
   re-order the AA quadratures too — a change I have not measured and that no
   evidence here supports.

So the surfdens PR should introduce its **own** named order near the quadrature
it governs, not import the AA one and not hardcode `100` at two call sites. The
tempting move — "there is already a shared constant, reuse it" — would have been
a coupling bug dressed up as de-duplication.

Recorded rather than acted on: the two-PR cap still holds, and this is now a
design note attached to a change whose evidence is already complete.

### 2026-08-10 — the eager-GL question, and a pre-existing numpy quadrature bug (gh#1289)

Two of my own queued plans were wrong, in opposite directions, and measuring
settled both.

**1. "Route eager through the GL rule" — I first had it as one PR with the order
raise, then dropped it entirely after reading `_quad_needs_backend`'s docstring
("scipy ... calls the integrand node-by-node so scalar-only potentials keep
working"; array-safety "NOT decidable"). Both readings were wrong.**

Forcing the GL route on eager torch over `test_potential.py -k surfdens`:
**39 s, 18 passed, 1 failed**. The one failure is `AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDisk`,
which deliberately does not opt in. The decisive part is that the guard at
`Potential.py:88-95` is a **general facility** — every potential either sets
`_backend_accepts_arrays` or raises `TypeError: Methods in X do not accept array
inputs` — and I verified it fires **loudly through composition and wrapping**
(bare / `Composite([Any, MN])` / `RotateAndTilt(Any)` all raise; none silently
wrong). So array-safety *is* decidable; what is undecidable is only the
composite's *top-level type*, which is all the docstring actually establishes.
A safe eager route is try-GL/fall-back-on-that-TypeError. Separate PR, gated on
the full eager suite.

The scipy control was SIGTERM'd at 508 s with no summary line, so `control >
508 s` is a lower bound and its counts are unknown — relaunched detached. Noting
it because the harness-backgrounded run was killed while the `nohup`'d one
survived, and because a killed run yields ZERO junitxml.

**2. A GL-vs-scipy table said `MWP14[0]` at (R=1,|z|=5) had 9.55e-06 error at
n=50 AND at n=100 — identical.** An error that does not move with order means
the rule has converged and the *reference* is the outlier. mpmath at 30 dps:

    mpmath                8.21245101525039e-09
    scipy quad (default)  rel 9.549e-06     <-- galpy's actual call
    scipy quad (tight)    rel 1.209e-15
    GL n=50               rel 1.225e-13
    GL n=100              rel 0.000e+00

`scipy.integrate.quad` defaults to `epsabs=1.49e-8`, which is **larger than this
integral's value (8.2e-09)**, so the absolute test passes on the first crude
estimate and quad returns success. Scanned: every |z| >= 5 for that potential is
wrong by 9.55e-06, while MiyamotoNagai and NFW (integrals ~5e-2) are at 1e-15.
The trigger is the integral's magnitude, not the potential or the geometry,
which is why no test catches it.

Filed as **gh#1289** — pre-existing, on the plain numpy path, so it is Jo's call
(numpy values are contractually byte-identical here). Same handling as gh#1276 /
gh#1277.

It also independently justifies the order raise: at |z|=20 GL n=50 degrades to
1.38e-08 where n=100 holds 2.01e-16.

**PRs:** gh#1285 re-running on `1f791a90` (patch-coverage test added; Windows red
already shown to be a flake). gh#1286 green but for the inherited FDM red.

   or off **tracedness** (`_quad_needs_backend` asks `under_trace`, explicitly
   not a concreteness probe). The single place data can appear --
   `c = _vertical_quad_split(...)` -- is guarded by `isinstance(c, float)`, so a
   tracer short-circuits to the `xp.where`.
2. *Helper placement.* Clean. The two new hooks sit on the base `Potential`, the
   override in `RotateAndTiltWrapperPotential`, the summations in
   `CompositePotential`. No new quadrature helper -- the existing
   `galpy.backend.quadrature` entry points are reused.
3. *Duplication.* One instance, kept deliberately. `CompositePotential._surfdens`
   and `._surfdens_poisson` share a four-line shape but differ load-bearingly:
   the first delegates to the **public** `pot.surfdens(...)` so each component
   picks its own route and its `_amp` is applied; the second delegates to the
   **private** `pot._surfdens_poisson(...)` to force that route, and must not
   apply `_amp` (it derives from forces, which already include it). Factoring
   them through a callable would hide exactly that distinction.

   Verified the bookkeeping empirically rather than by reading: composite `_amp`
   is 1.0, `composite.surfdens` matches the component sum to 3.09e-16, and the
   Poisson route matches **exactly**.

### 2026-08-10 — AdiabaticContraction lead CONFIRMED (and two invalid probes on the way)

Settled the lead I refused to file unverified last wake. It is real, and it is a
*different* bug from gh#1289's first instance.

`AdiabaticContractionWrapperPotential.__init__` integrates
`-numpy.interp(r, rgrid, new_rforce)` -- a piecewise-linear interpolant on **302
nodes** -- with `integrate.quad`. QUADPACK cannot resolve 302 interior kinks
inside its default `limit=50`, hence the "maximum number of subdivisions"
warning. Where gh#1289's first case has quad returning *immediately* (default
`epsabs` already satisfied), this one has quad trying and giving up.

    trapezoid (closed form)   -1.4176059533961423
    quad (as called today)    -1.4176051147516373   rel 5.9e-07
    quad (limit=20000, 1e-13)                       rel 5.1e-07

The integral of a piecewise-linear interpolant IS the trapezoid sum on its own
nodes, so the exact value is free. Validated the arbiter independently rather
than trusting the algebra -- dense Simpson converges onto the trapezoid value
(8.1e-11 -> 4.9e-12 -> 3.0e-13), not onto quad's. Posted to gh#1289 as a
separate instance with its own mechanism and fix. Impact stated plainly: `Phi0`
is the zero-point, so forces and orbits are untouched and only energies shift.

**Two of my probes on the way there were invalid, and both would have produced a
confident wrong answer:**

1. First probe rebuilt the integrand from `p._Rforce(r, 0.0)`, which is `nan` at
   r=0 -- every comparison came back `nan`. Caught because the output was nan
   rather than plausible.
2. Second probe picked the interpolation grid out of the closure with
   `min(arrs, key=lambda x: x[0])`. **Both** closure arrays start at 0.0 (the
   constructor prepends 0.0 to each), so it grabbed the force array as the grid
   and produced a "26x disagreement" that looked like a spectacular finding.
   Caught by disbelieving the magnitude and re-deriving: identify the grid by
   its ENDPOINT matching the integration limit, not by its start.

The second one is the dangerous class -- a plausible-looking wrong number, not a
crash ([[reproduce-the-assertion-not-a-proxy]]). Also hit
[[galpy-class-shadows-submodule]] again: `import
galpy.potential.AdiabaticContractionWrapperPotential as ACW` binds the CLASS, so
monkeypatching `ACW.integrate` silently patched nothing; `importlib` fixes it.

### 2026-08-10 — premise check: the whole-line test is COVERAGE, not a gate (and a 33x scare that was my own bug)

Before writing the whole-line test I queued last wake, checked whether it would
actually discriminate the order change. **It would not.** Backend-vs-numpy parity
on `surfdens(R, z=None)` measured at the CURRENT default (n=50):

    MiyamotoNagai  6.73e-13     Hernquist  5.65e-16
    NFW            1.27e-15     MWP14[0]   2.92e-11

All far inside any sane tolerance, so a parity test passes at n=50 **and** at
n=100. So last wake's "the PR must carry its own test for the whole-line branch"
was overstated: it is worthwhile **coverage** for a documented public spelling
that the suite never exercises, but it is not a gate for the order raise. The
order raise's real gate stays what it was — the traced 0-flip run, the
discriminating unit test that fails at n=50, and the mpmath table.

**And a scare I nearly reported as a finding.** `MWP14[0]`'s whole-line surfdens
reads `7.316e-14`, which is below scipy's default `epsabs`, so I suspected a
third gh#1289 instance. Integrating `_dens` with mpmath gave `2.439e-12` — a
factor **33** off. That looked like a serious defect for about a minute. It was
my own omission: `surfdens` returns `self._amp * integral`, and I had integrated
`_dens` without the amp. 2.439e-12 x amp = 7.316e-14. No defect.

What is left after correcting for that is real but mild: scipy's default-tolerance
whole-line integral is off by **2.9e-11** where `epsabs=0` gives 5e-16 — the same
mechanism as gh#1289 at low amplitude, and it explains the 2.92e-11 GL-vs-numpy
gap above as **scipy** being the outlier, not GL. Not filing it: one mild
instance adds nothing to an issue that already documents the mechanism with a
9.55e-6 case.
