### 2026-08-10 — de-risked the eager-GL design and it FAILED the check

Before building the eager-GL routing PR I probed its central assumption. It does
not hold, and I would have built the PR on it.

I had concluded: "the `_backend_accepts_arrays` guard is a general facility, so
array-safety **is** decidable; eager can try-GL and fall back on the declared
`TypeError`." Measured:

    MiyamotoNagai        declares False  -- but works fine with arrays
    AnyAxisym            declares False  -- correctly opts out
    Composite(Any, MN)   declares False  -- components [False, False]
    RotateAndTilt(Any)   declares TRUE   -- while WRAPPING a scalar-only potential

Unreliable in **both** directions. A wrapper forwards through its own
undecorated `_Rforce` and so *looks* array-safe — which is precisely what
`_quad_needs_backend`'s docstring says, and which I had dismissed as applying
only to the composite's top-level type. **The docstring was right; I was wrong.**

Second problem: the rejection is not pre-flight. The `TypeError` arrives **after
one integrand call**, and reaching `symmetric_quad` directly on a bare AnyAxisym
raises `AttributeError` instead. So a try/except route needs a broad catch
around a numerical routine — the kind that masks real defects.

Corrected both [[traced-surfdens-gl-order-too-low]] and STATUS.md, which
recorded the wrong conclusion as settled. The eager-GL PR now needs a different
mechanism (verified per-potential opt-in, or a cheap array probe) and should not
be built on "catch the declared TypeError".

**None of this touches the order raise**, whose case rests on the mpmath table
and the traced gate. `backend-jit/gl-order-100` stays push-ready.

Also: the Windows flake re-run is still refused — `job cannot be rerun` while
the parent run has 3 jobs in flight (18 completed, 0 queued, 3 in_progress). An
explicit refusal this time rather than a silent no-op.

### 2026-08-10 — a replacement design for eager-GL that survives the check

Having refuted the declarative design, tested the obvious replacement: a **cheap
dynamic array probe** — call `_dens` once on a 3-element array, compare against
the elementwise scalar results, cache the verdict per instance. The question
that decides it is whether any potential *silently returns something wrong*
rather than raising, which is the hazard `_quad_needs_backend`'s docstring
names.

    MiyamotoNagai / Hernquist / NFW / Plummer / DoubleExpDisk / PowerSphwCutoff
                          accepts, matches elementwise EXACTLY (0.0e+00)
    Composite(MN, Hern)   accepts, exact
    DehnenSmooth(MN)      accepts, exact
    Composite(Any, MN)    RAISES TypeError   (correct — AnyAxisym leaf)
    RotateAndTilt(Any)    RAISES TypeError   (correct)
    RotateAndTilt(MN)     RAISES TypeError   <-- wraps an ARRAY-SAFE potential
    AnyAxisym             no `_dens` at all (razor-thin; `_sdens`)

**No silent wrongness anywhere in the sample.** Where the probe says "accepts",
it matched to the last bit. Failures are conservative — `RotateAndTilt(MN)`
raises even though `MiyamotoNagai` is array-safe, so we would simply keep scipy
there: a performance cost, not a correctness one.

`RotateAndTilt(MN)` is also the sharpest evidence yet that the declarative flag
is untrustworthy: it declares `_backend_accepts_arrays=True` and is scalar-only
in fact, in the direction that would have caused a wrong answer.

**Stated carefully:** 12 potentials is a sample, not a proof. The probe also
evaluates at one (R, z), and a potential could in principle be array-safe there
and not elsewhere. So the design is *viable and evidence-backed*, not *proven*.
Any PR built on it needs the probe applied across the full potential registry,
not this hand-picked dozen.

Net from two wakes of de-risking: one design refuted before it was built, one
replacement identified and given supporting evidence. No code written on a bad
premise.

### 2026-08-10 — full-registry probe sweep: 0 silently wrong (and my metric cried wolf 4 times)

Closed the "12 potentials is a sample, not a proof" gap by probing **every
constructible potential** in `galpy.potential`:

    constructible potentials probed: 46   (unconstructible skipped: 8)
      accepts array + matches elementwise : 39
      raises (conservative, keeps scipy)  :  1
      no usable _dens                     :  6
      SILENTLY WRONG                      :  0

The first pass reported **4 silently wrong** — `CompositePotential`,
`KeplerPotential`, `NullPotential`, `SphericalShellPotential`. All four were
artifacts of my own comparison, and I checked instead of reporting:

* `Kepler` / `SphericalShell` return the correct `[0., 0., 0.]`; their density is
  zero away from the origin/shell, so my **relative** error was 0/0 -> `nan`,
  which my threshold read as a failure.
* empty `CompositePotential()` and `NullPotential` return a **0-d** `array(0.)`
  rather than shape (3,) — the value is right and broadcasts equal.

Same failure class as the earlier near-misses: a *proxy* metric (relative error)
that breaks exactly where the quantity is zero. Verified by comparing values
directly with `array_equal(..., equal_nan=True)` after broadcasting.

Two things this hands the future eager-GL PR:

1. The probe design is now backed by a **full-registry** sweep, not a sample —
   0 silent-wrongness in 46 potentials.
2. A concrete requirement: the probe must **accept a 0-d return as valid** (an
   identically-zero density legitimately returns a scalar) rather than demanding
   an exact shape match. Demanding shape equality would have mis-classified
   `NullPotential` and the empty composite as unsafe.

Residual caveat, unchanged: the probe evaluates at one (R, z). A potential could
in principle be array-safe there and not elsewhere.

### 2026-08-10 — the Windows "flake" DIAGNOSED: a marginal tolerance, not RNG (gh#1290)

gh#1286's re-run failed on the same test, which finally made me pull the actual
assertion values instead of re-running again. **My RNG-desync speculation was
wrong.**

    assert array([4.38726353e-08]) < ((0 * 1e-05) + ((1 - 0) * 1e-08))
      where 4.38726353e-08 = fabs(11.62525101 - 11.62525097)   # kpc

The two values agree to **8 significant figures**. The bar is 1e-8 **absolute**
on an 11.6 kpc distance -- ~4e-9 relative -- because

    _NUMPY_1_22 = (V > 1.21)*(V < 1.23) + (V > 1.23)*(V < 1.25)

is 1 only for numpy 1.22/1.24 (a deliberate loosening for those versions) and
therefore **0** on numpy 2.x, selecting the tight branch. The comparison is
between two **independently constructed** objects, so their agreement is bounded
by constructing the stream track twice, not by the kpc round-trip. ~4e-9
relative is right at that limit, and runner arithmetic decides it.

That fits every observation better than "flake": the same-SHA push/pull_request
split, failure on a ledger-only PR, one PR's re-run clearing and another's
failing twice. It is **runner-sensitive**, not 50/50.

Filed as **gh#1290** with the numbers. Deliberately did **not** change it:
loosening a tolerance on a `main`-lineage test to turn my own PRs green is
precisely the edit that should be Jo's call, not mine, however good the
justification. Re-running stays the lever until then.

Corrected [[windows-streamgapdf-sample-flake]], which had recorded the RNG guess
as "plausible, not yet confirmed" — now replaced with the measured mechanism.

### 2026-08-10 — profiled the AndTilted cost: it is Lever 1, with numbers

The AndTilted null result said "these need vectorisation". That is only
actionable if I know *what* to vectorise, so I profiled one representative call
(`RotateAndTilt(MWPotential2014)._surfdens_poisson` under eager jax):

    1 call = 2.054 s, 1,665,601 Python function calls

    scipy _qagse                 2.033 s   <- but only 21 integrand evaluations
    per integrand evaluation     ~97 ms
    conversion.py:1069 wrapper   1325 calls  (physical_conversion)
    _input.py:153 wrapper        1325 calls  (backend_input)
    coerce_coords                6175 calls, 0.579 s = 28 % of total
    RotateAndTilt _2ndderiv      42 calls, 1.488 s cumulative
    phi2deriv / R2deriv          189/42 each

**The cost is not the number of quadrature nodes — it is per-call overhead times
fan-out.** 21 integrand evaluations become 1325 decorated calls and 6175
coercions, because RotateAndTilt dispatches to 3 MWPotential2014 components and
each needs `R2deriv`/`z2deriv`/`phi2deriv`/`Rzderiv`, and every one of those pays
the decorator + coercion tax.

That is **Lever 1** (standing task: "eager-backend per-call overhead is ~5 ms
FLAT, 186x on a scalar call") — now confirmed as the dominant cost for the
largest remaining ledger cluster, with a concrete multiplier attached. 1325
decorated calls at ~1.5 ms is ~2 s, which is the whole measurement.

Two consequences for the roadmap:

* Raising or lowering the GL order cannot touch this. Neither can the eager-GL
  routing on its own — that removes the *scipy node-by-node* path, which would
  help, but the fan-out tax is paid per component-derivative regardless.
* The real lever is either batching the component fan-out (one call carrying all
  four derivatives, or all three components) or making the decorator/coercion
  path cheap enough that 1325 crossings stop mattering.

Recorded because it converts "needs vectorisation" from a label into a target.

### 2026-08-10 — Lever 1 quantified, and cProfile's 28% was inflated

Followed the profile into numbers. Instrumented `coerce_coords` over one
`RotateAndTilt(MWP14)._surfdens_poisson`:

    coerce_coords calls        5300
    coordinates seen           5300
      already backend + right dtype + right device   5172   (97.6 %)
      plain python scalar                             128
      numpy / None                                      0

**97.6 % of the coercion work is redundant** — those coordinates are already jax
arrays of the target dtype on the target device, and `coerce_coords` calls
`asarray_on_device` on them anyway. An early-exit is obviously available.

But I then measured what it would actually buy, instead of quoting the profile:

    asarray_on_device(already-correct array)   18.65 us
    early-exit dtype check                      0.54 us   (35x cheaper)
    5172 x 18.65 us                            96.5 ms of a ~1400 ms call = ~7 %

**So the cProfile reading of "coerce_coords = 28 % of total" was inflated by
profiler overhead** (cProfile charges per-call bookkeeping to a hot, tiny
function). The avoidable part is ~7 %, not ~28 %. Worth having the correction on
record before anyone plans work around the bigger number — including me, who
quoted it last wake.

The arithmetic points somewhere else anyway:

    1400 ms / 1325 decorated calls = ~1.06 ms per decorated call
    of which coerce_coords is ~60 us  =  ~6 %

**The dominant cost is the decorator machinery itself** (`physical_conversion` +
`backend_input` wrappers), not the coercion inside it. A coercion early-exit is a
genuine but ~7 % win; the real Lever-1 target is either fewer decorated calls
(batch the component fan-out) or a cheaper wrapper path.

Not opening a PR for this — the queue is four deep and CI-starved, and a hot-path
change to merged `galpy.backend` code deserves its own gate rather than being
squeezed in. Recorded as groundwork with the numbers attached.

### Eager-GL routing: prototyped, and REFUTED a second and third time

Built the successor to the refuted declared-flag design on a local branch
(`backend-jit/eager-gl-probe`, worktree `/var/tmp/eager-probe`, never pushed).

`integrand_accepts_nodes(xp, integrand, a, b)` in `galpy/backend/quadrature.py`
evaluates the node-wise integrand at two distinct points and compares against two
scalar evaluations — so it is not a bare `except` around a numerical routine, it
is a verified equivalence. `_quad_needs_backend` gained a third regime: numpy
always scipy (byte-identity untouched), traced always GL, eager decided by probe.

**It works for what it measures.** Routing table, both backends, x64:

    MiyamotoNagai / MWP14[0] / Composite(MN,NFW)   -> GL     3e-15 .. 9e-12 vs numpy
    RotateAndTilt(Any)                             -> scipy  (the flag says True)

That last row is the case the declared flag gets backwards, and the probe gets it
right. But **array-safety is necessary, not sufficient**:

    Composite(Any, MN).surfdens(0.8, 0.2)   numpy 0.1110   GL 0.1805   = 62% WRONG

The probe passes cleanly and the answer is wrong — no exception, no shape error.
So I tried the obvious repair, an n-vs-2n convergence check, and **it fails too**:

    case                numpy(scipy)      GL50       GL100      GL200   |100-50| |200-100|   err
    MiyamotoNagai       2.220158e-01  2.220158e-01  ...        ...      2.1e-15  4.3e-15   0.00e+00
    Composite(Any,MN)   1.110079e-01  1.804913e-01 1.804913e-01 1.804913e-01  1.4e-15  2.6e-15  6.26e-01

GL50, GL100 and GL200 agree with **each other** to 1e-15 while all three are 62 %
off. The rule converges to the wrong answer. A razor-thin disk's vertical density
is a spike at the mid-plane; every order with the same node distribution misses
it identically, so self-consistency is blind to it — the classic aliasing failure
of fixed-node quadrature.

**Conclusion: the eager-GL route is closed on all three mechanisms.** The ~28x
would need an adaptive backend rule or a human-verified per-potential opt-in.
The AndTilted ledger cluster is not reachable this way, so vectorisation is now
the only live lever on the jax ledger.

Two measurement bugs of my own, both previously recorded and both repeated:

* the probe built its node array from a **Python list**, which is float32 under
  torch and float64 under jax-x64. The f32-vs-f64 gap alone made torch and jax
  disagree on the same potential (1.5e-7 relative) and read exactly like a
  broadcasting defect. Fixed by handing `asarray_on_device` a typed numpy array.
* the first convergence script **reconstructed the integral by hand and dropped
  `_amp`**, reproducing the same 33x phantom as before. Redone through the real
  `pot.surfdens` call path with `n` injected into the rule.

### #211(B) prep: is a vectorised interpRZPotential grid build byte-identical?

gh#1274 merged (`b68c3ec9`), unblocking #211(B). Jo is about to rebase
main -> feat/backends -> feat/backends-develop, so this wake's work on it is
**measurement only, no PR** — nothing pushed, no CI added.

The seven grid-build loops (lines 246/274/302/333/358/383/408 of
`interpRZPotential.py` on main) are structurally identical: fill an `(nR, nz)`
array by calling `evaluateX(origPot, rgrid[ii], zgrid[jj], use_physical=False)`
one cell at a time. The rewrite is a `meshgrid` + one call. **The question that
decides the design is whether that is byte-identical**, since this is the numpy
path.

Measured across a 19-potential zoo x the 7 quantities, `numpy.array_equal(...,
equal_nan=True)` on a 9x7 grid, worktree at `origin/main`:

    BITEQ   94      <- vectorising is BIT-IDENTICAL wherever it works
    DIFF     5      <- all AnySphericalPotential
    RAISED   9      <- DoubleExpDisk (5), RazorThinExp (3), AnySpherical/Pot
    SHAPE    0

(Non-axisymmetric entries — DehnenBar, SpiralArms, RotateAndTilt — reported
`loop-err` because my harness called them without `phi=`. They are out of scope
for interpRZPotential anyway, so those rows carry no information either way.)

**The 9 RAISED are the easy class**: a `try/except` falling back to the loop is
safe, because the fallback is the *identical* computation, so nothing is masked —
a genuine error resurfaces in the loop.

**The 5 DIFF are the dangerous class.** `AnySphericalPotential` does not raise on
array input; it returns different numbers from the loop in **19 of 20 cells
(95 %)**. A `try/except` would sail straight past that and build the whole
interpolation grid from wrong values. So #211(B) needs a **value** check, not
just an exception check — the same conclusion the eager-GL work reached today,
arrived at independently.

**Correction to my own measurement.** I tried to settle which of loop/vectorised
is *correct* by comparing against an "analytic Hernquist" arbiter, and the
arbiter was invalid: I passed `dens=1/(4*pi*r^2*(1+r)^2)`, which is neither
Hernquist nor NFW, so it described a third profile. It duly showed loop and vec
*equally* far from it (1.167e+00 both) — i.e. it discriminated nothing.

That does not weaken the finding, because **the arbiter was never needed**:
byte-identity is defined against today's numpy path, which *is* the loop. So
`vec != loop` is disqualifying regardless of which is more accurate, and the
95 %-of-cells disagreement stands on its own. (Which of the two is physically
right is a separate question about `AnySphericalPotential`, not about #211(B).)

Also worth noting: on the **main** lineage `AnySphericalPotential` sets no
`_force_accepts_arrays` and none of its methods carry `_galpy_scalar_only` — the
flag exists only on `feat/backends`. So there is no declared signal at all here.

**Proposed design, to implement after the rebase:** vectorise, then verify the
result against loop evaluations of **one full row** (nz of nR*nz cells, ~0.4 %
overhead at the default 251x251) and fall back to the full loop on any mismatch.
A full row is deterministic over that row rather than a probabilistic sample of
scattered cells, and it is cheap. Fall back on exception as well.

### gh#1276: the fix is a substitution, not a higher order (measured)

`RazorThinExponentialDiskPotential`'s quadrature integrand contains
`sqrt(R^2+z^2-k^2+sqrtp*sqrtm)`, which goes to 0 at `k=R` as z->0: a square-root
singularity sitting exactly on the panel boundary. Fixed-order GL converges only
algebraically against that, which is why the error jumps discontinuously the
moment the `|z|<1e-6` handover gives up the exact Bessel closed form.

Arbiter: the exact z=0 closed form, validated against an mpmath (40 dps) quad of
the same integral at z=1e-9 -- they agree to 2.8e-9 / 1.3e-9 / 2.3e-10, so the
closed form IS the z->0 limit and is a valid reference at z=1e-6 to ~1e-6, far
below the errors being measured.

Relative error at z=1e-6:

    R    | n=100 SHIPS   n=300     n=1000    n=3000  | sub n=100  sub n=300
    0.5  |    5.21e-03  1.67e-03  7.54e-04  1.03e-04 |  5.38e-05   3.09e-06
    1.0  |    3.38e-03  1.08e-03  3.13e-04  4.02e-05 |  3.14e-05   1.38e-06
    2.0  |    8.94e-04  2.89e-04  6.43e-05  5.28e-06 |  3.89e-06   2.48e-07
    4.0  |    1.42e-05  4.63e-06  9.78e-07  9.81e-09 |  6.90e-08   2.57e-09

**The substitution `k = R(1-v^2)` on [0,R] and `k = R+u^2` on [R,10] at n=100
beats raising the order to n=3000, at the SAME number of integrand
evaluations.** ~100x accuracy for free. Raising `glorder` is the wrong lever:
it buys roughly one digit per 10x nodes, because the convergence is algebraic.

Residual after the substitution is 5.4e-05 at R=0.5, so this is a 2-digit
improvement, not a cure -- at exactly z->0 the integrand also has a jump in
`(k-R)/sqrtm` that a square substitution does not absorb. `sub n=300` reaches
3.1e-06 if the default order is ever raised. Both numbers go in the PR.

**Two harness bugs of mine, both caught by validating the arbiter, both of which
would have produced a confident wrong answer:**

* the first adaptive reference returned `nan` at z=1e-9 and nothing converged to
  it at z=1e-6 -- that reads as "all methods fail" but meant the REFERENCE was
  broken.
* the mpmath rebuild came out exactly 2x off, because **galpy's weights are
  `(hi-lo)*glw`, twice the standard GL weights**, with the factor absorbed into
  the `-2*sqrt(2)` prefactor. The clean 0.500000 ratio is what exposed it.
  Reconstructing a galpy quadrature from scratch: copy its weight convention,
  do not assume the textbook one.

Also mis-set my own pass gate to 1e-9, tighter than mpmath reaches on an
endpoint-singular integrand, and it reported "arbiter STILL BROKEN" on a
reference that was fine.

### gh#1277 DIAGNOSED, NOT FIXED: R2deriv is a Hadamard finite-part integral

`AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDiskPotential.R2deriv(R, 0)` carries ~1e-5 relative
error at small R, ~1e-9 at large R. Four hypotheses tested, three refuted:

1. **Already fixed on develop by gh#1278's panel grading?** No. main and develop
   give *identical* values (9.90e-06 at R=0.2 on both), so gh#1278 addressed a
   different aspect and a real fix is still needed -- and belongs on main, since
   the rebase will carry it into develop.
2. **A truncating tolerance, as in gh#1289?** No. `epsabs=0, epsrel=1e-13,
   limit=2000` reproduces the shipped value to 3 digits. The quadrature is
   converged; it is converged to the wrong number.
3. **Catastrophic cancellation in the integrand near a=R?** No. The two
   numerator terms sum to within 2e-15..1e-10 of mpmath at 40 dps, and
   `|t1+t2| ~ |t1|` -- no cancellation at all.
4. **A bad reference (the quadosc arbiter)?** No. I suspected the `zeros=`
   argument, since the integrand mixes J0 and J1 but the issue passes J1 zeros.
   Recomputing with J0 zeros gives the *identical* value, so the Hankel
   reference is robust and galpy is genuinely the one that is off.

**What it actually is.** The integrand diverges as `~1/(a-R)^2` with the SAME
SIGN on both sides:

    a-R=1e-04:  f(R+d) = 2.5656e+07    f(R-d) = 2.5686e+07

so the two sides add rather than cancel: the integral does not exist as a proper
integral, only as a **Hadamard finite part**. galpy evaluates it with
`integrate.quad(..., 0, 2R, points=[R])`, i.e. QUADPACK's QAGP, which is built
for *integrable* singularities (log, 1/sqrt). The finite number it returns is an
extrapolation artifact -- accurate to ~1e-5, and better at large R where the
singularity is relatively weaker. That is exactly the observed R-dependence.

**A correct fix subtracts the `1/(a-R)^2` and `1/(a-R)` parts analytically and
integrates the smooth remainder.** That is real work, well beyond a tolerance
tweak, and matches the issue's own "low priority" framing. NOT attempted here.

**One more harness error of mine, for the record:** I "checked the cancellation
between the half-integrals" by calling `quad` separately on [0,R] and [R,2R].
That is NOT galpy's computation -- `points=[R]` on a single call selects QAGP,
and splitting into two calls discards it. My split returned ~1e7 where galpy
returns 0.6, which is how I caught it. **When reproducing a scipy quadrature,
reproduce its ARGUMENTS, not just its interval.**

### gh#1295 audit follow-up + gh#1277 leading coefficient derived

**Audit of my own main-side PRs**, the check Jo asks for at merge time:

* **gh#1294 clean** -- `_grid_eval` covers all 7 sites, no residual grid loops
  anywhere in `galpy/potential/*.py`, one helper, no duplication.
* **gh#1295 had duplication I introduced** -- the substituted node/weight
  construction was verbatim in both `_Rforce` and `_zforce`. Hoisted to
  `_inner_nodes` / `_outer_nodes` (net -4 lines) so the rationale lives once.
  Gate: full `test_potential.py` **1328 tests, 0 failures**, then pushed.
* **No `if`->`xp.where` array-input issues** in any of the five: gh#1293/gh#1295
  are numpy-only paths on main, and gh#1294's only branch is structural
  (try/except + shape check on Python objects, not values).

**gh#1277: derived the leading singular coefficient analytically.** Writing
`d = a-R`, `s = a+R`, at z=0 `a^2-R^2 = d*s`, so the numerator factors:

    N = d^2 s^2 [ (2R^2 - 2Rd - d^2) E(m) + d^2 K(m) ]

and with `D = 2R^2 d^4 s^3` the whole integrand collapses to

    f(a) = a Sigma(a) [ (2R^2 - 2Rd - d^2) E + d^2 K ] / (2 R^2 d^2 s)

`d^2 K -> 0` (K is only log-divergent) and `E -> 1`, so as `d -> 0`

    f -> R Sigma(R) 2R^2 / (2 R^2 d^2 2R) = Sigma(R) / (2 d^2)

**The singular part is `C/(a-R)^2` with `C = Sigma(R)/2`** -- half the surface
density at the evaluation radius, no elliptic integrals left. Verified by
averaging the two sides at d=1e-5 (cancels the odd 1/d term): agreement 1.7e-08
at R=0.2 down to 8.2e-10 at R=2.

What remains is the *second* expansion: after subtracting `C/d^2` and adding
back its Hadamard finite part over the symmetric panel (`C * (-2/R)`), the
residual still carries `1/d` and `log|d|/d`. Those are odd about a=R so they
vanish in principal value, but `scipy.integrate.quad` does not compute a
principal value, so they need the same treatment. Posted both the diagnosis and
this derivation to gh#1277 so it is a starting point rather than a dead end.

### gh#1277: z=0 solved (470x), but it must not ship alone

**Second coefficient derived.** Expanding E and K about m->1 with
`1-m = d^2/s^2` and `L = ln(4s/|d|)`:

    f = C/d^2 + B/d + integrable(incl. log),
    C = Sigma(R)/2,   B = [2 R Sigma'(R) - Sigma(R)] / (4R)

B verified to 4e-06..5e-05 (residual is the O(1)/log terms leaking in at finite
d). Notably **no log/d term appears** -- the log enters only at O(1), which is
integrable.

**Working formulation, and it needs no Sigma'.** Symmetrising about a=R cancels
the odd B/d term exactly, so only C has to be subtracted:

    int_0^{2R} f da = int_0^R [f(R-u) + f(R+u) - 2C/u^2] du - 2C/R

Measured vs the mpmath Hankel reference: shipped 2.99e-06 -> **6.39e-09** at
R=0.1, 9.90e-06 -> **2.11e-08** at R=0.2. ~470x at the worst point.

**But it must NOT ship as a `z == 0` branch.** The inaccuracy spans the whole
band `|z| <~ 1e-5`, not just the mid-plane:

    |z|     0      1e-10    1e-08    1e-06    1e-04    1e-02
    rel  9.9e-06  3.3e-06  1.9e-05  1.2e-05  3.9e-09  2.7e-14

so a z==0 branch would leave z=1e-8 at 1.9e-05 while z=0 became 1e-08 --
introducing a discontinuity the size of the bug. Same trap as gh#1276's handover.

**Refuted: peak-aware `points`.** Passing `points=[R +- z, +-3z, +-10z, ...]`
to tell QUADPACK where the narrow peak sits is CATASTROPHICALLY worse --
3.40e+08 at z=1e-10, 4.85e-02 at z=1e-08. Fragmenting [0,2R] destroys the
extrapolation QAGP performs across the singularity, which is doing real work and
is why the shipped code lands within 1e-5 instead of diverging.

Remaining: the z-dependent version of the subtraction, so one formulation covers
the whole band. All three results posted to the issue.

### gh#1277 root cause: the node offsets are not representable

Two more schemes tried for the small-|z| band, **both catastrophically worse**
below |z| ~ 1e-6 while helping above it:

    |z|      shipped   graded points   tan-substitution
    1e-10   3.25e-06      3.40e+08         1.70e+08
    1e-08   1.90e-05      4.85e-02         1.84e-02
    1e-06   1.15e-05      5.12e-05         8.39e-07
    1e-04   3.91e-09      2.03e-10         4.48e-10

That shape -- help above, explode below -- is the tell, and it is NOT the
quadrature. The integrand is parameterised by `a` and recomputes `d = a - R`
internally. At R=0.2 the float64 spacing is 2.78e-17, so:

    intended d   recovered a-R          rel err     -> in d^2
    1e-08        9.9999999947364415e-09  5.26e-10    1.05e-09
    1e-10        1.0000000827403710e-10  8.27e-08    1.65e-07
    1e-12        1.0000056338554941e-12  5.63e-06    1.13e-05

and `1/(d^2+z^2)^2` amplifies it. **Any scheme placing nodes at R +- eps with
eps << R is limited by this** -- the node cannot represent its own offset. It
also explains why the shipped code degrades gracefully instead of exploding:
QAGP spreads nodes over the whole [0,2R] and never probes d ~ 1e-10, so it never
touches the cancellation; it just extrapolates and lands ~1e-5 off.

**The complete fix therefore starts with a reparameterisation**, not more
analysis: express the integrand in `d` as a primary variable (`a = R+d`,
`a^2-R^2 = d(2R+d)`, `(a-R)^2+z^2 = d^2+z^2`, `(a+R)^2+z^2 = (2R+d)^2+z^2`), so
the offset is never formed by subtraction. Then symmetrise (kills the odd term,
no Sigma' needed) and subtract the singular model with its finite part. That one
formulation covers z=0 and the band together, with no handover discontinuity.

Step 1 is mechanical rather than analytical, which makes the remaining work much
better defined than it looked. All four results posted to the issue.

### gh#1277 prototype: large win over most of the range, one decade unsolved

Reparameterised the integrand in `d = a-R` (so the offset is never formed by
subtraction), symmetrised about d=0, and used `d = z*sinh(t)` for the peak
region -- `tan` fails because `arctan(R/z)` sits within ~5e-10 of pi/2 and is
quantised there, which is the SAME representability trap one level up.

    |z|      shipped    d-param prototype
    0       9.90e-06        1.92e-10     <- 51,000x
    1e-12   1.00e-05        5.85e-04     <- WORSE
    1e-10   3.25e-06        2.31e-06     <- marginal
    1e-08   1.90e-05        5.48e-08     <- 350x
    1e-06   1.15e-05        1.18e-09     <- 10,000x
    1e-04   3.91e-09        6.06e-12
    1e-02   2.72e-14        1.78e-15

**Honest state: a large win for z=0 and |z| >= 1e-8, a regression below ~1e-11.**

I hypothesised the residual at z=1e-12 was cancellation of the ~C*pi/z peak mass
(~1e12) against the rest, and added the analytic model subtraction
`2C/(u^2+z^2)` whose integral over [0,R] is `(2C/z) arctan(R/z)` -- exactly to
handle that mass in closed form. **It did not help** (2.48e-04 -> 5.85e-04), so
that explanation is NOT confirmed and the last decade is still unexplained.

Stopping the hypothesis loop here rather than iterating further on guesses. What
is solid: the reparameterisation and symmetrisation are clearly right (they buy
2-4 orders across most of the range), and the z=0 case is essentially solved.
The `|z| <~ 1e-11` decade needs its own diagnosis, and for a razor-thin disk it
may be worth asking whether |z| that small should simply be treated as 0 -- but
that is a modelling call, not a numerics one, and it is Jo's.

### CORRECTION: run-level status is not a throughput metric

I reported "nothing completed in 41 minutes, the pool is starved by hung jobs".
The first half was measured at **RUN** level and is misleading; the second half
over-generalised.

Inspected the three remaining in_progress runs job-by-job:

    Linux/Mac build        2 active of 26 jobs   (24 done)  36-38m on test_orbit shards
    All-backend tests      3 active of 44 jobs   (41 done)  13-26m on slow jax shards
    Test doc notebooks     5 active of  5 jobs              22-31m

They are **progressing normally**. A run with 44 jobs stays `in_progress` for
hours while steadily completing work, so counting completed *runs* shows zero
throughput while dozens of *jobs* finish.

The two runs I cancelled WERE genuinely anomalous -- 4/4 jobs stuck 99-115 min on
one step, vs 22-31 min here -- so that action stands. But "the pool is full of
hung jobs" was the wrong generalisation from them.

**Metric to use:** `gh run view <id> --json jobs` and count active-vs-total jobs
plus per-job step age. Compare a job's age against its peers on the same workflow,
not against the run's age. `gh run list --json status` alone cannot distinguish
"44-job run grinding through" from "wedged".

### Stale attempt-1 CANCELLED entries are not a blocker

gh#1291/gh#1292 each showed **44 CANCELLED checks**, and I read that as "these
cannot go green until re-run". Wrong on two counts:

* `gh run list --json conclusion` showed **zero** cancelled runs on those
  branches -- because the cancelled entries belong to a run whose OVERALL
  conclusion is not `cancelled`. Resolving the check `link` back to its run id
  showed all 44 came from a single `All-backend tests` run.
* Those runs are already at **attempt 2, queued**. `gh run rerun` refuses with
  "This workflow is already running". The 44 entries are attempt-1 records that
  attempt 2 supersedes.

**How to read this:** a `CANCELLED` state in `gh pr checks` is per-attempt, not
per-check-name. Map the check's `link` to its run id and inspect
`gh run view <id> --json status,conclusion,attempt` before concluding anything
needs a restart -- consistent with the existing note that `run_attempt` is the
only reliable confirmation.

### gh#1277 SOLVED end-to-end

The missing piece was not more analysis -- it was measuring whether the last bad
decade is physically distinguishable from z=0. It is not: the mpmath reference
moves only **5.94e-09** between z=0 and z=1e-10, and ~1e-11 by z=1e-12. So
snapping |z| < 1e-9 to the z=0 branch is legitimate, with a bounded ~6e-9 error,
~3 orders below the 1.9e-05 defect.

Final scheme = reparameterise in d (kills the representability cap) + symmetrise
about d=0 (kills the odd B/d term, so no Sigma' needed) + `d = z*sinh(t)` for the
finite-|z| peak + snap below 1e-9.

    |z|        0      1e-12    1e-10    1e-08    1e-06    1e-04    1e-02
    shipped  9.9e-06  1.0e-05  3.3e-06  1.9e-05  1.2e-05  3.9e-09  2.7e-14
    new      1.9e-10  1.3e-10  5.7e-09  5.5e-08  1.2e-09  6.1e-12  1.8e-15

**Better everywhere, worst case 5.5e-08 vs 1.9e-05.** No regression at any row.

NOT opened as a PR: five are already queued and the pool is saturated, so it
waits for that batch rather than adding ~150 checks. Posted to the issue in full.

### z2deriv fixed too, via a shared helper

`_z2deriv` shared R2deriv's defect (6.47e-07 at R=0.1). The derivation fell out
cleanly: **at z=0 its K term carries a z^2 factor and vanishes entirely**,
leaving `-a Sigma(a) E(m) / (d^2 (a+R))`, so the singular coefficient is
`-Sigma(R)/2` -- exactly minus R2deriv's. Verified numerically to 5e-10 BEFORE
writing any code.

    R       0.1       0.2       0.3       0.5       1.0       2.0
    before  6.47e-07  5.06e-07  9.32e-08  2.42e-07  5.13e-08  3.62e-09
    after   4.66e-11  2.97e-11  1.05e-10  8.78e-11  3.37e-12  5.36e-13

~14,000x at R=0.1.

**Applied the gh#1295 audit lesson up front rather than after review:** hoisted
the quadrature machinery into a shared `_finite_part_quad(integrand_d, R, az, C)`
instead of copying it. The two derivatives now differ only in their integrand
and the sign of C. `_Rzderiv` is odd in z and vanishes at z=0, so unaffected.

Branch `fix/anyaxisym-r2deriv-finite-part` now has 2 commits, still UNPUSHED
pending runner capacity.

Jo pushed back on my claim that the 44 CANCELLED checks were harmless. They were
not. Actual state:

    run 31408896025 (gh#1291):  status=queued  attempt=1  jobs: 44 cancelled, 1 queued
    run 31409010327 (gh#1292):  status=queued  attempt=1  jobs: 44 cancelled, 1 queued

**attempt=1, not attempt 2.** I had conflated these with the two notebook runs I
re-ran (which genuinely were at attempt 2) and asserted the same of these without
checking. My earlier "stale attempt-1 records that attempt 2 supersedes" was
simply wrong, and **both PRs could never have gone green**: my blanket
cancellation killed 44 of 45 jobs, the 45th stayed queued so the run never
reached a terminal state, and `gh run rerun` refuses a non-terminal run.

`gh run cancel` did not resolve it either -- the run stayed `queued` because its
remaining job is itself queued and had not been picked up.

**Fix:** an empty commit on each branch, producing fresh runs on a new SHA
(gh#1291 -> c1daacb7, gh#1292 -> 823d5041). Respects the no-force-push rule.

**Lesson:** `gh pr checks` state alone cannot distinguish "superseded by a later
attempt" from "wedged and never coming back". Resolve the check's `link` to its
run id and read `status` + `attempt` + the job-state histogram. A run that is
`queued` with mostly-cancelled jobs is STUCK, not pending.

### Empty commit -> 99 checks not ~151: build.yml push: is PATH-FILTERED

Jo asked why gh#1291/gh#1292 showed 99 checks when a PR usually has ~151. The
runs on the new SHAs were **all `pull_request`; the 3 `push`-event runs per
branch were missing.**

Cause: `build.yml` (and siblings) declare

    on:
      push:
        paths: ['**', '!*', '*.py', ...]
      pull_request:
        paths-ignore: ['doc/**']

An **empty commit changes no paths**, so the `push` trigger never fires. The
`pull_request` trigger is `paths-ignore`-based and still matches. Missing ~52
checks == exactly the push-event build jobs.

**This turns out to be harmless, and arguably better.** `all-clear` is written to
succeed once every check *that exists on the commit* has finished and passed --
its own header says it "transitively requires all CI workflows ... without having
to list any of them". So 99 checks gate on 99. The merged gh#1286 had 154 only
because it carried BOTH event families, i.e. the same jobs twice -- the duplicate
push+pull_request matrix I had already flagged to Jo as a workflow-scope wish.

So the empty commit accidentally produced the lean variant: same coverage, ~35 %
fewer jobs, gate still correct. Worth knowing deliberately rather than by
accident: **an empty commit re-triggers pull_request workflows only.** Use it
when you want a clean re-run at lower cost; use a real (path-touching) commit if
you specifically need the push-event runs.

### Adopted the empty-commit recipe; gh#1294 restarted on it

Jo endorsed the empty-commit trick as standing practice, so gh#1294 was brought
back that way rather than by `gh run rerun` on its cancelled runs. Two reasons:

* re-running cancelled runs is what produced the half-cancelled **wedge** on
  gh#1291/gh#1292 (a run left `queued` with 44/45 jobs cancelled cannot be
  re-run and never becomes terminal);
* a fresh SHA gets the lean check set, since `build.yml`'s `push:` trigger is
  path-filtered and an empty commit matches no paths.

gh#1294: `6444da90 -> 10acf0b7`, 0 cancelled checks. Verified there were no
prior-SHA runs left to cancel (parking had already stopped them).

Mechanism confirmed on the MERGED gh#1286 rather than assumed: its 154 checks
were 8 runs on ONE SHA -- `Linux/Mac build`, `Windows build` and
`Test documentation notebooks` each appearing TWICE (push + pull_request), plus
`all-clear` and `All-backend tests` which are pull_request-only. So the recipe
removes exactly the duplicated half.

Recorded as memory `empty-commit-halves-ci`, including the two constraints:
the empty commit must be its OWN push (a combined push computes `paths` over all
commits), and you must NOT instead cancel the head SHA's push runs (that leaves
CANCELLED checks on the head, which fails all-clear -- the original wedge).

The z2deriv rewrite spliced `s[index('def _z2deriv'):index('def _surfdens')]`.
**`_Rzderiv` sits between those two anchors**, so it was silently removed. The
full `test_potential.py` still passed **1327 / 0** -- nothing in that file
exercises AnyAxisym's `Rzderiv` -- so it would have gone into the PR invisibly.

It surfaced only because I went to verify a claim I had already asserted TWICE on
the issue from reasoning alone: "`_Rzderiv` is odd in z and vanishes at z=0, so
it is unaffected". Instead of a number I got `PotentialError: '_Rzderiv' function
not implemented`. Checking the "obvious" claim is what caught it.

Restored verbatim from main; it needed no change. Verified against the Hankel
reference `-2pi Int k^2 J1(kR) exp(-kz) Sigmatilde dk`: 2.4e-11 at z=1e-6 down to
1.6e-16 at z=1e-1 -- already accurate. The regression test now pins Rzderiv too,
so a future splice through this region fails loudly.

**Two durable lessons** (memory `def-to-def-splice-deletes-methods`):
* a green suite is NOT evidence a method still exists;
* after any structural edit, diff the method SET against the base --
  `diff <(git show origin/main:$F | grep -o "def _[a-z_]*" | sort) <(grep ... )`
  is one command and would have caught this immediately rather than an hour later.

### Would the FULL CI have caught the _Rzderiv deletion? Measured: NO

Jo asked. I had generalised from one file ("a green suite is not evidence a
method still exists"), which was over-broad. Checked properly -- three
structural reasons, and the answer is still no:

* `test_potential.py`'s generic Rzderiv checks are `hasattr(tp, "_Rzderiv")`
  guarded (~1505, ~2504) -> deletion becomes a SKIP, not a failure.
* `test_orbit.py` explicitly EXCLUDES AnyAxisym ("has bad behavior for odeint
  and isn't really meant for orbit integration", line 263, plus two
  `rmpots.append`). Verified by deleting the method and running that file's
  AnyAxisym tests: **2 passed**.
* `test_quantity.py` only exercises unit handling on `surfdens`.

So the correct, narrower lesson: **`hasattr`-guarded generic tests convert a
deleted method into a silent skip**, and a potential excluded from the orbit
suite has unusually thin derivative coverage. Both together make the deletion
invisible to the whole matrix, not just to one file.

That also means the gold-value test I added is doing real work: it is now the
ONLY thing in the suite that would fail if AnyAxisym's Rzderiv disappeared.

### The "vectorise SCF/Multipole eval" roadmap item is MIS-AIMED

STATUS.md has listed "vectorisation of SCF/Multipole/wrapper eval, where the
1440-2641 s entries live" as the only live lever on the jax ledger. Checked it
before the rebase, and it is aimed at the wrong thing.

**1. SCF's backend eval is ALREADY vectorised.** `_evaluate_expansion`'s backend
branch says so explicitly: "flatten the broadcast coords to 1-D and evaluate ALL
points in one batched `_compute_at_point` call (no per-point Python loop, so no
O(P) unrolled XLA graph / per-call retrace)". Only the numpy branch still uses
`numpy.ndindex`, and that is byte-identity-constrained anyway.

**2. The slow tests are not multi-point evaluations.** `test_Cautun20` and
`test_DehnenBinney98` build `mwpotentials` models (DehnenBinney98 builds FOUR)
and call `vcirc` at single radii. Measured, DiskSCF(N=10,L=10):

           construct        20x vcirc
    numpy    0.269 s          0.030 s
    jax      7.309 s          5.348 s
    ratio      27x             178x

**0.267 s per scalar `vcirc` call.** Vectorisation across points cannot help a
sequence of separate SCALAR calls -- the batching never engages. So the real
lever for these entries is **per-call overhead**, which is already tracked as
task #79 ("eager-backend per-call overhead is ~5 ms FLAT, 186x on a scalar
call"), plus a 27x construction cost that no eval change touches at all.

**Harness flaw in my own measurement, stated so it is not reused:** the
`import mwpotentials` row (numpy 52.3 s vs jax 0.000 s) is meaningless -- the
module was already imported and cached by the numpy pass, so the jax arm timed
nothing. Only the explicit construct/eval split above is valid.

Action: retarget the post-rebase roadmap from "vectorise SCF eval" to
"per-call overhead + construction cost", and stop citing vectorisation as the
remedy for the 1440-2641 s entries.

### Root cause of the 1440-2641 s jax entries: the scan is TRACE-ONLY

Profiled a single scalar `vcirc` on DiskSCF(N=10,L=10) under eager jax
(10 calls, cProfile, sorted by tottime):

    12290 calls  0.345 s self / 0.441 s cum   jax ufunc_api.__call__
      300 calls  0.043 s self / 0.844 s cum   galpy .../gegenbauer.py:25

~**1229 jax ufunc dispatches per scalar vcirc call**, funnelled through
Gegenbauer, which dominates the call tree.

Reading `galpy/backend/special/_fallback/gegenbauer.py`: it ALREADY has a
`lax.scan` fast path -- but it is gated on `under_jax_trace(x)`. **Eager jax
takes the Python loop**, running the three-term recurrence N-1 times with several
`jnp` ops each; SCF stacks that over L orders, hence ~1e3 dispatches per call.

So the slow entries are:

* NOT missing point-vectorisation (SCF's backend eval is already batched),
* NOT a missing scan (it is written and used under trace),
* but the scan **only engages under trace**, and the eager suite never traces.

That is consistent with the standing "no internal jit" directive
([[no-internal-jit]]): galpy is jit-COMPATIBLE, not jit-ing. Under that rule
these entries are **structurally slow under eager jax**, and no amount of
vectorisation work changes it.

Honest options, for Jo:
1. accept them as permanently ledgered (status quo, zero work);
2. let the EAGER path use the rolled recurrence too -- but a `lax.scan` in eager
   jax is still a jax call and would change eager numerics/behaviour, and it
   edges toward internal jit, so it needs Jo's sign-off;
3. reduce per-dispatch cost generally (task #79) -- helps everything, hardest.

Recorded rather than acted on: option 2 crosses a standing directive.

## 2026-08-10 ~20:20Z — found a real defect in MY OWN gh#1277 branch

Drafting the gh#1277 PR body meant re-reading the diff rather than my notes about
it, and the diff contained a line I did not intend:

    -    @check_potential_inputs_not_arrays
         def _Rzderiv(self, R, z, phi=0.0, t=0.0):

**My "restore `_Rzderiv`" commit (6c069b00) put the method body back but dropped
its decorator.** Confirmed by counting the guard across the file: base `main` has
**6**, my branch had **5**.

This is the *second* instalment of the same mistake. The first was the def-to-def
splice deleting the method; I "fixed" it and added a gold-value pinning test — but
that test calls `Rzderiv` with **scalars**, so it passes whether or not the guard
is attached. I pinned the method's existence and its numbers, and never its
contract.

**A/B, both directions measured:**

    decorator PRESENT  -> new test PASSES
    decorator ABSENT   -> new test FAILS: "ValueError: The truth value of an
                          array with more than one element is ambiguous",
                          raised from inside the integrand at line 59
    decorator ABSENT   -> the gold-value test still PASSES  <-- the blind spot

That ValueError is exactly what the decorator exists to prevent: without it an
array call dies deep in the quadrature instead of raising a clean TypeError.

**Fix + the test that would have caught it** (commit `cb4ae823`): restore the
decorator, and pin the **contract across the whole set** rather than one
decorator's presence — each of `__call__/Rforce/zforce/R2deriv/z2deriv/Rzderiv`
must work on a scalar (so a deleted method cannot masquerade as the TypeError we
want) and must raise `TypeError` for an array in either R or z. Guard count is
back to 6 = 6 vs base; all 12 AnyAxisym tests pass; full `test_potential.py`
re-running now.

**Lesson worth carrying:** when a method is restored or spliced, diff the
**decorator set**, not just the method set. `git show --stat` and a green suite
both show nothing. Extends [[def-to-def-splice-deletes-methods]].

In the pre-merge audit I noted that `transformed_quad` and `nested_quad` keep
`n=50` while `symmetric_quad` moves to `_QUAD_N=100`, and called it "deliberate
scope, not an oversight". That was a reasonable guess, not a check. Checked it.

**Every backend quadrature call site in galpy passes `n` explicitly**, so those
`n=50` defaults are unreachable from galpy's own code — they are API defaults for
external callers only:

* `transformed_quad` — **zero external callers.** Only `symmetric_quad` calls it,
  and it threads `n=n` through, so the finite branch already gets 100.
* `nested_quad` — 6 call sites (osipkovmerrittdf, diskdf x3, sphericaldf x2), all
  passing `n=_QUAD_N_VMOM2D` or `n=_NQUAD`.
* `fixed_quad` — swept every call with a paren-matching scan rather than a line
  grep (most are multi-line). Two apparent hits, both false positives:
  `constantbetadf.py:550` is a **comment**, and `galpy/util/quadpack.py:128` is
  **scipy's** `fixed_quad` (`from scipy.integrate import fixed_quad, quad`),
  passing n positionally as scipy's 5th argument.

So `symmetric_quad` was the *only* one of the four whose default was actually
reachable — from `Potential.py`'s three sites, which is exactly what gh#1292
changes. **The PR's scope is complete, not merely narrow**, and there is no latent
"other quadrature still at 50" follow-up hiding behind it.

Worth noting the distinction that made this checkable: reaching a low default is
not itself a defect — it only matters if that integrand needs more. What the sweep
establishes is *reachability*, which is the part that could have hidden a second
instance of the gh#1289/gh#1292 accuracy class.

used at **both** line 268 (`_R2deriv`) and 313 (`_z2deriv`), while its comment

because the two derivatives do not behave alike near z=0 — for z2deriv the
first-order correction integral `int k^3 J0 Sigmatilde dk` does not converge, so
its z-dependence is not linear a priori.

Measured against the mpmath Hankel reference (relative movement of the TRUE value,
z=0 -> z=1e-9):

    R      R2deriv    z2deriv
    0.2    5.9e-08    1.9e-09
    1.0    2.4e-09    4.5e-09

**Finding 1 — the floor IS safe for z2deriv**, in fact safer: it moves less across
the floor than R2deriv does. My concern was unfounded, but it was worth the check
and is now documented rather than left to be inferred.

**Finding 2 — the comment understated its own bound by 10x.** It measured the
movement between z=0 and **z=1e-10** and concluded "snapping costs ~6e-9". The
floor is at **1e-9**, and the movement is ~linear in z, so the worst case is
~6e-8. The 5.9e-09 number was not wrong — it was quoted at the wrong point. (It
also cross-validates: my 5.937e-08 at 1e-9 is exactly 10x the comment's 5.9e-09 at
1e-10, so both measurements agree.)

Fixed in `3655d816` (comment only, no behaviour change; 12 AnyAxisym tests still
pass). Branch now **6 commits @ 3655d816**.

* **checks passed / total** — worst: the denominator grows as runs get scheduled,
  so the percentage can go *backwards* while work is being done.
* **runs completed** — better, but quantised: a 25-job run reads 0 until its last
  job lands, so a PR can look frozen for an hour while ~50 jobs finish.
* **jobs within started runs, plus a count of not-yet-started runs** — the honest
  one. Queued runs genuinely have no job count yet, so report them separately
  rather than pretending a single percentage exists.

its components do, since the evaluator just sums them. **No special case is
needed, and adding one would be dead code.** Only a composite *containing* an
array-unsafe component falls back, which is correct.

What invited the misreading was my own docstring: it described the fallback as

"composites" if the qualifier is dropped. Now stated explicitly with the sweep

IS the overhead: measured **0.251 s vs 0.008 s, 31x**, for
`DoubleExponentialDiskPotential`. That is the ~15 % build slowdown disclosed in
the PR.

corners, interior) plus both diagonals to break lattice alignment so a
stride-periodic disagreement cannot hide between samples. **19 cells at any grid
size.** Stated the trade honestly in the docstring: now probabilistic for a
*sparse* disagreement where two rows were not, but not for the failure actually
being guarded against — a broadcasting bug is whole-array, and the one real
instance disagrees in 95 % of cells, which 19 samples miss with probability 5e-25.

## 2026-08-11 ~02:35Z — Jo: backend precision must MATCH numpy/scipy precision

Jo, on discovering that `_bk_dispatch` reuses scipy for plain concrete backend
values: *"this seems fine, although I didn't realize it and I'd rather in general
that backend accuracy/precision matches non-backend (numpy, scipy) precision."*

**New standing directive**, saved as memory `backend-precision-must-match-numpy`:
a GL path materially worse than scipy on the same input is a **defect to fix**,
not an acceptable price for differentiability. Do not ledger such a gap as
"backend is approximate".

**Measured the current gap for AnyAxisym**, both paths against an mpmath Hankel
reference (not against each other):

    regime            scipy            GL(backend)
    z != 0            1e-15 .. 5e-14   1e-16 .. 5e-15   <- GL EQUAL OR BETTER
    z == 0 exactly    1e-8  .. 1e-5    2.8e+03 .. 3.4e+05

**So the directive is already satisfied everywhere off the plane** — the GL rule
is at machine precision and often beats scipy. The single violation is at exactly
z=0, where GL is not imprecise but WRONG by 3-5 orders of magnitude. That is the
existing ledger entry `jax-jit test_2ndDeriv_potential[AnyAxisym]`, whose own
comment reads "the TRACED potential is wrong at exactly the disk plane".

And it is the same mathematics gh#1296 fixes on the scipy side: at z=0 the
integrand is a Hadamard finite part (`C/d^2`, same sign both sides). So the
`_gl` port is now well-specified rather than vague — apply the finite-part
treatment (reparameterise in `d`, symmetrise, subtract `2C/d^2`, add back
`-2C/R`) to `_R2deriv_gl` / `_z2deriv_gl`.

### Three probe errors of mine along the way, all self-inflicted

1. **float32.** First probe omitted `JAX_ENABLE_X64=1`; jax silently ran f32 and a
   near-singular quadrature returned inf/nan that looked like a galpy bug.
2. **`is_backend_array(output)` proved nothing.** It returned True while the work
   ran through scipy — the numpy branch casts its result back to a backend array
   on exit. Had to instrument which `_X_numpy`/`_X_gl` method actually executes.
3. **`TracerArrayConversionError` was MY callable.** I reported that `_gl` "raises
   under jit"; it was my `lambda R: numpy.exp(-R/0.3)` surfdens, which cannot take
   a tracer. With `get_namespace(R).exp(...)` both jit and grad work fine.

That third one surfaced a real constraint worth documenting: for potentials built
from a **user-supplied callable**, the differentiable path is only as
backend-agnostic as that callable. Not a galpy defect, but it means any probe must
pass an agnostic function or it measures its own mistake.

Verified the dispatch does what it claims — jax.grad, jax.jit and torch
`requires_grad` all take `_R2deriv_gl`; plain values take `_R2deriv_numpy`; and
both autodiff grads match a finite-difference reference to all printed digits
(+8.335430e-01).

created at torch's *default* dtype rather than at the input's, losing ~7 digits.

`hyp2f1`) — the likely common cause is a constant materialised inside a special
function's fallback. NFW/MiyamotoNagai, which use no special functions, are exact.

**This is a direct violation of Jo's new precision directive**
([[backend-precision-must-match-numpy]]) and is NOT ledgered — nothing tests it,
because the suite runs with torch's default dtype set to float64.

## 2026-08-11 ~04:15Z — REAL DEFECT: backend hyp2f1 silently wrong for 0 < z < 1

Jo asked for more develop PRs and pointed at "the smaller issues". Chasing the
torch f32 lead (logged above) led somewhere bigger.

**`galpy.backend.special.hyp2f1` returns a badly wrong answer for every z > 0**,
on BOTH jax and torch (both route to `hyp2f1_fallback`; jax via
`_NATIVE_UNRELIABLE`, torch via `_NATIVE_MISSING`). Measured against scipy:

    z      -2.0    -0.5     0.1      0.4      0.8      0.95
    rel   7e-15   6e-15   5.1e-03  8.6e-02  3.9e-01  6.4e-01

20 of 30 sampled (a,b,c,z) wrong; **every** z<0 point exact, **every** z>0 point
wrong. The returned value is exactly `1 + (ab/c)z` -- the first-order Taylor
series. The fallback's own docstring says **"2F1(a, b; c; z) for real z <= 0"**,
so this is a documented domain restriction being *silently violated* rather than
broken code.

**Severity: latent, not active.** Instrumented `TwoPowerSphericalPotential`: galpy
only ever passes z in [-15.8, -0.06]. Nothing in-tree is affected -- which is
exactly why no test catches it, and exactly why it is a landmine for the next
caller.

**Fix (in progress, worktree /var/tmp/nogl):** enter through Pfaff,
`2F1(a,b;c;z) = (1-z)^{-a} 2F1(a, c-b; c; z/(z-1))`, which maps 0<z<1 onto the
z<=0 domain the existing three routes are built for. Both branches are evaluated
at a z valid FOR THAT BRANCH (never the raw z) so `xp.where`'s eager dead side
cannot feed a nan back through a gradient. Verified per parameter set:

    0 < z < 1 : 6.7e-15 .. 9.9e-07   (was 5.1e-03 .. 6.4e-01)
    z <= 0    : 4.17e-06 UNCHANGED   (pre-existing, at (1.5,0.5,3.0,-15.0))

## 2026-08-11 -- codecov: two reds, one real and one phantom

Both gh#1294 and gh#1297 went red on `codecov/patch` in the same window. They
are NOT the same problem, and the discriminator is worth writing down because I
got the first one wrong.

**Read the check-run TITLE, not the compare API.** I pulled the compare
endpoint on gh#1294, saw `patch/diff: [1, 15, 15, 0, 0, '100', ...]`, and called
it a phantom. That `'100'` is the BASE side of the totals object -- not head
patch coverage. codecov's own title said the opposite and was right:

    codecov/patch:   91.89% of diff hit (target 99.93%)
    codecov/project: 99.93% (-0.01%) compared to b68c3ec

**gh#1294 -- REAL.** `_grid_eval` has three fallbacks and only two were
reachable from the potential zoo: the try/except (AnySphericalPotential raises
on an array) and the bit-for-bit spot check (the non-broadcasting potential).
The third, `grid.shape != (nR, nz)` -- a vectorised call that SUCCEEDS with the
wrong shape -- has no potential in the zoo that does it, so it was dead code as
far as the suite was concerned. Covered with a synthetic evaluator that returns
a bad shape for array input and behaves normally for scalars; the test asserts
the vectorised call happens exactly once, the result is the cell-by-cell answer,
and it is not the zeros the bad call returned. A/B'd: fails with the guard
disabled. Pushed as 735ca0f3 (+ empty commit e64f9a4d, superseded runs
cancelled in tandem).

**gh#1297 -- PHANTOM, and provably so.** `codecov/patch 16.66%`,
`codecov/project 86.01% (-13.95%)`. A ~14-point project drop from a 20-line
change to one special function is not physically possible. The mechanism is
visible in the job list rather than guessed at: the entire patch lives in
`galpy/backend/special/_fallback/hyp2f1.py`, which is exercised ONLY by
`tests/test_backend_special.py`, and the shard running that file
(`build (ubuntu-latest, 3.14, tests/test_backend*.py, ...)`) was still
in_progress when codecov scored the commit. The coverage for the patch had
simply not been uploaded yet. Expect it to self-heal; re-run all-clear after.

That is the general rule for separating the two: a phantom has a MISSING
UPLOAD you can point at (a shard still running, or a head/base session-count
split), a real drop has uncovered LINES you can name. Don't classify on the
size of the number alone -- but do let an impossible-looking magnitude prompt
the check.

### jax: all 33 failures are ONE boundary, not 33 defects

Every jax failure is in the single `test_quantity`/`test_coords` shard, and 31
are the same error:

    jax.errors.TracerArrayConversionError: __array__() was called on traced array

plus `TypeError: ... 'DynamicJaxprTracer' and 'PrefixUnit'` and one kingdf units
assertion -- the same wall in three spellings. Failing names are
`test_potential_method_returntype` / `_returnunit` / `_value` and their
planar/linear twins.

An astropy `Quantity` must hold a CONCRETE array; constructing one calls
`__array__`, which a tracer refuses by construction. **Units and tracing are
mutually exclusive at the astropy boundary** -- no amount of backend work fixes
it. This is the "not-traceable by design (units)" category I had previously
inferred from two tests; it is now measured at full scale.

They are currently UNLEDGERED: the jit ledger holds just 2 `test_quantity`
entries, so these re-report every traced run.

**I am not writing 33 ledger entries for one systemic cause** -- that is exactly
the duplication Jo asked me to avoid. The right shape is a harness-level rule:
under `--jit`, skip the units-returning tests as a class, so the jit ledger stays
a list of REAL traced gaps. That is a design call about what the ledger means,
so it goes to Jo rather than being decided unilaterally. Recorded as memory
`units-quantity-not-traceable`.

the refs differ only by the change under test, run the byte-identical command in
both arms, and compare failing NAME SETS rather than counts. A "regression" that
disappears when the test runs alone is state pollution, not a defect.

**gh#1298**: `codecov/project` went -15.10pp -> **99.95% (+0.00%)** once its shards

### Stream-track flakiness: my mechanism was WRONG

I proposed that the two flaky stream-track gradient tests fail because the FD arm
evaluates `q0 +- h` through an ADAPTIVE diffrax solve, so a step-sequence
difference between the two perturbed solves leaks into the finite difference. The
fix would have been to pin `rtol`/`atol`.

**Refuted before writing any code.** The driver already defaults to
`rtol = atol = 1e-12` (`Orbits.py:2173`, "matching galpy's C integrators
(_parse_tol)"). Step-size noise at that tolerance is ~1e-12/(2e-4) ~ 5e-9 --
NINE orders below the 3e-3 bar the test asserts. Solver tolerance cannot be the
mechanism, and pinning it would have been a speculative edit to a delicate test
that fixed nothing while looking like a fix.

Remaining candidates, none measured, so none acted on:
  * the two arms use DIFFERENT `max_steps` (20000 direct vs 200000 recursive) and
    different adjoints -- they are not the same solve;
  * `_determine_stream_track_backend()` contains an eigendecomposition
    (`_meandO`/`_dsigomeanProgDirection`) whose branch/sign could flip.

Leaving the tests as-is. They are proven flaky by a same-SHA re-run (2 failed ->
6302 passed), so the operational answer -- re-run first -- already works, and a
speculative "robustness" change without a measured mechanism is exactly the kind
of edit that makes a delicate test worse. Recorded so the next person does not
re-derive the refuted hypothesis.

## 2026-08-12 -- gh#1298 merged; gh#1299 conventions registry (task #36)

**gh#1298 merged** into `feat/backends-develop` as **bf520538** after a clean
audit (no new conditionals, `as_numpy` is the existing shared helper, already
imported; plus an incidental `ruff format` reflow of one `integrate.quad(...)`
line, called out in the squash message).

Cron `6a357c84` alive, created 2026-08-11 -> **expires ~2026-08-18**.

### Task #36: the conventions registry had drifted 15 / 48

`tests/test_backend_conventions.py` enforces "no bare numpy in a migrated
potential's compute methods". It was gated on a hand-maintained `MIGRATED`
allowlist holding **15** classes, while **48** potential modules declare
`_backend_compatible = True`. The other 33 were entirely unchecked.

Registering them was not possible as-is: the visitor flagged **64 sites across
10 classes**. I triaged all 64 before writing anything, and **every one is a
false positive**, in exactly two classes:

  * **31 scalar constants** -- `numpy.pi` (bit-for-bit `math.pi`), `numpy.e`,
    `numpy.inf`, `numpy.nan`, `numpy.newaxis` (which IS `None`). No array
    semantics; correct under every backend. The visitor flagged any
    `numpy.<attr>` and could not tell a constant from an array op.
  * **33 uses in a numpy-guarded branch** of a dual-path method: the `else` of
    `if is_backend_array(r):`, the body of `if xp is numpy:`, the tail after an
    `if xp is not numpy: return ...`, and the numpy side of a
    `... if xp is numpy else xp....` ternary. All four dual-path modules
    (AnySpherical, interpSpherical, MultipoleExpansion, Potential) use the
    documented pattern correctly.

**Zero real defects.** So the fix was the checker, not the potentials -- gh#1299
touches no `galpy/` source at all.

What landed in the PR: a self-policing `SAFE_NUMPY_ATTRS` allowlist (a test
asserts each entry is a float/None, so an array function can never be slipped in
to blind the check); a visitor that tracks backend-reachability through `if`
guards and ternaries; and `CHECKED_MODULES` **derived** from
`self._backend_compatible = True` rather than hand-listed, so a newly migrated
potential is covered the day it lands. **15 -> 50 modules**, with all 15
previously-registered classes verified still covered.

### The A/B that mattered

An exemption is only safe if it is not over-broad, so I injected a bare
`numpy.*` call on the **backend** side of each dual-path module. First run:
three CAUGHT, `Potential.py` **MISSED**. That looked like a hole in the branch
logic. It was not -- line 816 is inside `_surfdens_poisson`, which is not in
`COMPUTE_METHODS`, so the visitor never looked at it. Re-injected at the real
`_surfdens` site (line 913): caught. All four now caught, and each of the six
guard forms ships as a *paired* case -- numpy-side exempt AND backend-side
flagged.

Worth keeping: a "missed" injection can mean the checker is blind, or it can
mean you injected somewhere the checker was never asked to look. Those are very
different bugs and only reading the enclosing `def` distinguishes them.

### Measured, deliberately not in scope

`COMPUTE_METHODS` is still a hand-list of 16 names. Across the 50 checked
modules, **100 further method defs (75 distinct names)** call `get_namespace()`
and are namespace-aware but unchecked. Measured them under the new visitor:
**0 unguarded sites**, so nothing is hiding there today. Not folded in, because
the obvious criterion ("any method calling `get_namespace`") pulls in
`__init__`, which is numpy-by-design and which the suite explicitly asserts must
stay unchecked. Filed as task #215.

    head d6898535: sessions=11  coverage=72.13   <- 16 shards not yet uploaded

Same `lines=48510` on both sides, so the "drop" is purely missing uploads. Then
watched it heal in place: **11 -> 26 sessions, 72.13 -> 86.02%**, with two
py3.14 `test_backend*.py` shards still to upload. No action needed beyond
re-running `all-clear` once it settles.

Note for next time: the session count lives at `totals.sessions`, NOT
`report.sessions` -- my first probe read the wrong key and returned 0 for both
sides, which would have told me nothing. Reading the wrong field looks exactly
like "the discriminator doesn't apply here".

### Task #49: one device anchor per CALL, not per coordinate

`@backend_input` coerced each declared coordinate separately, so `device_of()`
saw one value at a time. A numpy/python coordinate has no device -> anchors to
None -> lands on the backend default device (CPU for torch), while a CUDA
sibling stays on the GPU. Reproduced on the TITAN Xp with a spy on `_Rforce`:

    R numpy 1-D + z cuda 1-D  ->  evaluator sees R=cpu,    z=cuda:0  (result CPU!)
    R cuda  1-D + z numpy 1-D ->  evaluator sees R=cuda:0, z=cpu

Not a crash for MiyamotoNagai -- something resolves it -- but the result comes
back on the CPU, i.e. the GPU is silently lost. Whether a potential crashes or
quietly transfers depends on its arithmetic; both are wrong.

Fix: compute the anchor ONCE over all declared coordinates (the wrapper already
collects them in `probe`) and thread it into `coerce_coords(..., device=)`.

**Why the existing CUDA test missed it.** `test_mixed_coords_cross_device_cuda`
already covered "mixed scalar/array coords" -- but with SCALAR R,z. torch
accepts a 0-dim CPU tensor in a binary op with a CUDA one, so a per-coordinate
anchor sails straight through. Only a **non-0-dim** numpy sibling exposes the
split. Extended that test with array siblings in both orders.

**A CI-runnable regression test without a GPU:** torch's `meta` device works as
a second device. `device_of(meta tensor)` = meta; a numpy sibling coerced with a
meta anchor lands on meta, and without one lands on cpu. So the property is
checked on every runner, not only where a GPU exists.

Both tests verified to FAIL without the source change:
  * `split anchor: R=meta, z=cpu, phi=cpu`
  * `assert 'cpu' == 'cuda'`

Gates (all complete, from finished runs): numpy `test_potential.py` **1324
passed**, forced torch **1288 passed**, forced jax **1276 passed** (57 min),
CUDA device test passed. Committed locally as 51a8def9 on
`backend-jit/coerce-device-anchor`; opens as a PR once gh#1299 lands.

Incidental: `git stash push -- <paths>` from a worktree is still repo-wide.
Used it for the A/B and it popped cleanly, but verified afterwards that the main
worktree's uncommitted `coords.py` was untouched. Two worktrees remain the safe
way to A/B.

## 2026-08-12: the units/--jit "policy" was a bug — 33 -> 8

Jo asked what the units/`--jit` harness-skip policy was. Answering it properly
meant checking the premise, and the premise was wrong.

**I had recorded these 33 jax --jit failures as "astropy Quantity cannot be
traced; units and tracing are mutually exclusive by construction; this is not a
galpy defect and no amount of backend work fixes it."** I inferred that from the
error text on 2026-08-11 and never tested it.

The real cause is decorator ORDER. Decorators apply bottom-up, so:

    @potential_physical_input      1. strip INPUT units
    @backend_input("R","z",...)    2. <- jit boundary
    @physical_conversion("force")  3. <- builds the Quantity, INSIDE the trace
    def Rforce(...)                4. body

`Quantity.__new__` calls `__array__`, which a tracer refuses. Traceback proves
the nesting: `traced_call` -> `_jit.py:159 shim` -> `conversion.py:1015 wrapped`
-> `astropy/units/quantity.py:526`.

**The A/B that settled it before any real work:** swapping the pair in
`Potential.py` ONLY moved the failure — `pot(1.1,0.1)` and `pot.Rforce(...)`
went from failing to PASSING, and it then failed at `pot.rforce(...)`, a method
in a file I had not swapped. Units attach fine once they attach after the trace
returns a concrete array.

**Fix:** 75 sites, 7 files, every one in the wrong order (Potential 49,
planarPotential 14, linearPotential 4, DissipativeForce 3, sphericaldf 2,
planarDissipativeForce 2, Force 1). Diff verified a PURE reordering: 75 added,
75 removed, identical as multisets.

**Measured (finished runs, not partial):**

    jax --jit test_quantity+test_coords :  33 failures ->  8
    numpy test_quantity                 : 244 passed, 0 failed
    numpy test_potential                : 1288 passed, 0 failed

**Structural invariant** added to `test_backend_conventions.py` (where the other
source-structure checks live, so no new home and no duplication): for any method
carrying both decorators, the units decorator must be the OUTER one. A/B'd —
reverting the source makes it fail on exactly the 7 files, naming the methods.
Covers all four `physical_conversion*` spellings; widening from 2 to 4 found no
further violations, confirming 75 was the complete set. Carries a glob guard so
an empty file list cannot make it vacuous.

**The residual 8 are a different mechanism** (task #217): `sphericaldf`'s
`vmomentdensity` and friends carry `@backend_input` but NO `@physical_conversion`
— they build the Quantity INLINE in the body,
`units.Quantity(as_numpy(out) * fac, unit=u)`, and `as_numpy` on a tracer is the
`__array__` call. No decorator to reorder, which is precisely why the invariant
cannot see them. Needs restructuring, not reordering.

**Lesson, now in memory:** "impossible by design" is a claim that needs a test
like any other. I was one step from ledgering 33 tests as permanently
unfixable — writing a policy for them — on the strength of reading an error
message. A five-minute decorator swap refuted it. Reach for the experiment
before the category.

Committed 9204e778 on `backend-jit/units-jit-boundary`, held until gh#1300
merges (one PR at a time). galpy-jax push access restored by Jo, 977 commits
pushed.

## 2026-08-12: gh#1300 caused a 180x perf regression — found only by durations

The forced-jax orbit group-5 shard on gh#1300 failed with two TIMEOUTS. Not
marginal:

    test_orbits.py::test_integration_dxdv_2d            develop 1.7 s -> 300 s
    test_orbits.py::test_integration_dxdv_2d_rectInOut  develop 1.7 s -> 300 s

Neither is ledgered anywhere, so both normally pass. Measured by pulling the
junit artifacts for the SAME shard from develop run 31601434841 and PR run
31601564919 and comparing `time=` per testcase.

**Cause.** gh#1300 computes one shared device anchor and hands it to every
coordinate's coercion. Correct for mixed devices — but a numpy/python coordinate
that previously got `device=None` now gets an EXPLICIT device, and naming a
device commits the array instead of letting the backend place it:

    asarray_on_device(..., device=None)  : 134.3 us/call
    asarray_on_device(..., device=<dev>) : 397.6 us/call   (3.0x)

My first guess was that `jnp.asarray(device=...)` was RAISING and hitting the
documented fallback path. It does not raise — it is purely cost. Worth checking,
because the fix differs.

**Fix (pushed, e9df1561):** ask the namespace once (cached) what device it places
a new array on, and drop the keyword when the anchor equals it. CPU-only runs go
back to the `device=None` fast path; a CUDA sibling on a CPU-default run still
gets the explicit anchor, so the mixed-device bug stays fixed. `default_device`
lives in `_namespaces.py` beside `device_of`/`asarray_on_device`.

**Could not validate locally.** Those two tests take >10 min on this box under
forced jax in BOTH arms — a ~350x discrepancy against CI's 1.7 s — so local
timing is not a valid instrument for them. I checked the obvious suspect and it
was WRONG: `_ext_loaded: True` in both worktrees, so it is not a missing C
extension (the .so files just are not at `galpy/*.so`). Verification therefore
goes back to CI, which is the instrument that produced the original numbers.

**The lesson worth keeping.** Every VALUE stayed correct here; only the time
changed. I had verified gh#1300 against numpy/torch/jax value suites and a CUDA
probe, and all of them passed. No value assertion can catch this class — it took
a duration comparison against the baseline shard. That is a concrete argument for
treating the perf/timeout shards as part of the gate rather than noise.

Also this wake: gh#1302 (an as_numpy fix applied directly to feat/backends) was
CLOSED at Jo's direction — fixes do not go to feat/backends; the eventual
develop->feat/backends merge (gh#1204, currently draft) resolves those reds. A
red there whose fix already exists on develop is EXPECTED state, not a task.
Recorded as memory `no-direct-fixes-to-feat-backends`.

## 2026-08-12 (evening): real GitHub stack; units arc closes 33 -> 2

### Stack #1304 is a REAL GitHub stack now

Jo: *"1303 doesn't show as a real stack"* — correct. Setting `--base <branch>` is
the OLD manual convention; GitHub has a native feature with its own extension:

    gh extension install github/gh-stack
    gh stack init --base feat/backends-develop <lower> <upper>   # adopts existing branches
    gh stack submit --auto                                       # -> "stack #1304"

`init` adopted both branches WITHOUT rewriting them (SHAs verified unchanged
before/after) and `submit` reported "up to date" rather than force-pushing, so
it is safe against the no-force-push rule — but check the SHAs anyway, because
submit pushes every branch and a rewrite would silently become a force-push of
an open PR.

gh#1300 deliberately stays OUT of the stack: independent files, so stacking it
would invent an ordering constraint that does not exist.

Jo also asked about merge cost: merging the bottom retargets the upper PR and a
cascading rebase changes its SHA, so it pays a FULL fresh CI run. N layers
merged one-at-a-time costs ~N^2/2 runs. Plan: let the stack reach 3-4 layers,
merge bottom-up in one sitting, one `gh stack sync` at the end.

### gh#1300: a 180x perf regression that no value assertion could catch

Covered in the previous entry; the fix (`default_device`, skip the device
keyword when it cannot change placement) is CONFIRMED by CI:
**300 s timeout -> 3.4 s / 3.5 s pass**. Residual ~2x vs develop's 1.7 s, which
is real and stated in the PR rather than glossed.

Then CI found a SECOND thing on the same PR, and this one was mine: adding a
keyword-only `device=` to `coerce_coords` broke two tests that monkeypatch it
with a positional-only `spy(xp, *coords)`. I have a memory that says to grep
tests/ for the changed symbol; I did not run it. Running it afterwards found a
SECOND spy that CI had not reached yet — so fixing only what CI reported would
have left a red for the next run.

### The units arc: 33 -> 2, and cause B is not a defect

gh#1301 (decorator order, 75 sites) took it 33 -> 8. gh#1303 (hoist the input
parse outside the boundary for sigmar/sigmat/beta/vmomentdensity) took it 8 -> 2.

Two of my own classifications were wrong along the way, both from reading error
text instead of reading the code:

  * I drafted gh#1301 believing its swap made df methods silently wrong under
    jit. **Develop is already wrong** (0.04439 vs the correct 0.14091,
    identical) — the swap is neutral and the bug predates it. Never measured
    the baseline before asserting causation.
  * I filed the kingdf `nan` as an independent numerical defect (cause C). It
    was downstream of the same cross-backend cached state as cause A. One
    mechanism, not two.

And cause B, twice mis-filed ("astropy is untraceable", then "units on stored
parameters"), is actually: **AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDiskPotential is DEFINED BY
a user-supplied callable**, evaluated inside the traced region, and the tests
pass numpy/units lambdas:

    surfdens=lambda R: numpy.exp(-R / (1 * units.kpc)) * units.Msun / units.kpc**2

`numpy.exp(tracer)` calls `__array__`; `tracer * PrefixUnit` is meaningless. No

### Defect 1 (pre-existing, numpy path): quad's absolute tolerance truncates

The old assertion was

    assert numpy.fabs((1.0 - expdisk.vcirc(...) / diskpot.vcirc(...)) < 1e-10)

— `fabs` wrapping the *comparison*, so it is `fabs(bool)`: every ratio above one
passed and only the too-large direction could ever fail. Fixing the parens made it
fail at **1.04e-5**.

Not the fix's fault. Surface densities agree to 2e-16; the disagreement is
R-dependent (5.7e-5 at 3 kpc → 1.3e-6 at 9 kpc). Cause: with `amp=1e10` carrying
the normalization, `_sdens` returns ~1.8e-12, so `scipy.integrate.quad`'s default
`epsabs=1.49e-8` is four orders LARGER than the integral itself and quad returns
early. Moving the 1e10 into the callable (`amp=1.0`, `_sdens` ~0.018) restores
**2e-13**. So AnyAxisym's accuracy depends on an arbitrary split of normalization
between `amp` and `surfdens` — silently. Same class as the surfdens 9.55e-6 case.
The test now compares in the O(1) form at 1e-10 and says why.

### Defect 2 (traced-only): z==0 loses the graded panels

Chasing a tolerance for the backend arm, found that at **z == 0** the traced force
is ~5.7e-5 off from numpy while eager is exact (eager reaches `_Rforce_numpy` via
`_bk_dispatch`; only the traced path runs the GL split). In `_bk_split_quad`,
`dmin = where(|z|>0, min(4|z|, half), half)`, so at z==0 `ratio = dmin/half = 1`
and all K=24 graded panels collapse to **zero width** — the quadrature degenerates
to 4 panels of GL-50. Deliberate (the comment cites an FD-in-R blow-up), but the
cost was never measured. It is now (task #218):

    eps      Rforce rel-err   Pot rel-err   FD-d2-in-R rel-err
    None      5.67e-05         4.17e-05      2.82e-04    <- current
    1e-2      5.67e-07         4.17e-07      8.77e-03
    1e-3      5.65e-08         4.17e-08      2.33e-02
    1e-4      3.94e-09         4.17e-09      2.34e-01
    1e-5      3.21e-08         4.18e-10      1.28e+01

Value accuracy buys 100–10000x; the R second derivative degrades 30–45000x. The
cusp the original comment warned about is real, so this is a genuine tradeoff, not
a free win — parked as #218 pending a measurement of analytic `R2deriv` and of
`jax.grad` (rather than the FD proxy) before picking an eps.

`tests/test_backend_anyaxisymdisk.py` asserts z==0 only in the EAGER test, which is

### Method note: a reference computed inside the forced block is not a reference

My first eps scan showed the baseline as *exactly* correct and every candidate as
5.6e-5 wrong — the opposite of the truth. I had computed the numpy references
inside `with use("jax", force=True)`, so the boundary coerced them onto the traced
path and I was comparing the traced path against itself. Recomputing the references
outside the block reproduced the earlier probe exactly. Same shape as the
`use()`-is-a-context-manager and value-checks-cannot-see-a-fallback traps: the
control arm has to be built where the thing under test cannot reach it.
