### Correction to my own ledger note: the grading IS the cause

`tests/backend_xfail.txt:319` documents the traced disk-plane defect and concludes,
from an A/B I ran earlier, *"the cause is common to both ladders and is NOT the
grading ... do not start from the quadrature ladder."* I started from the
quadrature ladder anyway (having forgotten the note), and the note is wrong.

The A/B swapped the **dyadic** ladder (`xp.maximum(Rp * 2**-k, dmin)`) against the
**geometric** one (`ratio = dmin/half`). But at `z == 0`, `dmin == half` in *both*,
so both arms collapse every graded panel to zero width. Neither arm had grading on
at the plane. The A/B varied the ladder's *form* while holding fixed the very thing
it drew a conclusion about — the same "arms must differ in one thing" trap, and the
byte-identical failure on both sides is exactly what a held-fixed variable produces.

Varying it properly (z-independent floor `dmin = eps*half` at z==0) and reproducing
the note's own quantity — one-sided `dPhi/dz` at R=0.5, dz=1e-8:

    eager (correct)   +4.436e-04
    current code      -8.285e+03     (note reports +7.35e+03; same pathology)
    eps=1e-2          -8.077e+01
    eps=1e-3          -6.184e+00
    eps=1e-4          +1.274e+00

and traced `Phi(z=0)` converges to the eager value as the floor tightens.

Not a finished fix — eps=1e-4 is still ~2900x off, and it trades against `R2deriv`,
which is *already* catastrophic on current code at the plane (traced -2.7e+04 vs
numpy -2.5788, the latter confirmed independently by FD-of-numpy-force to 6 digits).
Traced `R2deriv` degrades progressively below |z| ~ 1e-4. So the honest statement is
that grading is the dominant cause and buys 100-6500x, the residual needs its own
treatment, and the objective (value + first derivative vs second derivative) has to
be chosen before picking an eps. Parked as #218 with the numbers rather than rushed
into the stack.

Worth noting what the AD column did: `jax.grad(Rforce)` **improves** 9.6e-5 -> 7.3e-8
under grading. My earlier "the second derivative degrades" line came from an FD
second difference — a different quantity from the first-derivative AD result, and I
had been about to treat them as one.

## 2026-08-13 — gh#1303 real red fixed (entry-point checker vs. the units hoist)

Cron re-arm confirmed working: `351c0c5a` fired on schedule at :13.

gh#1303's py3.14 `test_backend*.py` shard went red on a REAL failure, not codecov:

    test_coordinate_entry_points_are_decorated_or_listed
    assert not ['sphericaldf.py::sigmar(r)', 'sphericaldf.py::sigmat(r)']

Self-inflicted, and structural. Hoisting unit parsing outside the trace boundary
turns a public entry point into

    @physical_conversion("velocity", pop=True)
    def sigmar(self, r):
        return self._sigmar_backend(conversion.parse_length(r, ro=self._ro))

    @backend_input("r")
    def _sigmar_backend(self, r): ...

`@backend_input` MUST sit inside the unit parsing (that is the whole point of the
PR), which moves it off the public method — so the checker saw sigmar/sigmat as
uncoerced.

Fixed the checker, not the source: an entry point counts as coercing if it hands
one of its OWN coordinates to a function carrying `@backend_input` in the same
module. Listing them in `_UNDECORATED_BY_DESIGN` would have been a lie — they are
not undecorated by design.

The "hands one of its own coordinates" clause is the part that matters. A rule of
"mentions a decorated helper anywhere in the body" would excuse an entry point
whose arguments never get coerced. Two synthetic negative controls, both still
caught: (a) no delegation at all; (b) calls the coercing helper with a literal
instead of its coordinate. So this is a STRONGER invariant than the one it
replaces.

Gate: `tests/test_backend_input.py` 26 passed on numpy, `--backend jax`, and
`--backend torch`. Pushed as 877fb5ad.

Process note: I never ran `test_backend_input.py` locally before pushing #1303,
despite the forced-backend-gate-before-push rule naming exactly that. CI found it
~7h later. The gate is cheap (15s) and I skipped it.

## 2026-08-13 (05:19Z) — what the two AnyAxisym xfails actually demand

gh#1303's fresh run after 877fb5ad is clean so far (149 pending, 0 failures); the
earlier codecov reds cleared with the new run, which is what the partial-upload
phantom reading predicted. gh#1305 still parked with cancelled runs.

Jo asked whether the two ledgered AnyAxisym xfails will be fixed. I gave a
qualitative answer last wake; here is the quantitative one, derived from the
assertions rather than from proxies (which is what tripped me up before).

`test_2ndDeriv_potential` has tol 10**-4.5 and **squares both sides**, so the
relative tolerance is 10**-2.25 = 5.6e-3. Its grid includes `Zs = 0.0`, and it
compares `evaluateR2derivs` against

    mRforcederivR = (Rforce(R) - Rforce(R+dr)) / dr,   dr = 1e-8

With |R2deriv| ~ 2.5 that allows ~1.4e-2 absolute in the FD, and the FD divides by
1e-8 — so it needs traced `Rforce` accurate to **~7e-11 absolute** (~3e-11
relative). Current traced `Rforce(z=0)` is 1.3e-4 absolute; the grading floor got
to 8e-9. Both miss by orders of magnitude. And `tR2deriv` itself is ~1e4 out,
which needs the finite-part port. **This test needs BOTH fixes, not one.**

`test_forceAsDeriv_potential` one-sided-differences Phi with dz=1e-8, so it needs
traced Phi to ~1e-12 absolute.

So both reduce to one requirement: **traced quadrature at z==0 must reach ~1e-11
to 1e-13 relative.** Panel grading cannot get there — that is now proven rather
than suspected, since the floor bought four orders and moved neither assertion. It
needs the ellipkm1 log singularity handled analytically inside a traceable
fixed-node scheme: port `_finite_part_quad`, plus an analytic treatment for the
evaluate/Rforce integrands, with the z==0 / z>0 branches selected by `xp.where`
(both arms evaluated, each at a harmless argument).

Structural framing worth keeping: numpy has TWO singularity treatments the backend
lacks — `_quad_apeak` (zforce, Rzderiv) and `_finite_part_quad` (R2deriv,
z2deriv) — and `_R2DERIV_ZFLOOR` is numpy-only. The backend runs one generic
graded-panel rule for all six. Also, `_bk_dispatch` routes CONCRETE eager backend
input to scipy deliberately, so "eager is correct" in the old xfail note says
nothing about the GL code: eager never runs it.

Honest assessment: this is a numerical-methods project, not a quick fix. scipy
reaches ~1e-16 on these integrals so the target is not absurd, but a fixed-node
traceable scheme has to earn it analytically. NOT started this wake — recording
the requirement was the useful output, and starting a speculative implementation
against an unquantified target is exactly how the grading floor wasted a cycle.

### Feasibility of fixing the two xfails: measured, and it moved twice

**First correction, to myself.** `test_2ndDeriv_potential` SQUARES both sides of
its 10**-4.5 tolerance, so the relative tolerance is 10**-2.25 = **5.6e-3**, not
the much tighter number I derived last wake. That changes the verdict on half the
problem.

**Arm (a), the R2deriv value — FEASIBLE.** Prototyped the numpy finite-part
decomposition with FIXED Gauss-Legendre nodes (i.e. traceable) against the scipy
reference:

    R=0.5   n=50 1.6e-4 | n=100 4.1e-5 | n=200 1.0e-5 | n=400 2.6e-6 | n=800 6.4e-7
    R=1.0   n=50 2.8e-5 | ...                                        | n=800 1.1e-7
    R=2.0   n=50 3.4e-6 | ...                                        | n=800 1.4e-8

Convergence is algebraic ~1/n^2, but 5.6e-3 is met at n=50 with 1.5 orders to
spare. So porting `_finite_part_quad` with plain GL nodes fixes arm (a). My
earlier "needs ~117k nodes" used the un-squared tolerance and was wrong.

**Arm (b), the FD-of-Rforce comparison — BLOCKED.** It needs traced `Rforce` to
~7e-11 absolute. Current is 1.3e-4; the grading floor reached 8e-9 and got WORSE
at eps=1e-5 (3.2e-8), so it floors near 1e-9 — about 100x short.

**Why no quadrature rule rescues arm (b).** The finite-part integrand is a
difference of two ~1/u^2 quantities and loses ~2 digits per decade. Measured at
R=1:

    u=1e-2 -> +0.6622   (cancelling 7.5e+02)
    u=1e-6 -> +1.0921   (cancelling 7.5e+10)
    u=1e-8 -> +1.7500   garbage
    u=1e-9 ->  0.0      total loss

Usable only for u >~ 1e-7. That is why tanh-sinh — the rule actually designed for
endpoint singularities — DIVERGES here: rel-err 1e6 at n=200, 1e21 at n=400, nan
at n=800, because its nodes reach u ~ 1e-20. The failure is floating-point
cancellation, not the quadrature. Plain GL survives only because its smallest node
happens to sit at the usable edge. Removing the cancellation analytically needs
Sigma'(R), which the file itself says is unavailable for a user-supplied callable.

**So: not fixable by quadrature engineering.** Two options, both Jo's call:
(1) obtain Sigma'(R) — an optional derivative callback, or FD the user's Sigma
(reintroduces error); an API change. (2) change the traced-path test contract —
both tests amplify quadrature error by 1e8 via a dr=1e-8 finite difference, and a
larger dr or a central difference tests the same physics without it; numpy passes
as written, so this is a deliberate weakening.

Total cost of settling this: about 40 minutes of prototyping, no code pushed. That
is the right trade against building a traceable finite-part port that would have
fixed one arm of one test and left both xfails in place.

### Local: the Hadamard rule exists and is measured

Added `finite_part_quad(xp, integrand, b, *, c, peak_width, n, device)` to
`galpy/backend/quadrature.py` (uncommitted). It returns the INNER integral only —
the `-4` prefactor and the `[R,inf)` tail stay with the caller, since those are
AnyAxisym conventions and not part of a general rule. Both branches are evaluated
with a guarded width because `peak_width` may be traced. `xp.asinh` confirmed
present on numpy, jax.numpy and array_api_compat.torch.

Validated against scipy's adaptive `_finite_part_quad` on the REAL R2deriv
integrand:

    R    z       rel-err n=100   rel-err n=400
    0.5  0       4.06e-05        2.55e-06
    0.5  1e-8    1.39e-07        1.23e-05   <- WORSE at higher n
    0.5  1e-4    2.47e-12        6.32e-10
    1.0  0       7.10e-06        4.47e-07
    2.0  0       8.70e-07        5.48e-08

Against the current traced path's **3.8e+03** at z=0 that is an ~8-order
improvement, and inside the 5.6e-3 the test needs.

Two things the numbers teach, both now written into the rule's docstring so the
next reader cannot undo them:

* **n=100, do not raise it.** At z=1e-8 the error GROWS with n (1.4e-7 -> 1.2e-5)
  because more nodes reach closer to the origin, where `sym(u) - 2c/u^2` is
  cancellation noise. Same floor that makes tanh-sinh diverge. It is a property of
  the integrand, not of the order.
* numpy's `_R2deriv_numpy` snaps `az` to 0 below `_R2DERIV_ZFLOOR = 1e-9` — which
  is why z=1e-10 reproduces the z=0 row exactly. The backend caller must apply the
  same floor, or the sinh branch gets entered at a width where it cannot work.

next. Still a correctness fix, still will NOT flip either xfail.

## 2026-08-13 (08:5xZ) — codecov caught a REAL bug I introduced

gh#1303 finished: 150 SUCCESS, `all-clear` FAILURE (it fails *because* codecov
does), `codecov/patch` green, `codecov/project` red. With sessions finally EQUAL
(28 vs 28) the phantom explanation was exhausted:

    head 877fb5ad  lines=48587  hits=48556  misses=31  99.93
    base 5b063cf6  lines=48520  hits=48500  misses=20  99.95

A real +11 misses. Per-file diff put ALL ELEVEN in `galpy/backend/_jit.py`,
0 -> 11.

**The cause is a bug I wrote earlier in this PR.** The namespace guard tested

    not getattr(xp, "__name__", "").startswith(mode)

and the torch namespace is `array_api_compat.torch`, whose `__name__` does NOT
begin with "torch". So under `jit("torch")` the guard matched EVERY call and
returned NOT_TRACED: **torch tracing was disabled everywhere**, and the torch
shim became dead code — hence exactly 11 uncovered lines.

No test caught it, and structurally no test could: the suites assert values, and
an untraced call returns the same values as a traced one. torch --jit stayed green
while tracing nothing. This is the same blind spot `assert_jit_matches_eager` was
written for (a value check cannot see a missing trace) — only coverage saw it.

Fix: use `name_of_namespace`, which already existed in `_namespaces` and maps
`array_api_compat.torch -> "torch"`. My guard had hand-rolled a worse copy of an
existing helper — the duplication class the loop tells me to audit for, and I
introduced it. Also allowed numpy coordinates to stay traceable (both jax.jit and
torch.compile accept them; only a DIFFERENT backend framework must stay eager),
which restores the pre-guard behaviour that covered those lines.

Gate this time (I skipped it when the guard first went in): 272 passed on each of
jax eager, jax --jit, torch eager, torch --jit; 26 passed on numpy. Pushed as
4fa9ba4b.

**Lesson worth keeping: do not dismiss codecov/project as phantom by pattern.**
Three checks in a row this run WERE phantom (sessions 6/55, 25/28, 27/28) and the
fourth was real. The session-count comparison is what distinguished them, and it
only becomes decisive once sessions are equal.

test checks the ROUTING instead:

    jit(jax)   -> jax traces, numpy traces, torch stays eager
    jit(torch) -> torch traces, numpy traces, jax stays eager

It reports the whole routing table rather than failing on the first mismatch,
which matters: a `__name__` prefix test gets the numpy entry wrong as well, and
stopping there would hide the torch entry — the one that was actually broken.

**A/B'd, because a passing test proves nothing.** Restoring `startswith(mode)`
makes it fail with

    jit(jax) routed the wrong namespaces -- numpy: eager (expected traced)
    jit(torch) routed the wrong namespaces -- numpy: eager (expected traced);
                                              torch: eager (expected traced)

so the numpy and torch regressions are each caught, independently. 28 passed with
the fix. Pushed as 0d721893.

This is the third time this class has bitten: a value-based check cannot see a
missing trace, a numpy fallback, or a silently-eager backend. `count_boundary_crossings`
and `assert_jit_matches_eager` exist for exactly this, and neither covered the
mode-vs-namespace routing. Now something does.

### Two verification lessons from this one

* **AST, not grep, for import checks.** Two shell probes in a row (grep on a
  40-line window, then an awk range) reported the `name_of_namespace` import as
  MISSING when it was present in all eight files. Parsing the file answers;
  pattern-matching the source guesses.
* **A racing waiter reports an empty run as a pass.** My first gate waiter polled
  `pgrep` for the pytest process, ran before pytest had spawned, found nothing and
  exited 0 — leaving a log with `### numpy` and no result line. Reading that as
  "gate complete" would have meant pushing on a run that never happened. A header
  with no result is not a pass. Re-armed on the PARENT bash pid, which cannot
  race, and that is the pattern to reuse.

## 2026-08-13 (21:19Z) — #66 characterised: narrow spikes, not RNG fragility

gh#1308: 54 SUCCESS, ~97 pending, codecov red at 54/153 (partial upload, not
decidable). Local work went to #66.

Three measurements, each correcting the previous:

1. **Is it batch-dependent?** No. The same x evaluated alone gives the identical
   3.576e-09, and BOTH arms are bit-identical in and out of batch (0.000e+00). So
   the error is a function of x.

2. **A uniform scan over [-3,3] found nothing** — max 1.1e-11, median 1.2e-16. I
   nearly concluded the spike was not reproducible. It was ALIASING: grid spacing
   0.025, and x=1.543 falls between samples at 1.525 and 1.550.

3. **Resolved properly** (361 points over [1.50,1.59]):

       peak         x = 1.543750   err = 3.590e-09
       FWHM         ~0.001
       local floor  5.551e-17   -> the spike is 6.5e7x the floor
       spikes at    x ~ +-1.54 and +-3.4
       fraction of a fine grid with err > 1e-10: 0.057%
       => P(>=1 of 100 normal draws hits a spike) ~ 5.6%

   Same order as the ~12% flake rate measured directly, so the model holds.

x = +-3.4 is exactly the stream/impact position coordinate, so these are geometric
coincidences rather than statistical tails.

**Conclusion: seeding would have been wrong.** It picks a draw that misses spikes
0.001 wide and buries a 6.5e7x local error blow-up in
impulse_deltav_general_curvedstream. #66 rewritten accordingly; the open question
is which arm is wrong at those offsets, to be settled against a high-accuracy
reference rather than by assuming the analytic Plummer arm is right.

Method note: a scan that finds nothing has to be checked against its own
resolution before it is believed. Mine had spacing 25x the feature width.

## 2026-08-13 (22:19Z) — #66 ROOT-CAUSED: scipy quad default tolerances, again

gh#1308: 108 SUCCESS, ~45 pending, head codecov 26/28 sessions — two short, not
decidable. Waiter armed.

Finished #66. It is not RNG fragility and not a tolerance-loosening job; it is a
real accuracy defect, and the filed fix ("seed or loosen tol") would have buried
it.

**Which arm is wrong** — settled structurally, then measured.
`impulse_deltav_plummer_curvedstream` has NO quadrature at all (closed form); only
the general arm integrates, via `_deltav_integrate` -> `scipy.integrate.quad` at
DEFAULT tolerances. A closed form cannot grow a 0.001-wide spike; a quadrature
can. Swapping only that call for the same integral at epsabs=1e-16, epsrel=1e-14,
limit=500:

    x=1.543750   3.590e-09 -> 2.776e-17     1.3e8 x better
    x=1.500000   5.551e-17 -> 1.110e-16     unchanged
    x=0.0        7.772e-16 -> 5.551e-17

The analytic arm never moves. So scipy's default tolerances silently under-resolve
the acceleration integral at isolated impact offsets, and the analytic reference
was right all along.

**This is the third time scipy.integrate.quad's defaults have bitten this project**
— surfdens shipping 9.55e-6, AnyAxisym's amp-split epsabs truncation, now this.
The pattern is always the same: it returns quietly with a wrong answer rather than
failing.

Fix is one call with explicit tolerances, after which the test needs no seed
because the spikes are gone. #66 rewritten with the full evidence chain and a gate
that includes the runtime cost (the quad runs 3x per star) and a check of whether
the fixed-order GL backend twin (_GENERAL_QUAD_N=100) shares the blind spot.

Two method notes from the chain, both already cost me a wrong conclusion once:
  * a scan that finds nothing must be checked against its own RESOLUTION — mine
    had spacing 25x the feature width and I nearly declared the spike unreal;
  * `galpy.df.streamgapdf` is the CLASS, not the submodule; importlib is required
    to reach `_deltav_integrate`. Same shadowing trap as galpy.potential.Potential.

## 2026-08-13 — task #188: assert_jit_matches_eager adoption (gh#1310)

Cron `351c0c5a` verified alive at the start of the wake (created 2026-08-13,
expires ~2026-08-20). Both PR slots were free — six PRs had merged in the prior
stretch (gh#1300, #1303, #1305, #1306, #1307, #1308) and nothing of mine was
open, so this was the right thing to land rather than a filler task.

**Scoped by classification, which is the whole point of the entry.** The task
note warned against treating the raw grep count as the backlog. Of 67 raw
`jax.jit` sites in `tests/test_backend_*.py`: 17 direct `jit(f)(x)` calls
(adoptable), 17 bound to a name, 9 AD compiles via `grad`/`jacfwd` (NOT
adoptable — the helper asserts a value match against eager, which is not what
an AD compile is testing), 21 other shapes. Adopted at six verified sites;
`test_backend_trace.py:58` was inspected and deliberately rejected because it
asserts `under_trace` fired rather than comparing a value.

**Why the swap is worth anything.** The hand-rolled idiom checks that jitting
does not change the value. It cannot see a trace that folded its arguments away
into a constant — that compares equal too. `assert_jit_matches_eager`
additionally walks the jaxpr and asserts the output genuinely depends on the
traced inputs. This is the same blind spot that let the torch-tracing bug (a
`startswith` against `array_api_compat.torch`) silently disable torch tracing
everywhere until codecov flagged 11 dead lines in `_jit.py`.

Gate, all three arms from a finished run (`### DONE` present, per the
never-report-a-partial-run rule): numpy 655 passed 32:22, jax 655 passed 32:18,
torch 655 passed 33:17. Committed tree re-checked with `--collect-only`: 655
collected. PR head SHA verified equal to local HEAD, base `feat/backends-develop`,
diff exactly six test files.

### Two self-inflicted errors, both caught by guards rather than by a green suite

1. Patch match-strings were built from output I had piped through
   `sed 's/^/    /'`, so they carried four extra spaces and matched nothing. The
   script **reported `SKIP: 0 matches`** — which is the only reason it was
   caught immediately. Contrast the earlier failure this trip where a patch
   script asserted and wrote nothing at all, surfacing as a `NameError` two runs
   later. Assert-and-report beats assert-and-die.
2. "Insert the import after the last import line" picked a line *inside* a
   multi-line parenthesized `from ... import (`, splitting it — SyntaxError at
   collection in three files. Fixed by AST-locating the last top-level
   `Import`/`ImportFrom` `end_lineno` instead of regex-matching line prefixes.
   The same pass revealed that my `"backend_jit_helpers" not in s` guard had
   silently skipped `test_backend_actionAngle.py`, which already contained a
   FUNCTION-LOCAL import of a *different* helper from that module — a
   substring guard cannot distinguish "already imported at module level" from
   "the name appears somewhere in the file".

Both are the same lesson in different clothes: textual heuristics over Python
source keep producing confident wrong answers, and AST parsing settles them.
That is now the third time this trip (the two `awk`/`grep` import false
negatives were the first).

Note recorded for honesty: pre-commit's isort reordered the import lines after
the gate had been launched, so the three arms ran against a tree differing from
the committed one by import ordering alone. Semantically identical; the
committed tree was re-verified by collection, not by a second 100-minute run.

### Same wake — gh#1311, the second PR: nothing was testing the test helper

While gh#1310's CI ran, I checked a claim I had just made in its description:
that the jaxpr dependence check adds signal a value comparison cannot. Passing
at six sites only proves the check DETECTED dependence; it does not prove it
would CATCH a folded trace. A/B'd it directly — a constant function returns
`depends_on_inputs = False` and `assert_jit_matches_eager` raises. So the claim
holds.

That prompted the real find: **22 test modules import `backend_jit_helpers`, and
nothing tests it.** `jit_output_depends_on_inputs` is never asserted outside its
own module. If it started returning True unconditionally — a jax release
reshaping `jaxpr.invars`/`eqns` would do it — all 22 adopters would quietly
degrade to plain value comparisons and CI would stay green. Textbook hollow
green, and squarely the class the mission is supposed to eliminate.

gh#1311 adds `tests/test_backend_jit_helpers.py`: 10 tests that each assert the
helper REJECTS something (constant trace, wrong `ref=`, out-of-tolerance from
both sides at 1e-8 vs 1e-12, `err_msg` on both failure paths, elementwise array
comparison so an all-but-one match still fails). Two boundaries recorded on
purpose: the check is "consumes ANY declared argument" (a partially-used
signature passes), and it is structural not numerical (`x * 0.0` still consumes
`x`). Gate: 10 passed on each of numpy / jax / torch.

Branched off develop `50dbf316`, file-disjoint from gh#1310 (verified with
`comm` over both PRs' file lists, not by eyeballing). Two PRs now open, which is

### 2026-08-14 — gh#1312 MERGED (develop c54fcb8f); FOUND the slow-skip cost driver

Ledger **169 -> 168**, in scope **100** (15 xfail + 85 slow-skip). Both slots free.

**The 276-1079s is a scalar double loop IN THE TEST, not in the backend port.**
`test_interpolation_potential_force`:

    rs = linspace(0.01, 2.0, 21); zs = linspace(-0.2, 0.2, 41)   # 861 points
    for r in rs:
      for z in zs:
        rzpot.Rforce(r, z)                            # scalar
        evaluateRforces(MWPotential, r, z)            # TWICE (numerator + denominator)
        rzpot.zforce(r, z)                            # scalar
        evaluateRforces(MWPotential, r, z)            # AGAIN in the next assert

~5 scalar backend calls x 861 points = ~4-5k calls, and the exact force is
recomputed 2-3x per iteration for the SAME (R,z). MWPotential is a 3-component
list so each call fans out further. ~5 ms flat per-call overhead
([[lever-1]] / #79) x ~5000 = the measured runtime.

**This changes the shape of the 85-entry campaign.** The slow-skip reason string
says "unrunnable until the backend port is vectorized", and I had taken that at
face value for weeks. The port is fine here — `_grid_eval` is already vectorised
(measured last wake: 3 vectorised, 0 fallbacks). The scalar loop is test-side.

Fix is safe and mechanical: evaluate all 861 points in ONE array call per
quantity (4 calls replacing ~5000), keep the identical tolerance and identical
sample points. Two cautions for the implementation:

* assert ELEMENTWISE and report the worst offender —
  [[assertion-comparison-outside-reducer]]: `all(fabs(d)) < tol` passes when
  wrong. Use max|rel| < tol with the argmax in the message.
* verify `interpRZPotential.Rforce` accepts arrays before assuming it (the module
  has scalar-wrapping code at its top), and confirm the vectorised values are
  bit-identical to the scalar ones, not merely within tolerance.

If this holds it un-defers entries by making the TEST cheap, which is legitimate:
the deferral exists because the test costs 18 minutes, and the 18 minutes are
avoidable without weakening a single assertion.

### 2026-08-14 (cont) — ROOT CAUSE: the bit-for-bit guard makes jax fall back ALWAYS

cProfile of the jax constructor:

    2 calls   _grid_eval    233.494 s
    2 calls   _loop         230.531 s     <-- the fallback IS taken
    80838     evaluateRforces + evaluatezforces   (= 40401 x 2 SCALAR calls)

Then confirmed WHY, directly:

    spot-check cells differing bit-for-bit under jax: 2/9
    worst relative difference: 1.639e-15   (~7 ULP at float64)

`_grid_eval` accepts the vectorised result only if it reproduces the scalar path
**bit for bit**. That holds on numpy. Under jax, vectorised and scalar reductions
associate differently, so the check fails on ~2 in 9 cells over a 1.6e-15
difference — and the fallback to 40401 scalar calls per quantity is therefore
UNCONDITIONAL on jax. That is the whole 1643x.

**I have to own the wasted wakes here.** My "3 vectorised, 0 fell back" probe ran
on NUMPY (never wrapped in `use("jax")`) and on MWPotential2014, not the test's
MWPotential. I measured the wrong path, published "the grid build vectorises
cleanly", and then spent four wakes hunting elsewhere — through the numpy-island
theory and the test-batching theory — because I had wrongly eliminated the one
place the time actually was. [[value-checks-cannot-see-numpy-fallback]] applies
to SPEED probes too: assert which path you are on before believing a timing.

**The fix, and why it is not a tolerance-weakening.** The guard's purpose is to
catch `AnySphericalPotential`, which mis-broadcasts in **95 % of cells**. A
relative tolerance of, say, 1e-12 still catches that by ~13 orders of magnitude
while accepting ULP-level reassociation. So:

* numpy: keep bit-for-bit exactly as now (the strict guarantee is preserved, and
  the numpy path stays byte-identical);
* jax/torch: tight relative tolerance.

This is backend-aware, not laxer. Per [[backend-precision-must-match-numpy]] the
numpy path must not move, and it does not.

**Scope: this is much bigger than 6 entries.** Any table-backed potential that
builds a grid under a forced backend hits the same unconditional fallback. It is
a plausible common cause across a large fraction of the 85 slow-skip entries.

### 2026-08-15 — Jo's design call on gh#1316: move the guard from RUNTIME to TEST TIME

Jo: *"fixing anyspherical and deleting the guard can work, but we have to make
sure to then test always for ALL potentials so we don't silently introduce a bug
on a new potential. So an approach similar to the test grids of potentials in
test_potential might be necessary? Regardless, please also work in parallel on
other ledger burndown so this doesn't fully block other progress."*

**This is a better architecture than what I proposed** and I want the reasoning
recorded, not just the instruction. `_grid_eval`'s spot check pays a cost on
EVERY grid build, forever, on EVERY potential, to catch a bug in ONE. That is a
runtime workaround for something a test should assert once. Moving it to a
parametrized all-potentials test:

* removes the 1643x fallback entirely (no tolerance, no discriminator, no
  numpy-vs-backend asymmetry, and LESS code);
* makes new potentials covered automatically, which the runtime guard only did
  probabilistically (~19 spot cells, and I proved that sampling is
  grid-geometry dependent).

`test_potential.py` already has the pattern: named lists (`_NORMALIZE_POTS`,
`_PICKLE_POTS`, `_FORCEASDERIV_POTS`, `_2NDDERIV_POTS`) fed to
`@pytest.mark.parametrize("potname", ...)`. The new one is `_BROADCAST_POTS`
with the same shape.

**Test design, corrected for the error that invalidated my first survey.** My
zoo survey compared jax-vectorised against jax-SCALAR with exact inequality —
which measures reassociation, the very thing I had already proven is
indistinguishable from a mis-broadcast by magnitude. It "found" 18 of 46
offenders including MiyamotoNagai, Hernquist, NFW and Isochrone, which
obviously broadcast fine. It also silently DROPPED `AnySphericalPotential`,
because it needs a `dens=` argument and both no-arg constructions failed.

The correct assertion compares against a KNOWN-GOOD reference:

    ref  = numpy, cell-by-cell          # ground truth
    got  = backend, whole-mesh
    assert allclose(got, ref, rtol=1e-10)

Reassociation lands ~1e-15; a real mis-broadcast lands ~1e-1. Those separate

### 2026-08-15 — AnySphericalPotential: UPSTREAM numpy bug confirmed on main, two sites

**Verified on `origin/main`, not inferred from the docstring** (which misled me once
already on this same class). Two `quad` calls collapse an array `r`:

    line  86  _rawmass:   integrate.quad(a^2*rho, 0, numpy.atleast_1d(r).flatten()[0])
    line 129  _revaluate: integrate.quad(rho*a, numpy.atleast_1d(r).flatten()[0], inf)

The docstring's "byte-identical to the historical closure -- an array ``r``
collapses to ``r[0]``" is accurate: this is PRE-EXISTING galpy behaviour that the
backend migration faithfully preserved. It is not a regression.

**Asymmetry that matters for the fix and the test:**

* `_rforce = -self._rawmass(r) / r**2` -> the collapsed SCALAR mass is divided by
  an ARRAY r^2, which broadcasts fine and returns **silently wrong forces**.
  Measured: max rel err **0.943**, 76/77 cells wrong on the CI's logR 11x7 grid.
* `_revaluate` is guarded by `if r == 0:` -> a multi-element array **RAISES**
  (ambiguous truth value) rather than returning garbage.

So the forces are the dangerous half. A test that only checked the potential
would have found nothing.

**Backend path is correct** (measured 1.3e-15 vs numpy cell-by-cell truth on two
grids) because it routes to in-backend GL quadrature node-by-node. So
`_grid_eval`'s guard is protecting the NUMPY path from a numpy defect, and on jax
it is pure cost -- the 1643x is paid to guard a path that was already right.
That inverts the diagnosis I started with.

**Fix design (PR -> main, then cherry-pick per Jo so it drops on rebase):**
`quad` needs a scalar limit, so the numpy path must evaluate per element and
reshape, at BOTH sites:

    rr  = numpy.atleast_1d(r)
    out = numpy.array([quad(..., 0, float(x))[0] for x in rr.flat])
    return out.reshape(numpy.shape(r)) if numpy.ndim(r) else out[0]

This DELIBERATELY changes numpy output for array input -- which is precisely why
it belongs in main as an upstream decision rather than inside the backend work,
where [[backend-precision-must-match-numpy]] would otherwise forbid it.

Test: whole-array vs per-element on NUMPY across several grid geometries. Must
cover forces (the silent half), not just the potential. This is the first
instance of the `_BROADCAST_POTS` check Jo asked for.

## 2026-08-15 (later) — the if->where class, measured across the exclusion list

Both PRs still in CI (gh#1322 81 pending, gh#1323 110 pending), so this wake
went to the follow-up gh#1323 surfaced.

**Mapped every potential on `test_potential_array_input`'s exclusion list to a
cause**, by catching the exception and reporting the raising line:

* **if->where class (real, fixable)** — `SphericalShellPotential`
  (`if r <= self.a`), `HomogeneousSpherePotential` (`if r2 < self._R2`),
  `RazorThinExponentialDiskPotential` (`if numpy.fabs(z) < 1e-6`).
* **by design, not a defect** — `DoubleExponentialDiskPotential` and
  `AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDiskPotential` raise `TypeError` from an explicit
  scalar-only input decorator in `Potential.py`. Consistent with
  [[anyaxisym-array-optout-is-deliberate]]. These stay excluded.
* **structural** — `FerrersPotential` keys a `hashlib.md5` cache on the
  coordinates themselves; scalar-only by construction.

Fixed the first two (branch `fix/potential-array-input-where`, `a07ce379`,
pushed, PR **not** opened — two-PR limit). Left RazorThin alone: its `|z|<1e-6`
branch is entangled with the accuracy issue in gh#1276.

Shape of the fix worth keeping: **keep the scalar path literally unchanged
behind `numpy.ndim(x) > 0`** rather than letting `numpy.where` handle scalars
too. `numpy.where(True, 1.0, 2.0)` returns a 0-d *ndarray*, not a float, so a
pure-where rewrite silently changes the scalar return type across the whole
potential API. The guard keeps scalars bit-identical *and* type-identical, and
matches the existing `numpy.ndim(R) == 0` split in `EllipsoidalPotential`.

Second thing: `where()` evaluates the dead branch, which here divides by the
radius while the origin sits in the *other* branch. Guarded the divisor and
verified with `RuntimeWarning` promoted to an error that no new warning appears
anywhere on the domain, including exactly at the shell radius. (The `r=0` raise
that surfaced is `SphericalPotential._Rforce` doing `_rforce(r)*R/r` — checked
the scalar call raises identically, so pre-existing.)

Drive-by: **`numpy.infty` was removed in numpy 2.0** and the repo tests against
2.4.3, so `SphericalShellPotential._rdens` and
`RazorThinExponentialDiskPotential._z2deriv` both held a live `AttributeError`.
Invisible because both sit in `# pragma: no cover` branches — a reminder that
`no cover` hides *breakage*, not just untested lines.

## 2026-08-16 (early) — caught a sweep bug before the jit run landed

Both PRs are clean of real failures: gh#1323 149 SUCCESS / 0 fail (Jo's to merge
on main), gh#1324's flake re-run cleared it. The dispatched traced run
(31914531334) is still fully queued -- 44 jobs, runners saturated by the two PRs.
That is a real cost of dispatching it now, and it was a deliberate trade.

### The sweep could not have read the run it was dispatched for

Checked the workflow before the artifacts land rather than after: artifacts are
named

    backend-junit-${BACKEND}-${SHARD_ID}      # BACKEND is just jax|torch

**jit mode is not encoded in the artifact name at all** -- `SHARD_ID` comes from
`backend_status_report.py --id`, which is derived from TEST_FILES. So a traced
run's artifacts are byte-indistinguishable *by name* from an eager run's.

My `jit_run = any("jit" in b for b in seen)` detection would therefore have been
**False for the jit run**, and the sweep would have skipped all 40 `-jit`
entries while holding exactly the data needed to evaluate them -- reporting "not
evaluable" over a run that cost 44 jobs. Silent, and it would have looked like a
correct result.

Fixed: `--jit` is now an explicit argv flag, and the mode gates *both*
directions -- an eager run cannot speak to a `-jit` entry, and a traced run
cannot speak to a plain one. `probe` strips the `-jit` suffix so `jax-jit`
entries look up `jax`-named artifacts. Regression-checked both ways:

    eager artifacts, no flag : 40 not evaluable, 0 stale   (unchanged)
    eager artifacts, --jit   : 51 not evaluable, 18 "stale"  <- MEANINGLESS

That second run is a deliberate misuse to prove the wiring; its 18 hits are the
exact category error the flag prevents. **The flag must match the data**; nothing
in the artifacts will tell you if you get it wrong.

### Also corrected a claim I had already published

Wrote in gh#1324's body that RazorThin's quadrature branch "would silently
return a scalar rather than raise" for array input. Then measured it: it raises
`ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (100,) (11,)`
-- 100 GL nodes against 11 coordinates do not broadcast. It would only collapse
silently in the degenerate case where the coordinate count equals the node
count. Body corrected. The substantive point stands (it is a coordinate x node
quadrature refactor, not an if->where, so it is correctly out of gh#1324's
scope) -- but I published the reasoning before checking it, which is the thing
to not repeat.

## 2026-08-16 — Jo: never decrease coverage, even by one line

**gh#1323's -1 line was not in any file gh#1323 touches.** Both changed source
files are 100 % on head (AnySpherical 61 lines/0 missed, quadpack 74/0; patch
coverage 7/7 and 8/8). The compare API localises it exactly:

    galpy/potential/interpRZPotential.py   misses 0 -> 1   (lines 517 -> 517)

Unchanged line count, file untouched. The cause is causal, not coincidental:
`_grid_eval` accepts the vectorised whole-mesh result only if it reproduces the
scalar path bit for bit, else falls back to the cell-by-cell loop -- and **the
only thing that ever triggered that fallback was `AnySphericalPotential`

and the branch dies.

So the guard never had a test; it was covered incidentally by another component
staying buggy. Replaced with a synthetic mis-broadcaster
([[pvar-negative-example-fragility]]: use a forced synthetic, not a real
potential) that neither raises nor returns the wrong shape. The test asserts the
guard rejected the vectorised answer *and* separately that the vectorised answer
really differed, so it cannot pass vacuously. Four docstring claims this PR
falsifies were corrected to past tense.

Measured, it is the other way round:

    gh#1204  feat/backends-dev  -> f/b     misses 15 -> 20   3 files worse

feat/backends **improves** on main. The +5 is entirely develop's, i.e. mine:

### Process failure worth recording

Committed the fix onto **gh#1324's** branch, because this worktree was still on
`fix/potential-array-input-where` from creating the stack -- and
`git push origin fix/anyspherical-array-mass` answered **"Everything
up-to-date"**, because it pushed a branch that had not moved. Only the
remote-vs-local SHA comparison caught it
([[verify-pr-content-not-push-success]]). Unpushed, so the repair was a plain
`reset --hard` + `cherry-pick`, no force-push. **Check `git branch --show-current`
before committing in a multi-branch worktree**; "up-to-date" is not success.


### The develop +5, pinpointed

All five located with `/report/?sha=<FULL sha>&path=<file>`, filtering
`v != 0`:

    galpy/df/jeans.py                             181   called_surfdens = 2.0 * fixed_quad_semiinfinite(
    galpy/actionAngle/actionAngleStaeckel.py     2630   except (TypeError, RuntimeError):
                                                 2635   delta2 = xp.stack([_delta2(R[ii], z[ii]) ...])
    galpy/potential/AnyAxisymmetricRazorThin*    345   except Exception:  # tracer: in-backend GL
                                                 346       pass

**Every one is a fallback / `except` branch on the backend path** -- the same
shape as gh#1323's `_grid_eval` fallback. None of them is newly-added untested
code; the compare API confirms no *diff* line lost coverage in any of the three
files (`change_summary` shows the loss, but the per-line `lines` payload spans
only diff hunks and is empty of misses). They are pre-existing lines that
stopped being reachable.

That is the real pattern, and it is worth stating plainly: **backend migration
loses coverage by making defensive branches unreachable, not by adding
untested code.** Those branches exist for conditions the happy path never
creates, so they need a forcing test in the same PR that introduces them.

### Correction: codecov `line_coverage` is NOT bogus

I had recorded that field as unusable. Wrong -- my filter was inverted. Entries
are `[line, value]` with **`value == 0` meaning HIT**. Validated both ways:
`jeans.py` (1 miss) yields exactly `[181]`; `HomogeneousSpherePotential.py`
(0 misses) yields `[]`. Two real gotchas remain: the endpoint needs the **full**
40-char SHA, and `/compare/` only carries diff-hunk lines. Memory corrected.


## 2026-08-16 — CORRECTION: the AnyAxisym "tracer leaks" are test-side

I reported that the traced run found **2 genuine traceability defects** in
`AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDiskPotential` (`TracerArrayConversionError:
__array__() called on traced array`). **That was wrong.** Chasing the third
coverage line put me in the same code, and the traceback lands not in the
dispatch but inside the differentiable GL integrand:

    _bk_dispatch -> _Rforce_gl -> _bk_split_quad -> fixed_quad -> rforceint
    rforceint calls sdens(a)  <- the USER-SUPPLIED surfdens callable

A/B that settles it:

    surfdens = lambda R: (1.0 + R) ** -3.0     value ok, jax.grad ok (0.408866)
    surfdens = lambda R: numpy.exp(-R / 0.3)   value ok, jax.grad RAISES

And the failing CI tests pass exactly the second form:
`tests/test_potential.py:14297  surfdens=lambda R: numpy.exp(-R / 0.3)`.

So the potential **is** differentiable and traceable when handed a
backend-agnostic surfdens; `numpy.exp` on a tracer is the caller's problem, and
for a class whose entire contract is "you supply the callable" that is the only
sensible behaviour. These are **test-side**, not library defects. The traced
tally is therefore: 2 test-side fixtures, 2 known AnyAxisym singularity
accuracy, 3 torch timeouts -- **zero new library defects**, which is a better
result than I reported and a worse one for my confidence in that report.

Lesson: I classified by exception *type* (`TracerArrayConversionError` -> "code
converts a tracer") without reading far enough down the traceback to see whose
code did the converting. Read to the innermost frame before naming a culprit.

### Third coverage line: probably dead, deliberately not rushed

`AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDiskPotential.py:345/346` (`except Exception: pass`)
is not reached by the concrete, `jax.grad` or `jax.jit` paths -- `under_trace` /
`requires_grad` divert tracers before the `float()` probe, and array input is
rejected upstream by `check_potential_inputs_not_arrays`. It looks genuinely
unreachable, in which case the right move is to delete it rather than contrive a
test ([[no-hiding-uncovered-code]] cuts both ways). Deleting a defensive branch
is a behaviour change, so it wants a caller audit rather than a quick edit; not
done this wake.

### My flake-rate measurement was biased low

Earlier I sampled 25 recent `build.yml` runs, found 1 failure of the symplectic
job, and reported "~4-10 %". **That method undercounts by construction**: the
runs/jobs APIs report each job's *final* conclusion, and a re-run overwrites a
failure with success -- so every flake anyone already re-ran is invisible. The
direct observation is 3 hits across my own two PRs inside a day.

To measure it honestly you have to walk each run's **attempts**
(`/runs/<id>/attempts/<n>/jobs`), not current conclusions. Memory corrected;
I should not have quoted a sampled figure as the incidence.

Worth Jo's attention at some point (not a phone-ping, re-runs clear it): the
test asserts *exact* bit-identity, and `leapfrog_c` is only reproducible to
about 1 ULP. An exact-equality assertion on a 1-ULP-reproducible quantity will
keep costing re-runs indefinitely.

    after    2 accuracy failures + 0 tracer errors

But only one of them was a *test*: `..._all_methods_reject_a` now passes.

could reach its own assertion, and with the fixture fixed it gets there and
fails on accuracy:

    Fz/limit = [9.99990899e-01 ... 2.65046238e+03 2.67711334e+13]

That is task #218 — the backend GL path lacking both of numpy's singularity

**Why I got it wrong.** I had A/B'd the *mechanism* (numpy.exp on a tracer
raises; an arithmetic surfdens does not) and then predicted the *count* from

more than one thing wrong with it and the first failure masks the rest. This is
the same shape as [[reproduce-the-assertion-not-a-proxy]]: a verified mechanism
licenses no claim about magnitude or count. The rule I am adding is narrower and
easier to apply -- **when a fix removes an exception, the count of tests it
fixes is not knowable until they are re-run, because the exception may have been

### 2026-08-16 — #218 diagnosed: a LOG endpoint singularity, not a missing treatment

Merged gh#1327 (develop `24500321`) and opened gh#1328 for the surfdens
fixture, then spent the rest of the wake measuring #218 properly. Its title is
wrong and should be rewritten: the backend GL path does **not** lack the numpy
singularity treatments. `_R2deriv_gl` already calls `_bquad.finite_part_quad`
(#219 landed). What it lacks is accuracy, and now I know why.

**Traced error at z=0** (mpmath gold, `jax.jit`):

        R      R2deriv      z2deriv
      0.1     2.00e-04     1.08e-05
      0.2     6.65e-04     8.40e-06
      2.0     5.57e-07     2.03e-07

**Two measurements localise it.** The semi-infinite tail contributes nothing
(n=400 and n=800 agree to three digits), so all the error is in the finite
part. And the finite-part error is exactly `1/n^2`:

    n     100        200        400        800
    err   6.65e-4    1.67e-4    4.18e-5    1.05e-5

Gauss-Legendre is *exponential* on a smooth integrand. Algebraic `1/n^2` is the
signature of a singularity the rule can still see. Reaching 1e-8 by order alone
would need ~25 000 nodes.

**What the singularity is.** After subtracting the `2c/u^2` model, the residual
`g(u) = sym(u) - 2c/u^2` grows by a *constant* 18.47 per decade of u:

         u       g          delta
     1e-03    4.947e+01
     1e-04    6.794e+01    18.47
     1e-05    8.641e+01    18.47
     1e-06    1.049e+02    18.47
     1e-07    1.234e+02    18.47
     1e-09    6.400e+01    (cancellation floor -- as the docstring warns)

That is `g = -Lambda ln u + const` with `Lambda = 18.47/ln 10 = 8.02`. So the
`c/u^2` subtraction removes the pole and leaves a **logarithm**, which is
precisely what makes GL algebraic.

**I mis-derived Lambda before measuring it,** and the error is instructive. I
predicted `Sigma(R)/(2R^2) = 6.42` by taking the log from `ellipkm1(m1)` as
`m1 -> 0`. Measured 8.02. The gap is `ellipe(1-m1)`, which is *not* smooth here
either: its expansion carries an `m1 ln m1` term, and `m1 ~ d^2/4R^2` multiplied
by the `2R^2/d^2` pole in front of it promotes that to an O(1) log. Both special
functions contribute. Deriving the coefficient by hand is exactly the kind of
step where a missed term is invisible; the constant-per-decade table is not.

**Why this does not have an easy fix.** The obvious moves are both blocked by
the float64 cancellation floor the helper's docstring documents:

* An exponential substitution (`u = b e^-t`) or tanh-sinh makes the log smooth,
  but drives nodes to `u ~ 1e-17 b`. `g` is a difference of two `~c/u^2`
  quantities, so its *absolute* noise is `~eps c/u^2`; weighted by `du ~ u` that
  contribution grows like `1/u`. This is the same mechanism that made tanh-sinh
  diverge (measured previously: 1e6 at n=200, nan at n=800).
* Pure geometric panel grading stopping safely at `u ~ 1e-7 b` leaves the last
  panel unresolved, worth `~Lambda * 1e-7 * b * ln(...)`, i.e. ~4e-6 relative at
  R=0.2 -- better than today but still short of 1e-8.

So the fix has to *remove* the log analytically, the way `2c/u^2` is removed:
subtract `Lambda (-ln u)` and add back its exact integral `Lambda b(1 - ln b)`.
The open design question is where `Lambda` comes from. Deriving it per caller is
what I just got wrong by 25 %, and it would have to be right for an arbitrary
user-supplied `Sigma`. Estimating it numerically from `g` at two probe points in
the safe band (`1e-5 b` to `1e-3 b`, where the table above is clean to 4 digits)
needs no analytic input, stays traceable and differentiable, and is the
direction I would take.

Not attempted this wake -- gh#1328 is open and this is a separate, larger PR.
What changed is that #218 is now a well-posed numerical problem with a measured
target, instead of a title that misdescribes the code.


### 2026-08-16 (later) — #218: the log subtraction works, validated for both callers

Prototyped the fix in numpy against the mpmath gold. Subtracting the residual
log the same way `2c/u^2` is already subtracted -- take
`h(u) = -Lambda ln(u/b)`, integrate `g - h` by the existing GL rule, add back
the exact `int_0^b h = Lambda*b` -- gives, at the CURRENT default n=100:

               current          with log subtraction
    R2deriv    2.0e-4..6.7e-4   5.6e-12..6.8e-11
    z2deriv    2.0e-7..1.4e-5   8.1e-12..8.2e-11

Seven orders on R2deriv, and no extra quadrature nodes: the whole gain is from
making the integrand smooth, which is the point -- GL was already exponential,
it just had a singularity to chew on.

**Lambda is estimated numerically, not derived.** A least-squares slope of `g`
against `-ln u` over five points `u = b*10^-k`, `k = 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5`. This
matters because Lambda is not a nice closed form: it ranges over 44.78 (R=0.1)
to 0.0002 (R=2.0) for the same potential, both `ellipe` and `ellipkm1` feed it,
and it has to be right for an arbitrary user-supplied `Sigma`. It is plain
arithmetic on integrand evaluations, so it stays traceable and differentiable.

**The window is not arbitrary and not a knife-edge.** Measured against three
alternatives:

    window          R2deriv worst   z2deriv worst
    k=3..5   (5pt)      6.8e-11         8.2e-11
    k=2..4   (5pt)      1.3e-08         2.4e-09
    k=4..6   (5pt)      1.4e-08         3.8e-09
    k=2.5..5.5 (7pt)    1.0e-09         3.5e-10

Both failure directions are explained: above `k~3` the `O(u)` term in
`g = -Lambda ln u + A + O(u)` biases the slope; below `k~5` the `c/u^2`
cancellation noise does (the same floor the helper's docstring already
documents, measured earlier at `u = 1e-9`). `k=3..5` sits between them with
~100x margin under the 1e-8 test tolerance.

**A transcription error worth recording.** My first z2deriv prototype gave
errors of order *unity* on both arms. That was not the method failing -- I had
written the z2 integrand from memory instead of copying `_z2deriv_gl`. Copying
it (at z=0 the `ellipkm1` term carries a `z^2` factor and drops out, leaving
`-a Sigma(a) E(1-m1) / (d^2 (2R+d))`) made the "current" column reproduce the
independently measured traced errors --- 1.07e-5, 8.40e-6, 2.03e-7 --- to three
digits. That agreement is the real check that the prototype is faithful, and it
only exists because there was an independent measurement to hit.
[[reproduce-a-quadrature-exactly]] again: copy the integrand, do not re-derive
it.

Not implemented yet. The remaining work is `galpy/backend/quadrature.py`
(the estimate must not NaN-poison the sinh branch, which is evaluated
unconditionally under trace), torch parity, and tests. Next PR; gh#1328 is
still in flight.

### 2026-08-16 — gh#1328 went red on torch; my regression, my skipped gate

CI caught a real failure on `backend torch tests/test_potential.py --splits 5
--group 5`:

    TypeError: exp(): argument 'input' (position 1) must be Tensor, not float

The fixture I "fixed" last wake, `surfdens=lambda R: get_namespace(R).exp(...)`,
is wrong on torch. Two things combine:

* Under a **forced** backend, `get_namespace` returns that backend's namespace
  even when handed a plain Python float (no array input to follow, so it falls
  through to the context).
* **`torch.exp` rejects a Python float; `jax.numpy.exp` accepts one.** So this
  whole class of bug is invisible on jax and only torch reports it.

The float gets there because AnyAxisym's concrete-scalar branch deliberately
routes to scipy's adaptive quad -- it calls the user's `surfdens` with ordinary
floats, by design.

The fix is the codebase's own idiom, and this is the part that stings:
`AnyAxisymmetricRazorThinDiskPotential._default_surfdens`, in the file I was
editing against, carries the comment **"Dispatch on is_backend_array (NOT
get_namespace)"**. It was written down, in the same module, and I used the wrong
one anyway. Adopted it, hoisted to a single module-level `_anyaxisym_surfdens`
rather than repeating the guard in two lambdas.

**How it escaped me: I skipped my own pre-push gate.** For that commit I ran
numpy and traced jax and stopped there. [[forced-backend-gate-before-push]]
says run the touched suites under forced torch AND jax, and the whole reason
that rule exists is that the two disagree -- a jax-only gate is structurally
incapable of catching a torch-rejects-float bug. Cheap check, skipped, cost a
red CI cycle.

Re-gated properly this time: `-k anyaxisym` is 13 passed / 1 skipped on numpy,
forced torch, AND forced jax (torch was 2 FAILED before). Traced jax unchanged
at 2 failed / 9 passed -- the two remaining are the accuracy failures this PR
never claimed to fix. Pushed as `66ece1e4`; the exact CI shard is also running
locally as a belt-and-braces check.

**Local shard result (finished):** `--backend torch --splits 5 --group 5` gives
**266 passed, 12 skipped, 0 FAILED** in 5:14. That reconciles exactly with CI's
pre-fix `264 passed, 2 FAILED` -- same shard, same two tests, now passing. CI
has restarted from scratch on `66ece1e4` and is fully queued.


### 2026-08-16 — #218's OTHER half diagnosed: panel edges collapse in float64

gh#1328's torch red is fixed and confirmed in CI (group 5 SUCCESS). The only
remaining red is `codecov/project`, and it is a phantom by the session test:
head has **24 sessions vs base's 28**, reporting 6837 misses against 15 and
85.94% against 99.96% -- an impossible 14-point drop from a change that touches
only `tests/test_potential.py`. 46 uploads still outstanding; it self-heals.
`codecov/patch` is already green.

So I took the half of #218 I had explicitly scoped OUT of the quadrature PR:
`test_anyaxisymrazorthin_smallz_limit`. Measured, R=0.5, Fz/limit:

    z         1e-5      1e-6      1e-8   1e-12     1e-20      1e-30
    numpy   0.999991  0.999999   1.0    0.999936  0.999936   0.999936
    traced  0.999991  0.999999   1.0    1.0       2650.46    2.68e+13

**Mechanism.** `_bk_split_quad` grades dyadic panels toward the a=R peak with
`dmin = min(4|z|, R/2)` and builds the edges as `Rp - d` / `Rp + d` -- in
ABSOLUTE terms. At R=0.5 the float64 spacing is 1.11e-16, so for `4|z|` below
about half an ulp (|z| ~ 1e-17) `0.5 - 4e-20` rounds to exactly `0.5`: the
innermost panels collapse to zero width and the `1/((a-R)^2+z^2)` pole is then
sampled at `a == R`, giving ~1/z^2. That is precisely the 1e-12-fine /
1e-20-broken boundary the table shows.

numpy avoids it two ways: `_quad_apeak` splits with scipy's `points=[R]` (which
stays finite), and `_zforce_numpy`'s integrand takes `d2` as a SEPARATE argument
computed from the offset, so `(a - R)` is never formed by subtraction. numpy
still stops resolving below 1e-12 -- it saturates at 0.999936 -- but it saturates
INSIDE the 3e-4 tolerance instead of diverging.

Note `_R2deriv_gl` / `_z2deriv_gl` already dodge this: their integrands are
parameterised by the offset `d`, and they carry `_R2DERIV_ZFLOOR = 1e-9` below
which |z| is snapped to 0. `_zforce_gl` has neither -- its integrand takes `a`,
and there is no floor.

**Two candidate fixes**, not yet implemented:

1. *Small.* Give `_zforce_gl` the same floor treatment. The z->0+ limit is
   analytically exactly `-2 pi Sigma(R)`, so below the floor return that
   (times sign(z)) rather than a quadrature that cannot resolve the peak. Error
   at the floor is O(z/R), far inside 3e-4. Backend-only, so no numpy
   byte-identity risk.
2. *Structural.* Parameterise `zforceint` by the offset and build the panels in
   offset space, as `_R2deriv_gl` already does. Fixes the cause rather than
   masking it, but changes `_bk_split_quad`'s contract and so touches
   `_evaluate_gl` and `_Rforce_gl` too.

(1) is what the sibling methods already do and is the honest match to the
tolerance; (2) is the better engineering. Leaning (1) now with (2) noted, but
this is a decision worth making deliberately rather than at the end of a long
wake.


### 2026-08-16 — CORRECTION: the smallz story is two mechanisms, and I overclaimed one

Before implementing the zforce floor I measured the collapse threshold across R,
to choose between an absolute and a relative floor. The measurement refuted the
tidy account I wrote earlier this session.

    R        first bad z/R (traced, rel err > 3e-4)
    0.01     1e-14
    0.1      1e-15
    0.5      1e-14
    2.0      1e-14
    10.0     1e-6      <-- eight orders earlier

R <= 2 is scale-free at `z/R ~ 1e-14`. R = 10 is not, so it cannot be one
mechanism. Checked the second one against numpy:

    R      -2 pi Sigma(R)    |Fz| numpy      numpy rel err
    0.5     -1.8646e+00     -1.8646e+00        4.55e-07
    2.0     -2.0714e-02     -2.0715e-02        1.55e-05
    10.0    -7.8199e-13     -9.4298e-09        1.206e+04

**numpy fails identically at R=10 -- the same 1.206e+04.** So that arm is not a
backend defect: `Sigma(10) = 7.8e-13` sits about four orders below the
quadrature's own noise floor, and the rule returns 9.4e-9 where the answer is
7.8e-13. Both paths cancel away the same digits. Identical failure numbers on
two independent implementations is the evidence that it is the formulation, not
the migration.

So:

* **Mechanism A (R <~ 2, traced only, z/R <~ 1e-14):** a real backend gap --
  numpy is accurate to 4.5e-7 exactly where traced diverges. This is what
  `test_anyaxisymrazorthin_smallz_limit` (R=0.5) exercises.
* **Mechanism B (large R, BOTH paths):** cancellation against an exponentially
  small local `Sigma`. Pre-existing, not mine, and no floor fixes it -- it fails
  at `z/R = 1e-6`, far ABOVE any floor worth setting.

**What I got wrong.** Last wake I wrote that the cause was panel edges `Rp +/- d`
rounding away below half an ulp of R, and gave `|z| ~ 1e-17` for R=0.5. The
measured onset is `~1e-14`, three orders higher, and that account says nothing
about R=10. The direction is probably right -- the innermost panels of the
geometric ladder degenerate before the very last one does, which would land
above the naive half-ulp figure -- but I stated a specific threshold the data
does not support, and I was one step from designing a floor on top of it.

The lesson is the one I keep relearning in this file: a mechanism that explains
the case in front of you is not thereby the mechanism. Varying the OTHER
parameter (here R, not z) is what separated a real backend gap from a
pre-existing numerical limit that was never mine to fix.

**Fix deferred deliberately.** A relative floor `|z| < 1e-8 R` would cover
mechanism A with ~6 orders of margin over the measured 1e-14 onset, and is
scale-free where an absolute floor would misbehave at small R. But I do not yet
have the exact onset law, and B needs separating out before any of this is
written down as a fix. Not implementing at the end of a long wake on a mechanism
I have just had to correct once.

### 2026-08-16 — smallz onset law pinned: scale-free at ~tens of eps

gh#1330 is queued (151 checks, nothing reported), and it holds the runners, so
no competing jit dispatch this wake. Local CPU work instead: pinning the onset
law I said had to come before designing any floor.

Half-decade scan of the traced zforce against the -2 pi Sigma(R) limit:

        R      onset z/R    in eps
     0.05      3.16e-15      14
     0.20      3.16e-15      14
     0.50      1.00e-14      45
     2.00      1.00e-14      45

Those two values are ADJACENT grid points, so within resolution the onset is
**constant in z/R over a 40x range of R** -- scale-free, at a few tens of
machine epsilon. That is the signature of a relative-precision effect, which is
what the panel construction (`Rp +/- d`, plus `(a - R)` formed by subtraction)
would produce. It also kills the absolute-floor option: an absolute floor is
wrong at small R for exactly the reason this is relative.

Note this REPLACES my earlier "half an ulp of R, ~1e-17" claim, which was three
orders low and derived rather than measured. The corrected number is ~45 eps,
measured, and consistent across R.

**Design now fully specified by measurement:**

* floor at `|z| < 1e-8 * R` (relative, scale-free)
* below it the answer is the exact analytic limit `-2 pi Sigma(R) * sign(z)`
* clean separation: the floor sits **6 orders above** the 1e-14 onset, so the
  quadrature is only ever used where it is accurate, and the limit's own error
  there is `O(z/R) ~ 1e-8`, four orders inside the test's 3e-4 tolerance.

Implementation sketch that avoids a dead branch entirely: clamp `az` from below
to `max(|z|, 1e-8 R)` and evaluate `Fz = sign(z) * (-4 * az_clamped *
I(az_clamped))`. Because `I ~ 1/z`, the product is the constant limit, and above
the floor it is bit-identical to today -- no `xp.where` arm that can NaN-poison
a gradient. Needs care around the existing exact-`z == 0` guard.

Deliberately NOT implemented this wake. The design is settled but this is the
third time I have had to correct my own account of this failure, and it deserves
fresh context rather than the tail of a long session. Mechanism B (large R,
cancellation against an exponentially small Sigma, fails identically on numpy at
1.206e+04) stays out of scope regardless -- no floor addresses it.


### 2026-08-16 — zforce relative floor implemented: smallz_limit passes

Implementation is a **clamp, not a branch**: `az = max(|z|, 1e-8 R)`, evaluate
the quadrature there, and return `-4 sign(z) az I(az)`. Because the integral
goes as `1/|z|` the product is the constant limit, and above the floor it is
unchanged. Clamping removes a hazard rather than adding one -- no second
`xp.where` arm holding a divergent integral that could NaN-poison a gradient.

the bad side was never actually run.

still rejects arrays and so keeps the branch reachable. It checks the fallback's
VALUES against a per-element reference assembled in the test, not just that the

the file at all before believing the number". That is WRONG as stated and I acted
on it twice. File locality is not causal locality — the entire dead-fallback
class works at a distance, by making someone else's `except` unreachable. The
right question is not "does the PR touch that file" but "could the PR change
whether that branch is ENTERED".

Both PRs are early in their runs (gh#1331 11/151, gh#1324 restarted), codecov
red on gh#1331 is the mid-upload phantom. So: local work.

Corrected the MEMORY that carried yesterday's wrong rule
([[dont-reflexively-rebase-disjoint-prs]]). It said "check whether the PR could
reach the file at all before believing the number", which I acted on twice and
which is false — file locality is not causal locality. Replaced with the right
question: *could the PR change whether that branch is ENTERED* (does it stop
something raising, stop a guard firing, make a slow path fast). Also recorded
that `main` is a path-filtered PUSH run while a PR is a pull_request run, so
session counts across the two are not comparable.

Then ran my own [[def-to-def-splice-deletes-methods]] check on the programmatic
splice I made into `tests/test_orbit.py` — and it reported a function DELETED
(`test_orbitint_planar_dynamfric_pythonfallback`). Chased it:

    grep -oP '^def \K\w+' | wc -l   ->  278    <- silently short by one
    grep -cP '^def '                ->  279
    git diff --stat                 ->  48 insertions, 0 DELETIONS
    ast.parse FunctionDef names     ->  279    <- correct

**Nothing was deleted.** `grep -oP` dropped one line, and because my splice
ADDED one name, the counts matched at 278/278 — so the count check would have
missed it and the set check produced a false positive instead. The function
extracts fine from that line in isolation, so it is a whole-file grep artifact,
not a property of the line.

Two lessons, both recorded in memory:

* Do the structural set-diff with **`ast.parse`**, never grep.
* `git diff --stat`'s deletion count was authoritative and disagreed with the
  grep from the first moment. I should have trusted it before spending four
  probes on the discrepancy.

The splice itself is clean: 278 -> 279 functions, exactly one added, none lost.

### 2026-08-17 — gh#1324's symplectic red: I nearly convicted my own commit

gh#1324's orbit shard failed, I re-ran it, and it failed AGAIN with the identical
`max|diff|=5.55112e-16`. Two identical consecutive failures undercut the "known
intermittent flake" reading, so I investigated properly instead of re-running a
third time.

**Two dead ends, both instructive:**

1. *"My coverage-test commit is implicated."* I compared the PR's two heads:
   `ef37f197` (before) succeeded, `651e75ed` (after) failed. Looked damning.
   **Wrong** — I collapsed each SHA to "did any run fail", ignoring that every
   SHA has TWO runs (push + pull_request). Separated:

        ef37f197   pull_request success   push success
        651e75ed   pull_request SUCCESS   push failure

   A pass/fail split at ONE SHA is the definition of a flake
   ([[same-sha-duplicate-run-is-a-free-ab]]). `ef37f197` having both arms pass
   is a 2-sample coincidence, not evidence of a regression.

2. *Local reproduction.* Running my test then the symplectic test locally DID
   fail — but so did the symplectic test **alone**, with nothing before it. This
   worktree has no C extension built, so `leapfrog_c` never ran as C at all
   ([[worktree-missing-c-ext-fakes-passes]] — here it fakes a FAILURE rather
   than a pass). The reproduction was measuring nothing.

Also checked the causal question the right way, having just learned that
"doesn't touch the file" proves nothing: `test_symplectic_dxdv_base_bit_identity`
uses **MiyamotoNagaiPotential only** — none of the three potentials this PR
changes. So there is no path from the diff to that test's numerics.

Requested attempt 3 on the push run. The pull_request arm — the one the merge
gate actually reads — is already green at this SHA.

**Lesson, and it is the third time this week a "free A/B" has misled me:** an
A/B is only valid if the arms differ in ONE thing. Here the arms differed in
commit AND in event type, and the event type was the confound. Before believing
any pass/fail split, enumerate what ELSE differs between the two samples.

### 2026-08-17 — gh#1316: the test encoded the contract the PR exists to change

The `test_interpRZPotential_grid_falls_back_for_nonbroadcasting_potential`
failure on the jax shard is not a tolerance that is still too loose. It is a
**necessary consequence of the change**, and I spent two rounds tightening
`rtol` (1e-12 -> 1e-14) against a test that no value of `rtol` can satisfy.

The mechanism, once measured on both sides:

    AnySphericalPotential, whole-mesh vs cell-by-cell, on the test's own grid
      numpy   76 of 77 cells differ, worst 9.4e-01   <- genuinely non-broadcasting
      jax      0 of 77 cells differ                  <- broadcasts CORRECTLY

So the potential the test is named after is only non-broadcasting on numpy.
On develop the guard compared with `numpy.array_equal`, which made the guard's
criterion and the test's criterion **the same predicate**: any ULP difference
forced a fallback, and a fallback returns the cell-by-cell loop by construction,
so the test's `array_equal` could not fail. That coupling — not the potential —
is what made it stable.

This PR deliberately breaks that coupling. It gives the guard a 1e-14
reassociation allowance, whose entire purpose is that a *correct* vectorised
result differing by ~1.6e-15 is ACCEPTED instead of triggering a 1643x fallback
on a 201x201 MWPotential build. Once a sub-allowance difference is accepted, the
shipped grid is no longer bit-identical to the scalar path, and a test demanding
`array_equal` fails. numpy keeps `rtol=0`, so it never sees this; only the
backend shards do. Passing in isolation and failing in the shard was CI's
floating point differing from my box's, nothing more.

Fix, in two parts:

* the fallback BRANCH now has a synthetic-evaluator test, matching how its two
  sibling fallbacks (bad shape, raises) are already tested in this file. It
  injects a 1e-13 relative error — 10x above the allowance so it must be caught,
  ~60x above the 1.6e-15 noise the allowance exists to tolerate — in two shapes:
  a whole-array offset, and a single wrong cell at a location
  `_spot_check_cells` is known to visit, which pins the sample/guard coupling
  rather than the guard alone. It multiplies by a **namespace-matched** mask:
  returning numpy here would send the guard down its `rtol=0` branch and quietly
  stop testing the tolerance arm at all.
* the real-potential test now asserts the contract that actually holds — the
  shipped grid does not deviate from the scalar path by more than the guard
  permits: bit for bit on numpy, within 1e-14 on a backend.

A/B, which is the only reason I believe any of this:

    guard rtol      numpy      jax        torch
    1e-14 (PR)      pass       pass       pass
    1e-12 (broken)  pass       FAIL       FAIL

numpy passing on both arms is the point, not a gap: it takes the `rtol=0` path
regardless, which confirms the new test is aimed at the backend arm. The old
test could not have produced that table — it was insensitive to `rtol` in the
direction that mattered and oversensitive in the direction that did not.

**The lesson worth keeping:** when a PR changes a contract, the test that
encodes the OLD contract does not "fail" — it disagrees. I read a red shard
three times as evidence my new tolerance was wrong, when it was evidence the
assertion predates the tolerance. The tell was there from the first run and I
walked past it: the guard and the test were computing the *same comparison*, so
the test could never have been measuring the guard.

    numpy   z=1e-8  -1.984938989098     (+5e-12 from z=0)
    traced  z=0     -1.984856120473     <- off by 8.3e-5
    traced  z=1e-8  -1.984938968073     (+2.10e-8 from numpy's z=0)

The disk has Sigma(0.5)=0.3347, so 2*pi*Sigma = **2.10295**, and galpy's own
`zforce(0.5, 1e-8)` returns **-2.102952**. The true Phi therefore rises linearly
off the midplane as `Phi(0) + 2.103*z`, which is exactly what
`Phi(1e-4)-Phi(0) = 2.10e-4` confirms.

So the two paths are wrong in DIFFERENT places:

* **1e-10 <= z <= 1e-6: traced is RIGHT, numpy is WRONG.** The traced-vs-numpy
  relative difference is `1.06e-10, 1.06e-8, 1.06e-6` at `z = 1e-10, 1e-8,
  1e-6` — dead proportional to z, with coefficient `2.103/|Phi| `, i.e. exactly
  the cusp slope. numpy's Phi stays FLAT across the |z| cusp at these scales;
  traced resolves it.
* **z exactly 0: traced is WRONG**, by 3-4e-5 relative:

        R      rel err (traced vs numpy, z=0)
        0.20   2.97e-05
        0.50   4.17e-05
        1.00   3.18e-05
        2.00   6.66e-06
        5.00   1.31e-08

  and by z=1e-4 and beyond the two agree to 1e-13.

The test then divides that 8.3e-5 by dz=1e-8 and gets 8.3e3. **The ledger
entries are legitimate and they name a real traced defect** — the same z=0
endpoint-singularity family gh#1330 fixed for R2deriv/z2deriv, but one level
down, in `Phi` itself. Eager escapes it because `_bk_dispatch` routes concrete
backend scalars to scipy; only a genuine `jax.jit`/`grad` trace reaches the GL
path.

Per the standing rule that a less accurate GL path is a DEFECT and not a
tradeoff, this is burnable, and it is the natural sequel to gh#1330 — same
technique (subtract the analytically-known singular part before the GL rule).
Not started: two PRs are already open. Queued as the next code PR.

*Method note:* the numbers above are `float()` of the same expression on three
paths, not a proxy — and the discriminator that settled which side was wrong was
galpy's OWN `zforce` and the far-field `Phi(1e-4)`, i.e. two independent
references rather than my expectation of what a razor-thin disk should do.

### 2026-08-17 — numpy Phi misses the midplane cusp (main PR, 07549c0a)

`_evaluate` integrated with plain `points=[R]`, so for |z| << R quad stepped
over the O(|z|)-wide peak at a=R and Phi came back FLAT off the midplane:

    Phi(z) - Phi(0) at R=0.5      before        after       expected
      z = 1e-8                  +4.436e-12   +1.876e-08   +2.103e-08
      z = 1e-6                  -9.637e-11   +2.103e-06   +2.103e-06
      z = 1e-4                  +2.1029e-04  +2.1029e-04  +2.1030e-04

The missing term is exactly 2*pi*Sigma(R)*|z|, i.e. the vertical force: Phi and
galpy's own zforce (-2.102952 at z=1e-8) contradicted each other below
|z| ~ 1e-5.

**Two hypotheses tested and REFUTED before the right one:**

1. *scipy epsabs truncation.* Tightening to epsabs=1e-14 does not move Phi(dz)
   at all (-4.9e-12) and returns NaN at z=0. Not tolerance-limited: the nodes
   never land in the peak, so the error estimate stays small and quad returns
   confidently wrong.
2. *ellipk(m) rounding alone.* Switching to the stable complement + ellipkm1
   WITHOUT resolving the peak still gives +8.2e-13 at z=1e-8. The complement is
   necessary (it makes the peak evaluable at all -- panelling the old integrand
   returns nan/-inf because m rounds to exactly 1.0 at a=R) but not sufficient.

**The fix was already in the file.** `_quad_apeak` does exactly this via the
substitution a = R + |z|t, and its own comment describes the identical failure
for zforce ("came back +1.9e-8 instead of -1.86"). It was wired into zforce and
Rzderiv and simply never into Phi. I had already written a NEW `peak_points`
helper into `galpy/util/quadpack.py` and wired it up before finding this;
reverted it. Search the file you are editing before adding a mechanism to it.

**And the test was passing on two cancelling errors.**
`test_forceAsDeriv_potential` probes the midplane with a ONE-SIDED difference.
Phi has a |z| kink there, so the one-sided slope is +2*pi*Sigma(R), not
dPhi/dz; the assertion `Fz=0 => dPhi/dz=0` only held because Phi was flat. With
Phi fixed it reads -1.876. Changed to a CENTRED difference at z == 0 only: 0
for a kink, -Fz for a smooth potential, O(dz^2) instead of O(dz). Both changes
in one commit because neither is correct without the other.

NOT byte-identical on the numpy path, deliberately, and flagged to Jo before
doing it.

### 2026-08-17 — the ladder must stay: clustering collapses on zforce's pole

I had proposed replacing `_bk_split_quad`'s 24-panel geometric ladder wholesale
with `transformed_quad(interior_point=R)`, on the strength of Phi at z=0 going
3e-5 -> 1e-12. **Measured on zforce under jit, that is wrong:**

    R=0.5      ladder      transformed_quad
    z=1e-2     6.394e-15   7.673e-15
    z=1e-4     1.309e-14   7.595e-12
    z=1e-6     8.221e-13   1.054e-05
    z=1e-8     3.801e-10   1.703e-02

The two integrands are not the same problem. Phi's peak at a=R is
LOGARITHMIC; zforce's is a 1/((a-R)^2+z^2) POLE of width ~|z|. The `X = xi^k`
(k=3) map clusters nodes polynomially, so its closest node to the peak is
~(1/n)^3 * R ~ 5e-7 at n=100 -- fine for a log, hopeless for a pole at
z=1e-8. The geometric ladder marches panel edges to `dmin = 4|z|` EXACTLY,
which is the whole reason it exists.

So the change is targeted, not wholesale: `transformed_quad` in `_evaluate_gl`
only, where the singularity is logarithmic and the ladder's grading is switched
off at z=0 anyway; `_bk_split_quad` untouched for Rforce/zforce. Phi under
transformed_quad also matches the ladder at every z>0 sampled (1e-8, 1e-4,
1e-2, 0.1, 1.0), so nothing regresses.

*Method note:* my first attempt at this comparison was invalid and I nearly
believed it -- it reported 0.000e+00 rel err for every quantity at every z,
because eager jax hands CONCRETE scalars to scipy via `_bk_dispatch`, so the GL
path was never entered. The probe has to be inside `jax.jit` to reach it. A
column of exact zeros should have been the tell, not the reassurance.

**Near-miss worth recording.** I wrote

origin/feat/backends-develop`. The `worktree add` failed — the branch was
already checked out at `/var/tmp/ledgprune` — so the `cd` failed, and because

project "branch already used by another worktree" is a routine way for `cd` to
fail. Memory updated. The fix stays mechanical: `git -C <path>` always.

different ways and develop's answer is the weaker one:

    main    galpy/potential/AnySphericalPotential.py

develop's own source comment states the defect outright: *"_rawmass closes over
scipy.integrate.quad with a SCALAR upper limit (r[0] of an array), so the force
is scalar-only -- an array input silently collapses to its first element."*

The workaround only governs how `Potential.mass` DRIVES the quadrature
(`vectorized=False`, node-by-node). It does not protect a direct
`evaluateRforces(pot, Rmesh, zmesh)`, which is why the measurement came back
**76 of 77 cells differing, max rel 9.4e-01** on develop and **0 of 77** on
main. So develop currently returns silently wrong numbers for array input to
this potential, and has since before the backend migration.

**Plan (not started — 2 develop PRs already open):** adopt `quad_over_limits` at
develop's equivalents of main's two sites, then drop `_force_accepts_arrays =
False` if the array path is genuinely correct afterwards. Gate on the same
whole-mesh-vs-cell-by-cell measurement, on numpy AND on both backends, plus
`test_potential_array_input`. Cross-check against gh#1316's freshly-landed
`test_interpRZPotential_grid_matches_the_cell_by_cell_path`: once AnySpherical
broadcasts correctly on develop, that test stops exercising a numpy FALLBACK and
starts exercising the accepted-vectorised arm — still valid, but for a different
reason, and its docstring says so explicitly and will need updating.

*Method note:* the structural signals (quadpack.py present, matching symbol
counts) said "already ported"; the behavioural measurement said the opposite.
The source comment was the tiebreaker and it had been sitting there all along —
[[read-code-docs-before-classifying]].
